Taking whiskey straight makes many a man crooked. If you should happen to want your ears pierced just pinch the baby. If a young woman's disposition is gunpowder, the Sparks should be kept away from her. What everyone wants, what everyone gives, what everyone asks, and what very few take 4—Advice. Tired father—" I might just as well talk to the Wind as talk to you." Indifferent son—" Well, you always were fond of airing your views." She—" I visit this romantic spot annually." He —"Are your stays long?" She—" None of your business, sir. I thought you were a gentleman." A big Yankee from Maine, on his paying his bill at a London restaurant, was told that the sum put down didn't include the waiter. " Wal," he roared, "I didn't eat any waiter, did I ?" A countryman visiting" the Surrogate's office, on Observing the huge volumes of wills on the shelves, asked if they were Bibles. "No sir, said the clerk, "they are testaments." Wife—" Keep quiet, Charlie. The new doctor says I must, not talk to you." Husband, feebly— " Mary I Mary 1" Wife—" What is it, Charlie ?" Husband—" Engage that doctor for our family physician." "It's too had that the Bloffets are moving out of the neighbourhood, isn't it?" "Too bad? Why, Bloffet was a terrible nuisance with his cornet." "Yes. but now that he is leaving the rents will go up." Doctor—" Take these powders as directed, and your cold will be gone in two or three days." Patient—" You seem quite hoarse, Doctor." Doctor —"Yes; I've had a bad cold for a month." Lady of the House—" Why, you are the same man to whom I gave a loaf of my home-made bread the other day ?" Tramp—" Yes, mum; and I merely came around to show you that I was still alive." Old Man: "Can't do it, But I'll tell you what you csn have. I'll try and get you a nice long icicle.' Some time ago the following conversation was heard between two lovers—Jock and Kirsty. Kirsty, thinking Jock rather long in popping the question, expressed herself thus :—" Wed, Jock, are you for me or no? 'cause I wis gaun to the market the morn, an' I wis thinkin' I maybe wid hae some chance there." Young Miss Wilgus "Where are you going, papa I " Rev. Mr. Wilgus—" To the temperance meeting. We intend to inaugurate a movement to save the young men of the country." Young Miss Wilgus—" Try and save a real nice one for me, will you, papa, dear ? " "And do you doubt my love?" he asked passion- ately. "No, George," she answered, with admir- able tact; "but when you say that the day you call me yours will usher in an era of lifelong devotion and tender solicitude, you—pardon me, dear—you put it on a trifle too thick. You seem to forget, George, that I am a widow." An Irishman recently stopped at a hotel where pretty high bills were charged. In the morning the landlord made out the amount of damages and presented it to Pat. After he had glanced it over, the latter looked the landlord in the face and ex- claimed— "You put me in mind of a snipe." "Why?" asked the landlord. "Because ye're pretty nigh all bill." The proper visiting hours are from 3 to 6 P.M. Formal visits first hour, friendly visits second hour, very friendly visits third hour. When making a first call, send your card to the lady, unless she is in the room where you are announced, or has expected you; in the former case, leave the card on the hall table as you go out, so that she may see your address, and your day (if any) for receiving visitors. On the occasion of subsequent visits, leaving a card will not be necessary. "I want to exchange this yard of ribbon; it is soiled in one place," said Mts. Slioppiugly to one of the young women behind the counter at Silk and Sattin's. "Fm not the lady you bought it off," was the reply; "I've just returned from my holiday in the country, and some other lady must have sold it to you. Here, Maggie—did you sell this woman a yard of orange ribbon? No? Well, see which of the ladies in our shop did sell it, then." The celebrated Asiatic explorer Dr. Wolff was not remarkable for the cleanliness of his personal habits. On one occasion, when he was going on a visit, his wife gave him lia,f-a-dczen shirts, with instructions to put on a clean one every day. On his return, the shirts were not to be found, and, when questioned about the matter, he said, "You told me to put on a clean shirt every day, and I did so; I have them all on now."

Years ago we were on friendly terms with an old sea captain who used to be in the Mediteranean trade. He took delight in spinning yarns of the vasty deep. One of his recitals was as follows: " I landed a cargo on the wharf of a Turkish town not far from Constantinople. It was toward evening and I suggested to the Mohammedan gentleman in charge of the quay that a guard be placed over the goods. "Have no fear," he declared, stroking his beard, "there is not a Christian within forty miles 1" Mark Boyd says :—I was accompanying my father over the field of Waterloo, when our guide, an old British soldier who had been in the battle, stopped us rather abruptly at what I should say was the north-east corner of Hougoumont. "Here, sirs, his the werry spot vere 'ls Majesty King George IV. said the werry cleverest thing that vas hever said afore hor since by hany king, hi doesn't care a morsel vere ye picks 'im. Veil, sirs, ven King George vas on 'is journey to 'Anover, he pay Waterloo a wisit, hand vas haccompauied by 'ls Royal Highness the Duke o' Clarence hand 'ls Grace the Duke o' Wellington. Just hon this eere snot the Duke o' Wellington's oss slipped hup hon the dry tuff hand a-throwed the Duke. 'ls Majesty vas for a moment hafeared, so vas the Duke o' Clarence; but the Duke o' Wellington vas hon 'is feet bin ha momenttt all sight. Van the King sees that, he says to 'is brother, 'Veil, Clarence, ve can say vat t'others can't, that ye seed Wellington a-floored hat Waterloo." "The jury wishes to be informed on a point of law, your honour," said the court officer. "Let them be shown into the court," replied the judge. "We wish to know," explained the foreman, "if a jug of whisky in the jury room, if paid for by our- selves, would L e contrary to law, your honour ? " "Certainly," thundered the judge, "I thought the Information you wanted was in regard to the case." "We haven't got to the case yet," said the foreman, and then they filed out. A Nebraska editor's barn was burned the other day, and he crowded out the latest news from Stanley in order to insert a two column account of "the lurid work of the lire fiend," as he expressed It. And he ended thus—" As the last dying flame flickered heavenward, we realised that the loss was 56 dollars—no insurance. Thus to great and small alike come the deeper tragedies of life that furrow the cheek and scar the heart. We hope the coyotes who are in arrears will now have the decency to pay up. Verbum sap." div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

It is no secret that Mr. Balfour regards the car- rying of the Irish Land Bill as his crowning work at the Irish Office. He has no great belief in beat government in Ireland, and will probably leave the task to be undertaken by his successor. At the first opportunity he will leave the Chiaf Secretaryship.

One of the many curiosities now exhibited in the British Museum is a Chinese banknote, issued dur- ing the reign of the Emperor Hung Wu, A.D.1368-99. This is the earliest specimen of a banknote known to exist in any country. It is 300 years earlier than the establishment of the first European bank which issued notes.

It is understood that a fresh hitch has arisen in the drafting of the Education Bill. Mr. Chamber- lain, outside the Cabinet, is urging the necessity of certain previsions which Mr. Goscheu from within is stubbornly resisting. In the meanwhile, every day that passes adds to the difficulty with which a measure of this magnitude can be passed in the current session.

There is, I understand, some question as to whether the latest born scion of Royalty can, or cannot be ranked as a Princess. The Queen is said to be against the recognition, while the authorities of the Home Office are in its favour. Anyhow, in the announcement of the birth to foreign Couits, the newly-born was mentioned as daughter of the Duke and Duchess of Fife!

Ladies may have wondered what will be the name of the Duchess of Fife's infant daughter. The name chosen by the parents is Alexandra, and as this selection has been approved by the Queen,there is little doubt that it will be accepted. Alexandra is the name not only of the Princess of Wales, but of her daughter. It is also the feminine form of the christian name of the Duke of Fife. The christen- ing will, it is anticipated, be performed in the Sovereign's presence in the Chapel Royal, Windsor, shortly after her Majesty's return from the High- lands.

lam sorry to hear from India that Mrs. Grim- wood, the wife ot the murdered Resident of Mani- pur, whose graphic narrative of her escape after the massacre will be remembered, is only just re- covering from a serious attack of brain fever, due to the shock which she received on hearing ot her husband's murder, following on the privations and dangers which she incurred during the siege of the Residency and the subsequent flight through a hostile country into Assam.

On the occasion of a banquet at Stralsund, Herr von BOtticher, the Prussian Minister, made in his speech the following remark : " It is the Emperor's intention to promote the public welfare with all his power ; and believe me, there is less reason for anxiety than one often hears in the country. The political horizon is clear Do not let yourselves be troubled by French or Russian exaggerations. In my opinion there is no rational reason for any one beginning war with us, and we shall never be the aggressors."

The Railway Rates Committee. in stern pursu- ance of duty, sat on Wednesday, albeit the House of Commons was making holiday. This is the Committee in which influenza made its first appear- ance in the House of Commons, the epidemic being introduced, it was understood, by a witness from Sheffield. Of the ten members of the Committee tour were stricken, the Chairman (the Duke of Richmond), Lord Belper, Lord Houghton, and Mr. Dickson. All have now recovered, and were present at Wednesday's meeting.

Whenever the Factories and Workshops Bill comes mrfor consideration on the Report stage an attempt will be made to secure an advance of the age of half-timers. The action of the Government in this matter is somewhat compromising. At the Berlin Conference, through the mouth of their dele- gates, they approved the principle of advancing the age, whilst in Grand Committee the Home Secretary succeeded by narrow majoiities in defeating amend- ments designed to carry out the recommendations ot the Conference on this head.

Before the Czar moves a cloud of police officers open and secret police,genA attues and spies,military and civil tchinovniks of the private guard. On Tues- day last week it became known that the Czar was coming to Moscow; on Wedne:,.day night the police officials were at work inquiring into all suspicious characters and visiting lodging-houses and prying everywhere. They entered private lioues and de- manded to be shown the garrets. In particular the houses looking on the great square where the review is to be held had to undergo their close scrutiny.

The four-shilling piece is to go out of circulation. One matter on which all people can be thought to agree is that the Jubilee coinage is a failure, and most people are unanimous in regarding the four shilling piece a, the greatest failure of the series. I suppose it is the ugliest coin we have produced for a. long time. It is ungainly, clumsy, and unin-

telligible. For long it as confused with the five shilling piece, owing to the absence of any stamp of value on its reverse, and now that people have become better acquainted with the two coins their prejudice against it still exists.

Lord Romilly, the peer,who has just died,suffocated in the tire at his own re,idence caused by the upset- ting of a limp, was a blameless baron,who,since the death of his dist iiguishect father 17 years ago, has not sought to place himself very prominently before the pubiic eye. He combin,-d in his own person the military and the legal professions. He was a soldier as a lad, and he subsequently joined the bar, and be- came Clerk of Enrolments in Chancery. Politically he was a Whig, but he never made much of politics. He was 56 years of age at the Owe of his death, having celebrated the 55A1 anniversary of his birth- day about six weeks ago. his successor is :27 years of age, and, like his father, is a soldier.

The Queen completed her 72n 1 year on Sunday. This age. has been exceeded by only two of our Eng- lish Sovereigns—George 11., who lived for 77 years, and George 111., who attained the age of 82. On the 20th of June next her Majesty will have reigned fifty-four years, or longer than any English Sove- reign except two—Henry lii., who reigned for fifty- six years, arid George W., who reigned for nearly sixty years. With the exception of the King of Denmark, who is one year older than the Queen, her Majesty is the oldest reigning Sovereign. The bells of St. George's Chapel and St. John's Church, Windsor, were rung in celebration of her Majesty's birthday. The firing of salutes was deferred till Monday.

As I announced a few days ago, on the resump- tion of the sittings in the Divorce Court, the formal business of making the decree absolute in the O'Shea case was disposed of. In the coming term there are several sensational cases down for hearing. Among them is that in which the Coun- tess Russell petitions fora decree of judicial separa- tion. The petitioner was married not more than about eighteen months ago. A long array of legal talent has been engaged on both sides, and the case is expected to be a very peculiar one. Two or three cases in which well-known members of the theatri- cal profession are concerned are down for hearing. In one case a leading comic opera artiste will make her appearance in the court for the third time.

An interesting anecdote is related about the stick with which Prince George of Greece knocked down the Japanese who recently attacked the Cezarewitch. The Prince cut the stick himself in the woods of the Greek island of Pares, and had it finished off at a manufactory. It was of such gigan- tic dimensions that. even in the hand of the hercu- lean Prince it looked ridiculous, and was the subject of conversation in the Greek capital. But, in spite of this, the Prince was very fond of his stick. When on his departure with the Cesarewitch he appeared with it in his hand, his tattier urgeptly requested him to leave the cudgel behind ; but the Prince would not hear of it, and the Cesarewitch asked the King to let him have his way. TAe Xing him- self is said to have told this story.

The experiment of stocking Lake Vyrnwy, that vast artificial reservoir which has been formed for the purpose of supplying Liverpool and its neigh- bourhood with water, appears to have been strik- ingly successful. It is about two years since the Liverpool Corporation put in some four hundred thousand Loch Leven fry, since supplemented by fry of the ordinary brown trout of the River Vyrnwy and its tributaries; and already corres- pondents of "The Field," report good sport in these waters, in spite of the unfavourable weather that has prevailed of late. Th. lake is four and. three- quarter miles long, half a mile broad, and pictures- quely surrounded by the Berwyn Alountains. It is very deep in the centre; but the whole margin,
ACROSS TEE ATLANTIC (No. 2)
IN THE INTERMEDIATE.

div.head: SCOTCII, nusH AND ENGLISH EMIGRANTS.
div.p: SCOTCII, nusH AND ENGLISH EMIGRANTS.
BY "TOWNSMAN."

Though only numbering 91, the intermediate pas- sengers for Boston U.S.A., by the Cunard Steamer "Cephalonia," were a more motley group in com- parison than the steerage people. The latter were overwhelmingly Irish, but the intermediates num- bered amongst them Scotch. Irish,English, Russian, and American representatives who, on the whole, made up a very happy family. All the 2nd cabin passengers, except three, were emigrants, and were bound for various parts of the States. The majority were undoubtedly English. who had been engaged in the Yorkshire Cotton Mills, and were seeking to mend their fortunes in the cotton districts of New England. About half of the intermediates were women and children, and six or eight family parties who were going out to join husbands and fathers already prospering in the United States. Quite a number of the children were little toddles who could just stand—toddles who caused the ship's officers to remark about their starting early on their travels, and who occasionally raised such choruses as drew from the merry stewards refer- ences to the "joy bells of matrimony." Most of the children who could take care of themselves got their sea legs early,and enjoyed the voyage more than any one, but one or two of the little folk only left their berths the day before the passengers landed. As there were only five saloon passengers, the captain very thoughtfully granted to the intermediates the use of half of the saloon deck and the saloon smoke room, and the privilege was very gratefully enjoyed by the passengers. Of the half dozen intermediates who joined the ship at Queenstown the most con- spicuous were

div.head: GUSHING YOUNG COUPLE
div.p: A GUSHING YOUNG COUPLE

who did nailing but make love to each other all through the voyage. The husband was a tall, thin, loud-voiced young fellow, evidently well-to-do, and his wife a well built brunette of medium height. Rumour had it that the couple came of aristocratic Irish families, and had not long been married. Their conduct seemed to confirm the latter sus- picion, for they were to be found in every quiet corner' spooning" away to their hearts' content. If they walked about, it was always arm-in-arm, and if they sat their arms were invariably entwined. They were scarcely ever separated, but if they did happen to Dart there was such a game of seeking as provoked the merriment of the company. The husband did break loose at times, and then he dis- played a propensity for asking far-fetched conun- drums, at the solution of which he laughed know- ingly. It ultimately became known that the couple had only been married a week, ana were I practically on their honeymoon.

div.head: GOING TO BE MARRIED.
div.p: GOING TO BE MARRIED.

Another interesting passenger was a dark, pale- faced, pensive-looking young lady, who was not sick at all. She seemed to enjoy the whole voyage, and was knocking about when the rest of the Intermediates were groaning in their berths. She proved to be a very pleasant-spoken, intelligent birl, and she took quite a fancy to my companion, because he reminded her of some one she knew. It was,however,only a fancy, because she was already engaged to be married. I seemed that years ago she was engaged to a young man who emigrated to the States, where he was charmed by another in- amorata, and ultimately married her. The union however only lasted six months, for the newly- made wife sickened and died, and once again the young man cast about for a wife. Remorse at his treatment of his former love appeared to have seized him, and at length he mustered courage to write to her in England. The result was that the discarded lover was again re-instated in his affec- tions, and she travelled the :3,000 miles alone to be married on the da3 of arrival.

div.head: FATHER AND SON.
div.p: FATHER AND SON.

Another remarkable character was an old factory overlooker " Ira Bradford." What his business in the States was I could not exactly make out, but I concluded he was "prospecting." He was going firstly to Providence, XI., to investigate their. mode of working, and then, in all probability, home across the continent, and round by Australia. lie was a tall, wiry, sort of man with iron grey hair and beard, and keen but sympathetic eyes. He spoke entirely in the Yorkshire dialect, and reminded me strongly both in personal appearance and tone of voice of a friend long since deceased, but who seemed risen again in the person of this factory foreman. tie was a very interesting and intelligent individual, who, although brought up from boyhood to factory life, had a strong liking for mechanics and engineering. But more interest was perhaps taken in this man's son than in the man himself. The boy was about 16 years of age, and was, as one man described him, " A perfect terror." He was very well dressed in what his father said was "a bit o' good cloth" but be had not been on board three days before he split his trousers across both knees. He was everywhere about the ship and in every- thing. He would climb everywhere and jump witk anyone. He was always eating, and if he could not get enough to pocket at meal times he would slide down into the steerage and beg food from the poor boys there. He was jumping one morning when he slit his trousers right up the middle, and had to wear his father's great coat to make himself presentable. His clothes were stowed away in the hold, so that he could not change his trousers and at length he tore his father's coat and was then sent to his berth for the rest of his voyage. The father said he had been obliged to bring the lad along as he dare not leave him at home because be was unmanageable. He had done everything he could to tame him, but without effect. Days to- gether he had kept him to his room, but the only result this produced was the remark "Wait till I get a bit bigger, and I'll give the old fellow --." The last glimpse I got of this lively youth was round a corner, where he was cheerfully changing his pants.
A MOTHERLESS FAMILY.

A factory family was amongst the intermediates, and they were on their way to Providence. The whole family were exceedingly respectable and well nehaved. They, however, lacked one thing,and that was a mother's love. The members were eight in number—the father, three sons, and four daughters—the children's ages ranging; from 22 to about 10. All except the youngest were fac- tory workers of the better class—sharp and intelligent— and the youngest girl, the baby, promised to be even sharper than all the rest. The lads were fortunately able to take care of themselves, and the girls were cared for by an elder sister about 18, who evidently occupied the mother's place. The father was a vigorous,thought- ful artizan, who was going to settle down with people from his own district. Be was of a class such as we can ill spare from England, and such as will help to make the boycott on English manufactures more strongly felt year by year. Only this week a dinner was held in New York at which it was boasted that every article used was of American manufacture.

div.head: SICK WIFE.
div.p: A SICK WIFE.

An interesting personage amongst our number was a sick Anglo-American wife. She was accompanied by her husband, a dapper little fellow of the Mark Tapley order— happiest under the most depressing circum- stances. He was always cheerful, cracking jokes with everyone—even his wife, whom he was fond of asking " What would she do without him ? " He, however, seemed to think a great deal of her, and was exceedingly attentive to her—as a good husband ought to be. The wife had been to England for six months with a lady companion to see if her native air would be beneficial to her, but her sojoern in our largest county had effected no improvement, and she was returning to her family. Both she and her companion seemed glad to get back to America, as their experience of an English winter had not been of the pleasantest description. During the last few days of the voyage the invalid appeared to improve wonderfully, and she was scarcely like the game person when she went ashore and made for her home in South Boston.

div.head: JEALOUS MOTHERS.
div.p: JEALOUS MOTHERS.

The stewards had a rare time with the mothers and their families, through the jealousy of the mothers. A fine-looking lady from London, with a regular cockney son—of about eight years, seemed able to get whatever she wanted from the stewards, and of course the others were not slow in taking knowledge of the fact and letting

the attendants know it. Their remarks were not always complimentary, but the stewards took it all in good part, and by a quick sally oftentimes managed to put every- body in a good humour. The difficulty arose chiefly over hot water to wash the juveniles, and but for the good temper and smartness of the stewards, the latter would have been constantly immersed metaphorically in the liquid. The stewards however, knew how to get at the mother's better nature, and by picking up a child, nursing it awhile, and gushing over it soon won over one mother to their side.
A THIRSTY JO/NBR.

A man of unenviable notority was a thirsty joiner. He was a maker of woodwork connected with looms,and the factory overlooker thought he was leaving England on account of his drinking propensities. If this were so, he showed no sign of improvement during the voyage. He was always in an obtuse state, with inflamed eyes. He had red hair, a red face, and rotund body, but his obesity was not natural. He had a voracious appetite, and was always waiting for the dinner bell to ring, when he was the first to respond. He seemed determined like a fellow voyager, to have his £7 worth out of the Com- pany. When not eating he was drinking, and if the bar was not open he was miserable. Nothing pleased him better than to hear the chief steward enter and announce that " the bar was open, gentlemen," when be would trip down to the bar and imbibe ale, beer, and porter until it closed. At all meals also he had a bottle, and during the brief intervals that abstinence was en- forced he smoked continually. For a young man he was thoroughly besotted, and sensual in all his desires. Look- ing at his watch on Saturday at four o'clock, someone wondered what the people were doing in England. " I know what I should have been doing "said he. " Well ! " queried the other. "I should have been paid off and been drunk. I've been drunk many a time at four o'clock on Saturdays! " and he gloried in the thought.

div.head: HOW SOME SPENT THEIR TIME.
div.p: HOW SOME SPENT THEIR TIME.

Three or four North of Ireland men, who scarcely had a word to say during the voyage, spent most of their waking hours in smoking, and the younger of them—a youth of 17—smoked more than the others. The Yankee, an Irishman, a Scotchman, and an Englishman made up a card party, and played away hour after hour, and day after day, their games only being suspended at meal times. Others eta studious turn read all they could lay their hands on, and all books, periodicals, and news- papers became common property. The ladies enjoyed themselves with games of 'tiddledywinks." and varied these with dancing, skipning, and swinging on deck. The ycung men of athletic tastes devoted themselves to jumping, " cockighting," and feats of skill; and when tired with these they assembled in groups and argued with each ether for hours. About once a day all amuse- ment would be suspended as a ship hove in sight, and until it was definitely ascertained what she was, they were not renewed. The evenings, however, were very dull, and, although we had plenty of talent, it was not until almost the last night on board that an entertain- rnent was organised. This passed off so agreeably that all regretted others had not been arranged earlier in the I trip.

div.head: TICE QUARTERS
div.p: TICE QUARTERS

The berths were very comfortable, and tho provisions plentiful and varied. The menu was changed every meal, and there was always enough and to spare. Certainly, if intending emigrants can afford it, the intermediate is preferable to the steerage in many ways, but this is a matter that must be regulated by circumstances. Any- one booking by the Cunard Line may be sure of every attention, and people I have seen hero agree that it is one of the best lines to travel by.
THE SALMON BEATS THE FISHERMAN.

A gentleman, a few weeks since, fishing on a northern Scotch river, hooked a fine salmon. He found the fish (evidently a clean one) very strong, as he played with great vigour ; but he had full confidence in himself as well as in his tackle. Sud- denly, however, the fish made a rush which there was no resisting, and before he could be controlled had reached a huge boulder in the river, around which he managed to get the line, and was fast. The gentleman turned to his gillie, asking if he would venture into the water and clear the line. The gillie, who was rather short of stature and knew the depth of the pool, declined to venture in. Not to be done,however, the gentleman handing his rod to the gillie, went into the water himself, but before he reached the big stone was up to his shoulders in the water. He succeeded, however, in clearing the line, and the fish, too, which was still on the hook. The lordly salmon,however,must have been of a rogish turn, says a correspondent of the Fishing Gazette, who sends the story, for no sooner was he free than he proceeded to make several evolutions round and round the angler, and soon had him firmly ried round both his legs. On trying to reach the shore he found he could not move,so firmly had the line been wound round him. The gillie saw the dilemma and the danger, and entering the water pushed out the rod, so that his I master could grasp it. This he did, and by dint of great exertion and strugg!ing he reached the shore in safety, only to find, however, that the salmon had broken off, taking the fly and cast with him. There is no doubt that but for the prompt assistance rendered the gentleman would have been drowned.

div.head: ARLEY HALL.
div.p: ARLEY HALL.
Mr. Alfred Rimmer writes as follows in the "Manchester Guardian ":

Arley Hall is situated some miles from any rail- way station. It can be reached from Lymm, North- wich, and Knutsford, but Northwich i the nearest, though this is more than five miles away. The latter drive is not as pleasant as the others, as it en- tails nearly two miles through the outskirts of Northwich. From Northwich we pass the pleasant village of Great Budworth. The houses are exceed- ingly picturesque, and quite convey the impression of an old-fashioned country town; but though some are very old, the greater part, I am told, were built and partly designed by the present "Squire of Arley Hall," Mr. Egerton-Warburton. If we take this road we shall pass Budwierth. Mere, one of the principal of the Cheshire lakes, ind shall at once notice how closely it resembles in all its featurex the great pools that are now forming round and in North wich. Budworth Mere, of course, was the result of many ages of quiet subsidence, but the Northwick sinkings are enormously expedited by the increasing demands of trade. The country round Arley Park is somewhat flat, and can hardly rank among the most picturesque parts el Cheshire, but the enclosed park itself, which is of very large dimensions, is extremely beautiful, and th 3 gardens and grounds are kept up with great care. There is one large and very curious walled garden, which I should call the Dutch garden, as it is an excellent example of the change in gardening that William 111. introduced from Holland when he came to Eng- land. There are yew trees cut in. shapes, but the most striking feature is wbat at first sight seems a row of gigantic buttresses of fanciful form that would seem to support a long wall, and are so ex- actly trimmed that but for the colour they might almost pass for old stone-work. Arley Hall has been the seat of the Warburtons for, 'it is said, more than four centuries. There is a deed executed at Arlegh as early as 1346, but the date of the erection of the old hall which seems most probable is 1495. It is described as being then a large quadrangular building enclosing a court- yard. This is the period when perpendicular archi- tecture, which is peculiar to England, flourished. In the fifteenth century large portions of Cheshire were covered with forests of heavy oak trees, and that accounts for the many black-and-white houses that existed in the country; along the east coast, where oaks were scarce and stunted, hones of the same date were built of brick, while in Northamp- ton and other counties where there were quarries they were built of atone. The remarkable part of the Cheshile black-and-white is the heaviness of the woodwork, which Contrasts with the lighter work in the South, and still more with the black- and-White that we see on the Continent. There is at Arley a fine old riding school with a heavily timbered oak roof. The beams spring nearly from the ground—a peculiarity which may be seen also at the celebrated old hall of Baguley, near N orthen- den. The ancient black-and-white Arley Hall has disappeared. It is a large residence, and of the best examples of modern Elizabethan archi- tecture in England; Jacobean it has been called, but the gables and general features more close- ly resemble the style which prevailed in Eliza- beth's days. The entertaining-rooms are of very large dimensions, and the ceilings are among the most elaborate and costly in. England. The domestic chard is of. fourteenth century architecture, and was designed by Street, the architect of the Law Courts.. It has a fine, venerable ap- pearance, and is capable of seating 200 persons. There is daily choral service, at which the public are free to attend; on Sundays it is crowded to the fullest extent. Altogether, Arley Hall is decidedly one of the most interesting of all the modern houses in Cheshire.

div.head: PERCIVAL GORDON;
div.p: PERCIVAL GORDON;
THE CHILD OF°IIIE REGIMENT. SYLVANUS COBB.
CHAPTER XIH. TREE LOVE.

While the two earls had been in conference, at that late hour, on the evening of the day of the funeral, the old warder of the castle had been called from his comfortable lodge by the fierce barking of his best watch-dog, a pure blooded mastifl, as intelligent as he was faithful—and faith- ful unto death. Instead of going out into the court, and thence to the great gate, at a side wicket of which the dog was giving his alarm, the warder slipped out by the rear way, leaving the court, by a postern, so that, by making a sweep away from the premises, he could came to the gate, on the outside, as though from the highway. He took with him a heavy blunderbuss, loaded half way to the muzzle, and directed his wife to summon a few of the men-servants, to move towards the gate, and be ready to come to his aid should he call for assistance. The faithful servitor had his reasons for this curious proceeding. He had been credibly in- formed that a plan had been laid for a wholesale robbery of the castle, the expedition to be headed by two thieving men-servants, who had been dis- charged for various offences, stealing being not the worst. After their discharge they had been taken in hand by the officers of law, tried and condemned, and placed in the stocks for twelve hours and then publiely whipped. These were the men—three of them—who had planned to rob the castle, and they were equal to the work. Their secret had been whispered into the warder's ear by a poor woman, wife of an unfortunate drunkard whom the rascals had engaged to assist them. Robin Cuthbert was the, warder's name,-5 stout, rugged old man of almost three-score, but as lithe and enduring as ever. He made the circuit of the grounds beyond the court, striking the broad carriage-path at a eafe distance from the gate, which point he carefuly approached, keeping him- self well under cover. As lie came near the old barbican, with had been carefully preserved from the day of knightly tourney, he saw a man, who had just turned from the gate, coming towards him ; and he was sure that another man, if not two or three more, had gone in the opposite direction. He could intercept the man corning his way, and that was all; and that he prepared to do. He stepped aside, beneath the shadow of a droop- ing linden, and as the Man approached he sprang to the middle of the path and presented his blunder- buss. The moon, in its first quarter, was very near its setting, but the stars were bright and clear, and objects could be quite plainly distinguished near at hand. Robin very quickly discovered that the man before him was not one of the discharged servants ;nor did he lock like a thief. He certainly wore the garb of a gentleman, and bore himself as such. However, the faithful servitor was deter- mined to know who'hed been prowling around the castle gate at that hour, and to ascertain his busi- ness if possible. " Halt I Another stop and I fire! Ha ! None of that! If you run I'll put a dozen bullets through you as sure as fate! My blunderbuss is full." The stranger had a pistol in his hand—so Robin thought—just drawn from his.pocket, but he seemed afraid to use it, evidently fearing the blunderbuss might get ahead of him. "Now tell me—who are you, and what do you here ?" the old warder demanded, when he had covered his man to his satisfaction. "in the name of wonder who are you ?" the man returned, with an indignation that staggered the honest servitor considerably. "Is this the way and manner Lord Wenham's guests are treated on his own grounds? Are you of his household ?" Old Robin was trembling at every joint. He had recognised the man as one of the guests of the day—the man who was very soon to be Earl of Oxton.

"Pardon, my lord!" he cried, lowering his pon- derous brazen weapon. "I am a member of the household, and I meant no harm. I heard my mastiff barking; and knowing that he would only bark at a stranger, I feared there might be trouble. Dangerous men are abroad, my lord, and I hoped that I might capture one of them. If you would like to go in at the great gate, I will open the way for you." But Matthew Egerton—for it was be—did not wish to go in. He said he had started to return home with his mother, but the beauty of the scenery had attracted him, and he had stopped over for the night at the village inn, not caring to intrude upon Lord Wenham in the season of his mourning. After taking tea, he had taken a faney to come up and see the • old castle by moonligot ; and he said he had been richly repaid. But, the moon was sinking, and he had started on his return' to the village. If he had let it go at that, and retired without further remark, it is doubtful if the old warder would ever have thought seriously of the matter again • but after he had started on his way, he stopped and turned. "Look you, my good man, there is no need that you should say anything of this to the earl. He might blame me that I did not abide with him." The old man bowed, and Matthew passed on. Robin watched him until he had disappeared, and then turned towards the great gate, walking slowly, and muttering to himself of the event which had just transpired. He was not quite satisfied. In the first place, ha knew Matthew Egerton's reputation among the servants of Oxton, and he had heard several stories to his disadvantage. Further, he had, on that very day, taken a fair look at the young man's face, and had not liked it. The fancy had seized him to compare his face with the face of the hand- some young captain who had come home with his lordship, the result of which comparison we can readily imagine. "Surely," he said to himself, as he came near the gate, there was more than him here when I first came in sight. I know that one man slipped off the other way • and, I think, two of them. There may have been three. What were they doing here? He wasn't close up under this great gate looking at the castle by moonlight I And then I needn't tell the earl of it ! What in the world should he care for the earl if he is honest? Think of Harry Maxwell caring whether such a block as that lodged beneath his roof or not! There is some- thing here that don't appear on the surface." He had stopped outside the wicket beside the great gate, and was thinking that he would go to the porter's lodge and get a lantern, by the light of which to make an examination of the premises, and see if other stragglers might be lurking near. He had just found the hidden spring by which the wicket was opened from the outside, when a new thought struck him. " Oho I Aha ! ha, ha! Now I have it ! Oho-o- -o-o I" And he laughed aloud, not more at the thought of his own lack of judgment than at the comicality of the situation. "Bless me! why didn't I think of it in the outset! I saw him hang- ing around the lady more than once this afternoon. Oho I that's the secret! It's the sweet lady of Elm- dale I Well, I don't wonder he is smitten. But —Lord save her !—I hope she won't come to his claim I"

With the problem thus solved to his entire eatisfaotion, Old Robin entered the great court, dismissed the menservants who had gathered there by his directions, and then, without loss of time, sought his couch. On the following morning Lady Caroline was early astir, and ready, by the time the sun had shown its agolden disc above the tree-tops, to descend to the garden. She had made no appoint- ment with Percival—had spoken not a word of arrangement for another meeting—but she wished very much—it was a great yearning of her heart—. to see him and she was sure that he would not fail to walk in the garden at that matin hour. The morning was bright and beautiful, as had been the morning before, with nature wearing her sweetest smiles, and breathing her rarest frag- rance. _ _

As she stepped from the marble platform at the foot of the veranda stairs she met her dear lover close at hand. Ile had been waiting for her. "My darling, I knew you would come." He offered to kiss her hand, but she raised her radiant, happy face and made a frank exchange of the loving salutation. They walked away arm in arm down one of the flower-bordered paths, and at length, when beyond the possibility of observation from the dormitories of the castle, the young soldier stopped, and took both the lady's hands, gazing into her upturned face with a fervent, yearning love that filled her with joy ineffable. "Caroline," he said, with a solemn earnestness that told how sincere and honest was his purpose, "Jet us be entirely frank and free, and hide nothing. I have not since those blessed days of our early childhood asked you directly if you would be my wife." " Ah, my love, you mistake," returned the maiden, teaching a hand to his shoulder. "When

you would know if I loved you, as I had once • loved, and when you dared to imprint a lover's kiss upon my lips, you surely asked me if I were.all your own. Your every look and tone, and every act was a declaration to me of your devotion. And, my Percival, when I returned your kiss, and laid my head upon your bosom in loving trust- fulness, I gave you all the answer my soul could speak." "Bless you, darling, bless you I" And he caught her to his bosom, and held her there in a fond and fervent embrace. By and by they moved on, and Percival touched upon the subject uttermost in his thoughts. "Dear Caroline, you must know the one thing that troubles me above all others. For Matthew Egerton I care not a farthing. I watched him ctosely yesterday; I marked his looks towards yourself; and I could not fail to see that he had already come to cherish a bitter hatred of myself. 01 I cannot believe that when the last moment of probation shall expire by limitation, your rather could find it in his heart to even desire you to be that man's wife. It is too monstrous! too cruel 1 Lord Elmdale is a merciful man, of noble heart, I know, and I will not believe that lie would knowingly and willingly consign his child to lasting shame and misery; for, surely, as wife of lisich a wretch, shame would be your lot. The calamity of shame and disgrace must come to that man, if he lives; and those closely tied to him cannot escape the sorrow and chagrin. Yet, for all that, your father may not look kindly upon me. In tact, dearest, we know he will not. Ah 1 did you mark how he started, and gasped, and turned pale yesterday, when my general introduced me? Yes, I know you did. But—tell me—has he spoken to you on the subject?" "Not a void, my love; but I know it must come."

"Aye—be sure of that. He has already spoken with Maxwell. He visited him in his library late last evening, after all the others had retired." "He spoke of us 2—of our love 2" "Yes. It was of us alone he conversed, and he must have poured out his whole heart to our good friend, the general. Maxwell assures me that only the articles of betrothment, signed by him nine years ago, now hold him to the compact whereby your baud was given to Oxton's heir. In his heart your father dislikes the fellow as much as you do, though he does not, probably, think him a villain. Further—only, darling, we must not build too hopefully upon it—the general told me that Lord Elindale would gladly withdraw from the old agreement, if he could do so with honour. In fact, he is unhappy in contemplating it.
"But, Carrie, you know your father better than I do. You can best tell how far his pride and his fear of wounded honour may carry him."

"Before papa would do anything openly db.- honourable," said the daughter, with an expression of infinite sweetness upon her beautiful face, "I think he would suffer anything. How far he might be induced to go towards insisting upon an abnegation of the old-time contract of marriage, I cannot say. But, darling, my mind is made up, my course of action is resolved upon. But, before I say more can you tell me how Lord Wenham spoke? IL you kuow what impression he made ?" " Yes ; he told me everything that transpired at the meeting, reserving only what he said concerning myself; but we can imagine what that must have been. I can only tell you, Carrie, that your father was deeply affected—affected even to tears— betraying plainly, as I have already told you, that the old deed of affiancement rested like a painful incubus upon him. In the end he had not stated what he would do. He had spoken of his honour as pledged to the fulfillment of the contract, when Maxwell—and I can imagine just how he spoke— bade take care him of his own honour, and at the same time leave you, his daughter, to care for hers. And with that he sent his visitor away to sleep upon it." "Percival 1" the lovitig girl cried, with the light of a great relief breaking over her face, "that brings me very easily to speak what further I had to say with regard to the course I had resolved upon. If my father will go his way, without regard to my peace and happiness, I must take the guiding- hand for myself. It would be painful to set myself up in opposition to my good papa; for 0 1 he is good—very, very good !—only he is proud, and would like to see his child very high in the eyes of the world. But my own lifelong peace is of most account to me. One thing is sure : I cannot be wed against my will. In the England of this day a maiden may not be sold and bound like a slave, if she has done no crime. No, I cannot be wed against my will. Should the worst come, I will take the authority into my own hands, and be my mistress. In one year more I shall have reached an age where the law sets me free. In one year more—aye, three mouths less than a year—l shall become sole mistress of my own property, to do with it as I please." "And I," said the joyous youth, his eyes spark. hug with the greatest hopes that uplifted his spirit, "in one year more shall have a squadron of hussars under my command with a connnission of Major o 1 Cavalry in the English army. 0 lit does not seem possible! Look at the veterans yet waiting for advancement, while I, scarcely more than a boy, have reached my majority—or I shall have reached it on my return to London." But the gentle neriden could not see anything wonderful in it at all. In her estimation he had richly won all the honour that had been conferred upon him. "One thing, at least, is teue," the soldier re- sponded, with noble pride. "I have had not a particle of so-called family influence. I have had frienda\—friends, perhaps, as power:el in moral weight and influence as any in the kingdom—but they have all been soldiers, and they have spoken only of my record on the battle-field and in the reports of my regiment. Still my preferment is wonderful. A majonof cavalry at twenty. "And you will be a major ?" "Yes, I am sure of it. Oar dear general will not return to the army; and the Duke of Welling- ton, who, besides his position as Master of Ord- nance is acting as Governor of Plymouth, has been pleased to signify that be would like for me to come upon his staff with the rank of major. The only question in the way has been the possibility of Maxwell's return, in which case he would not give me up." "0 1 my hero! my hero !" cried the maiden rapturoasly, looking into his face with love un- speaeable, " fot what rack of empty name on eerth would I eechange the name you have so gloriously won for yourself! It is a preasant thing to be a titled lord, if one comes legitimately and honestly to the title; but it is a far pleasanter and a better thing to be a hero, brave and gallant, with one's honour the creature of his own life and Percival !—my love ! my hero ! my own I—thoe4a all the world beside should may me nay, 1 wouid cling to you and be your wife. So, my own true heart, know that this hand is you- s ; and I will call you hushaud just as soon as we anall both decide that the proper time has arrived." The lover's heart was full, and in response to this he could only take the noble girl to his bosom and hold her there, while he kissed her and blessed her. A little later they met Lord Wenham, who had come forth for a breath of the fresh morning air. To him they frankly told what they had been doing—told him the pledges they had exchanged and the plans they had laid, and he sustained them. "I may be wrong," he said, "in thus advising, but Ido not feel so. If I could be made to think that I was giving my countenance to anything that could, directly or indirectly, mar the interests of your father, 1 should hold myself guilty of gross error; but, upon may life, I do believe, hon- estly and sincerely, that what you two propose will be, in the end, for Richard Archer's best good; certainly for his peace of mind and self- satisfaction. Were he to consign his daughter to the man to whom he was so ignorantly and foolishly led to affiance her, he would live to repent in sack- cloth and ashes."
They walked on, Caroline once more taking the arm of their host; and so they came back to the castle and re-entered the great hall, and it so hap- pened that the Earl of Elmdale was there to see _ _

hem; and when he saw his daughter upon the general's arm a glad look gleamed in his azure eyes; but when, a moment later, he caught the effulgent brightness in Caroline's face, and the joy. beams that leaped from her eyes and danced in her lovely dimples, and saw a corresponding love-light in the handsome face of the youthful captain, his countenance fell. Yet he greeted them all plea- santly, and went so far, when they turned towards the drawing-room, as to take Percival's arm. After breakfast, upen the opening of the morn- ing's mail-pouch ana a reading of the letters, Lord Wenham had a glad surprise for hie youeg aide. "Captain, Tom is on his way to us, and wiii be here to-morrow." A glad light flashed in the youth's eyes. E host spoke of their dear old friend, Tom Craw' whilom sergeant of the —th Hussars, now beh.iie the responsible and honouraMe position of ordnee, sergeant at 'Woolwich. "Dear old Tom I" cried Percival.
" It will do

me good te see him. I hope he will not forget to bring the packet with him." "I should think not, seeing that that is the only excuse of business I could make for him in asking for his furlough," returned the general, looking up from the letter which he had not quite read through. Had our hero been looking at him a moment later, he would have seen a marked change in his countenance. All pleasant emotion left it, and an expression of pain, deep and poignant, came in its place. But he spoke no word. A pitying look towards his youthful aide he gave, and then turned away and went on with his reading. Later, as Percival was enjoying a few moments with Lady Caroline before her departure, he said to her: "You remember Tom Crawford?"

She remembered him very well. "He was my guardian," the youth went on, "and in his hands, when he became stationed at Woolwich, I left a packet of papers that are of great importance to me." Anti he described to her their character. _ _

"As you are aware," he continued, after that, "my grandfather—my father's father, Captain Archibald Gordon,—was younger son of a wealthy baronet; but from that source I can have no ex- pectations, as four elder brothers have left a nu- merous progeny. But, darling, Maxwell feels sure I have bright prospects in another direction. My grandmother, Captain Archibald's wife was a Patten, and granddaughter of Sir William Patten, of Ambleton, in Devonshire. The present baronet of Ambleton is an old man, and childless, and it is possible that lam his nearest living relative. If I am, being a lineal descendant of Sir William, I must come to the title and estate. For myself, dear Carrie, I care but little; but for your father's sake, and for your sake—Hush mean, with regard to your feelings for your father,—not for yourself,—for your sake, I hope the general may be right. Sir Edward Patten is the present bar- onet, over threescore-and-ten, and fast failing. 0 I Heaven send I may never wait for dead men's shoes; but if these shoes come to me, I will wear them."

---- And Lady Caroline went away happy and hope- ful,—the more happy because she could now meet her father with better grace in defence of her soldier lover. For herself, truly, she did not care for this prospective honour. She almost wished that it might not come, for then she could show to the world that she loved and prized her husband for the manhood that was his own. _ . .
_ What was to come neither she nor Percival, nor any other person, had the least shadow of thought or suspicion. (To be continued. )

div.head: RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.
div.p: RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.
TWINS!

Aw've known Jack o' Joanie's a while, He's fond ov a bit o' good life; For everyone he'd a jooak an' a smile, An' sooa hed his good-tempered wife. But lately he's changed. Hey, poor lad! It's but seldom neaw 'at he grins. An' his wife—Peg o' Molly's,—hoo's welly as bad; Au' t' change is thro' nowt nobbut twins!

Clooase to, they lived, quate an' content, An' childless, a good toothry year ; An' th' landlord, whenever he coed theer f3r t' rent, Kept axin' " Is t' babby nod here ?" They lafft at sich jooakes, blunt an' free, An' chaffed back, they cuddnd do less, An' weel aw remember Jack once sed to me,— "Hey, weddin's a gradely success !" Good childer they booath allus liked, An' often they sed ther fun, They wodn'd ha' cramd uns at o, cause they skriked, Yet wished i' ther hearts 'at they'd one. Ther dreom o' contentment's gooan by, Fooak mornd allus ha' tiler own way; For a couple o' babbles seet up a rare cry, While Jack wur at wark t'other day. Aw never, i' o ml born days See th' equal o' th' do 'at ther wor, For th' wiwmin abeawt wur o chatterin' like jays, Those childer they fair med 'em stun Fooak seemed to ha' gooan mad i' th' fowd,— At thowt on't, 0, heaw ini heyd spins ! I craze seemed to leet uppo booath young an' owd, When they heeard Peg o' Money's hed twins! 0 th' gossips kept scutterin' abeawt, Ther word-mekkers fairly on t' drive; An' heawse after heawse they nopt in, an' coom eawt, As busy as bees in a hive. Aw cuddn' tell wod to mek on't, 'Twur puzzlin' wed caused sitch ado, Till limpin' Susanna bawled up, just I' t' front 0' th' heawse, "Heigh, yo' lasses l—ther's two !" Then sumbry went off to tell Jack, At th' factory, o t' good joyful news ; Dear me ! beam fooak lafft when thad runner coom back,, An' sed Jack had coed 'em o foo's. lie wodn'd believe t' news at o Tilt he heeard id fro' Owd Doffer Sam, Then went back to wark wi' a rayther long jaw, An' sed 'twur too awkerd for gam.' When time coom for th' factry to lose, 0 th' gadders went lorryin' hooam, For, teen as a rule, wimmin's rayther too fawso Than let husbands know heaw they roam. When warkers seet deawn to tiler meals, An' heeard th' news, they o seemed so glad; Aw kornd tell heaw t' fayther o twin childer feet:, But know he lookt terribly bad.

He walked up afi white as a sheet, Just like a chap beawn to be hung; An' ever sin then he's bin run off his feet, An' getten a bit o' t' wife's tongue. It's penance, he ses, for his sins, An' often he sighs—wi' a groan,— " Beawt childer it's grand, but this weddin' wi' twins It's t' wost failure ever wur known !"
JACK 0' ANN'S.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
Hoisi OF COMMONS.-MONDAY. -
The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past

three. TUB VACANCY IN WEST DERBYSHIRE.—On the motion ef Vicount Wolmer, a new writ was ordered to issue for the election of a member of Parliament for West Derby- shire, in the room of Lord Edward Cavendish deceased. MANIPUR.—Sir JOHN GORST intimated to Mr. Crawford that if he would move for papers showing the precise political relationship of Manipur to the Government of India they would be laid on the table.—Mr. CRAWFORD also asked whether the Government would undertake that no one would be put to death in retaliation for the murder of Mr. Quinton and his companions until the circumstances had been considered by Parliament. -air John Gorst was surprised that such a question should be put. There would be no putting to death in retaliation, but adequate punishment would be meted out to those found guilty of crimes, without waiting for discussion in Parliament. M. DE COBAIN.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, in reply to Mr. T. M. Healy, said it was the intention of the Government to allow a certain limit of time to Mr. de Cobain in which to appear in his place, and if he failed to do so it would be for the House to take such further measures as might be thought fit under the circum- stances. NEW CoINAGE.—Mr. Goscuax informed Mr. Causton that the departmental Committee on the new designs for the coinage did not propose to make any report at pre- sent. It was proposed to invite certain artists to send , in by the 31st October next designs for the sovereign, half-sovereign, crown, half-crown, florin, and shilling. 1 Ile understood the Committee recommended the with- I drawal of four-shilling pieces. SUPPLY.—The House then -went into Committee of *apply, and a vote on aczount of four millions for the Civil Service and Revenue Departments being asked for. LABOUCHERE moved to report progress, as a protest against the treatment of the House by the Government, liir WILLIAM HARCOURT concurred in this. The reti- cence and blundering of the Government, he contended, 'were very unjust to the House. Mr. JAMES Lovrrnen said votes on account were now too frequent. Mr. Gos- cenx,replying to the various comments,said he could not answer the question as to the introduction of the Educa- tion Bill till the return of the leader of the House. The Motion to report progress was rejected by 122 to 67, and a further motion by the same proposer, to reduce the 111iti for surveys ef the United Kingdom by £20,000, was :41ecatived by 119 to 61. Mr. PRITCHARD MORGAN moved 111 reduction in the Woods and Forests Departments, for the purpose of calling attention to the gold mining royal- ties in Wales. In a long speech, he described how he had waited five years upon the promises of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, who had, however, done nothing. Mr. Gowning was able to assure Mr. Pritchard Morgan that Something had been done, and that an arrangement was about to be submitted which he thought would go a long way towards giving satisfaction. The Motion was with- driwn. The House adjourned at 12 15. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TernSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at & quarter-past four. THE NEWFOUNDLAND FISHERIES BILL.—Lord DxNsien said that on the third reading of this Bill he gave notice teo move that it be read this day four months. MITMENCE IN CRIMINAL CASES.—The Lord CHANCELLOR Moved the second reading of a Bill enabling the husband sr wife of a person criminally charged to be a competent witness on every hearing at every stage of such charge, 'whether the criminal was arraigned solely or jointly 'with others.—Lord DisxmAn, believing the Bill to be un- tonstitutional, said he would oppose it to the utmost ef his power, and moved that it be read this day ten months. r--Lord Herschell, Lord Esher, Lord Coleridge, and Lord Ashbourne supported the measure.—The Bill was read a •econd time. _ _

The House adjourned at 5.20. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TuEsner. As it was a morning sitting, the Speaker took the chair at five minutes past two o'clock. NIWFOUNDLAND.—Mr. Stavelev Hill presented a peti- tion from the Newfoundland delegates praying to be heard at the bar of the House with respect to the Fisher- ies Bill before proceeding with the measure, and intim- ated that on the second reading he would move that the prayer of the petition be granted. Mr. GOSCHEN ex- plained that the Newfoundland Legislature proposed to legislate for only one year. which proposal the Govern- ment could not accept. After hearing the member of the delegation, the debate would probably be adjourned, and the discussion of the Bill in that case would be re- Aimed on Friday. Tni DERBY.—Lord auto, in a very amusing speech, proposed that the House on its rising do adjourn till Thursday, which .was seconded by Major Rasch.—Sir Wi LFRED LAWSON, who opposed the motion, asked why the House should adjourn for "a gambling festival" like the Derby —Mr MORTON said that the Derby, though he had never seen it,WILLIAM was a "sink of iniquity."—Sir 101.4 COURT said the Governmene could prevent the adjournment it it chose, and if it did not the country would understand that all the talk about obstruction WAS hypocritical.—The motion was carried ny 137 votes t. 109.

CUSTOMS BILL.—The Chancellor of the Exchequer moved the second reading of tha Customs and Inland Revenue Bill, upon which Sir W. HARCOURT alleged that While Mr. Goschen is an able financier, he has, by his craving to appear eriginal,departed from all the old land- marks, and thrown the finances of the country into a itate of chaos Mr. A. H. Forwood, replying to the in- dictment as regards the navy, showed that the estimates as far as the Government dockyards were concerned had been unprecedentedly accurate, while as regards con- tract work there was ample explanation of the discrep- 'sees. Mr. Goschen replied to the various charges point by point, and demonstrated that the financial policy of the Government was not only economical beyond that of ,any preceding Administration,but that the accounts had Men made perfectly intelligible, except to those who Wished not to understand. Mr. Conybeare talked out the second reading. EyworNo Sim/ie.—At the evening sitting a resolution by Mr. James STUART proposing an alteration of the law tO enable women to sit on County Councils was dis- ettssed, amid repeated endeavours to count out the House. The motion was defeated by 78 to 52. The House adjourned at 12.5. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the wool-sack at a quarter past four o'clock. BILLS ADVANCED.—A Bill for the amendment of the jUdicature Acts was read a first time. The second read- 19g of the Drainage and Improvement of Lands (Ireland) till was postponed for a week. The Evidence in Criminal Cases Bill paFsed through committee witkout amend- pent, and the report was received. Lord de Ramsey informed Lord Lamingtnn that a decision would shortly be arrived at as to the transmission of cards with adhe- live halfpenny tamps through the post. Their lordships rose at twenty-five minutes to five **clock.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.:—THunsDAT.

The Spe7ker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. LOCAL Btu..—The Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway Bill was read a third time and passed. QugsrioNs,-&c.—Mr. Beixoutt informed Sir G. Camp- bell that there was no limit to the number of advances that could be made to one tenant purchaser in Ireland. Mr. RITCHIE, replying to Mr. Causton, said he hoped to be able to introduce in a few days the bill postponing the County Council elections, substituting March for January. Mr. Hicas BEACII informed Mr. Furness, lb reference to the alleged transfer of British steamers to foreign flags and subsequent overloading, that instructions had been Issued to detaining officers. FRES EDUCATION, &C.-Mr. SMITH expressed the hope that on Monday he would be able to name the date for the introduction of the Free Education Bill. Child labour, the reporting of the Labour Commission's pro- ceedings, Drlashonaland, and the order of public business formed the subject of further questions, Mr. Smith agreeing tc postpone this e• e second reading of the Factory and Workshops Bill, so as to enable Mr.l'Mundella to take part in the discussion. A new writ was ordered for the Cii!y of London. NEWFOI7IsTDIAND FISH/MISS.—Mr. W. H. SMITH stated that an understanding had been arrived at which would obviate the necessity of the Newfoundland delegates be- ing heard at the bar of the House. Mr. Smith afterwards Moved the second reading of the Newfoundland Fisheries Bill, and the action of the Government was vigorously assailed by Mr. Sts,vely Hill, Sir W. Harcourt, 'and others. Ultimately the Government accepted a motion by Mr. Brrce, to the effect that, inasmuch as the New- foundland Legislature had taken steps for giving effect to the agreement with France and for settling the diffi- culty, the House should not proceed to the second read- ing of the bill. The H.,!,,,,,fi-orwnras went into Committee of Supply.

div.head: LIVERPOOL TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE LIVERPOOL TRAGEDY.

FUNERAL OF THE VICTIM. The funeral of the murdered boy Nicholas Martin took place on Sunday afternoon at the Roman Catholic Cemetery at Ford.near Liverpool,and was made the occa- sion of a great demonstration. Bridgewater-st., where the parents live, was crowded from end to end, and many thousands struggled to get into St. Vincent's Church during the service. Along the whole route to the cemetery crowds lined the thoroughfares, and much sympathy was manifested towards the bereaved family. Tho deceased boy's school-fellows joined in the procession and six of theta carried the coffin from the hearse to the grave. FURTHER EVIDENCE.

The detectives under Mr. Allbutt are busy getting the evidence into form for the investigation before the coroner and the stipendiary. A very important piece of evidence was procured on Monday by Mr. Allbutt. In the afternoon he and several officers subjected the house in Stanhope-st., where the murder is alleged to have been committed, to another thorough search. The lower room was used by the accused Conway as an office in connection with the Seamen's and Firemen's Union. In Searching his apartment on Monday the officers came across a concealed cupboard. This was prised open,and Mr. Allbutt found therein a scrubbing brush such as is used by housemaids to scrub floors. The brush was covered with what is evidently blood, and taken in con- nection with the marks on the flon of the room where the deed is supposed to have been committed, the detectives believe that the brush in question was used for the purpose of cleaning up the blood stains. This brush, as well as other articles,has been sent to the pub- lic analyst for examination. The police have found a lad who saw the prisoner Conway talking to the murdered boy Martin, shortly after nine o'clock on the night when the murder is sup- posed to have been committed, at the corner of Bridge- water-st.,near the boy's home. Another bey has come for- ward who saw the prisoner on Saturday night with a pair of boots in his hand, near the scene of tbe murder. Other important discoveries have been made in connec- tion with the murder. One of the missing boots have been found in a marble yard near the scene of the tragedy, it having been thrown over the wall from the street. It is apparently bloodstained. The second boot was brought to the detective office, having been found in the Corporation stone-yard, not far from the scene of the murder. It also is stained with blood. In a stable yard near the same place a razor has been found, which had evidently been thrown over the wall on Saturday night. The only missing article now is the boy's cap. The police have also discovered a man who states that on Saturday night week he saw the prisoner come out of a public house, and call to a boy who was playing ball in Bridgewater-st. He told the boy to come and never mind the ball, and gave him sixpence. The boy and man then went away in the direction of Stanhope-st.,and he lost sight of them.

div.head: TWO MEN WANTED AS WITNESSES.
div.p: TWO MEN WANTED AS WITNESSES.

It has transpired that on Whit-Monday two men who had the appearance of plumbers were seen to enter the house in Stanhope-st., between twelve 'noon and one o'clock. The police are now endeavouring to find these men, because their evidence would be of the highest im- portance. There had been a dispute as to the water supply, which had been cut off, and the landlord of the premises had declined to grant the request made by Con- way for getting the water-pipes put right. It is now presumed that the prisoner met these two men and induced them to go to the house and do what was necessary to the pipes to enable him to obtain a tempor- ary supply of water.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: INQUEST.

- The inquest concerning the death of the boy Nicholas Martin, whose mutilated body was found in a sailor's bag in the Sandon Basin, on the 19th inst., was resumed en Thursday ,before Mr. Clarke Aspinall,and a jury. The father and mother of the deceased gave evidence as to the circumstances under which the boy was last seen,and stated that fourteen years ago John Conway, the man who is in custody, lodged with them. Hugh M'Donald, gateman at the Huskisson Dock, said that at one o'clock on the morning of the 19th inst. he thought he heard a splash, and remarked to some one. "What's that?" At about two o'clock he noticed something black float- ing in the water, and on its being brought to the side it was found to be a sailor's bag containing a boy's body, with the legs sawn off below the knees, there being also in the bag a pair of blankets and a knife and saw. Mary Patterson,second-hand clothes dealer,Bs, Park-lane, gave evidence as to the prisoner Conway having pur- chased the bag and blankets on the 18th inst. Rcse Ann Brown, 58, Bridgewater-st., stated that Conway lodged with her and acted as secretary to the Seamen's and Fire- men's Union. At ten o'clock on the morning of the 18th inst. he went out, saying he was going on an excursion, but returned and complained of being sick. He afterwards went out, returning about 10.30, and going, to bed about half-past eleven. When witness got up at half-past nine next morning Conway had gone out. He returned about half-past eleven, and on that and the following day complained of being ill. Dennis Murphy, a fellow-lodger, stated, in the course of his evidence, that on the Tuesday merning in question Conway was in bed when he went out at half-past eight. Other witnesses gave evidence as to seeing Conway talk- ing to the deceased and giving him money on the night of the disappearance, while a cabdriver deposed to driv- ing Conway and the bag to the Landing-stage on the Monday night. Conway was also identified as the pur- chaser of tne knife and saw found in the bag. The in- quest was adjourned until next day.
THE WOMEN'S LIBERAL FEDERATION.
LETTER FROM MR. GLADSTONE,

The annual meeting of the Women's Liberal Associa- tion was held on Wednesday night, at St. James's Hall, London. The large hall was well filled. Mrs. Gladstone presided, and among those on the platform were the Earl and Countesss of Aberdeen, Earl Spencer, and the Coun- tess Spencer, Lady Plowden, Lady Trevelvan. Lady Stevenson, Mrs. Shaw-Lefevre, the Countess Tolstoi, Lady Hayter, Mrs. Gilzean Reid, Mrs. C. B. M`Laren, Mrs. Bryant, Mrs. Theodore Fry, Mr. T. Fry, M.P., Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.P., Szc. _ _ _

Mrs. Gladstone, in opening the proceedings, said she did not intend to make a speech ; but she would do some- thing better—she would read a short letter from her husband, Mr. Gladstone (cheers), which was as follows :

Three weeks ago I:looked forward, with cordial in- terest, to addressing to-day the ladies assembled at the meeting of their Liberal Federation. The present Parlia- ment has sat long. Its whole term has had the con- tinuing interest of a single prolonged crisis,and that crisis, as months and years roll on, seems only to become more and more acute. Nor is this wonderful. The unsatisfied wants of England, Scotland, and Wales continually accu- mulate their arrears in the House of Commons,which,not- withstanding most perilous changes in precedure, which have restrained the ancient liberty of debate, continues to stagger under the unmanageable mass of its engage- ments. And in this state of things the majority of that house insist upon maintaining a system under which Ire- land (intent upon obtaining the management of her own affairs,and thereby enabling us to manage ours) occupies, in despite of herself, about one half of the available time of Parliament. And when the dissolution finally arrives, our opponents will demand an indefinite prolongation of this extraordinary condition of affairs, and will make this the basis of theirclaim to the confidence of the coun- try. Such is the subject on which it would have been my duty to speak to the meeting. The care necessary in order to complete recovery from my attack of influenza has made this impossible, but it will readily be believed how I shall be present, at least in heart and spirit, and how earnestly I hope that the meeting may serve the great purposes of the cause.— (Signed). W. E. G. The reading of the communication was received with cheers. A report was then submitted, which set forth the work carried out during the past year. Last year it was stated, the committee reported an aggregate of 143 asso- ciations, having a total membership of 51,300, of whom 45,350 were women. This year there were 177 affi- liated associations, with a membership of Kra, includ- ing 51,734 women. The Countess of Aberdeen, in moving 'the adoption of the report, said their disappointment at Mr. Gladstone's absence was great, but that disappointment had not chilled their ardour or damped their enthusiasm in the cause on whose behalf thy had gathered together. (Cheers.) Referring to Ireland, she expressed the opin- ion, as the result of a recent visit to that country, that the cloud which had recently overcast the cause of Ire- land, was beginning to be effaced, and that the Liberal cause would ultimately triumph. (Cheers.) The motionavas seconded by Mrs. C. B. M'Laren, sup- ported by Mrs. Bryant, and carried. On the motion of Mrs. Theodore Fry, seconded by Mrs. H. Gilzean Reid, the meeting adopted the following resolution with acclamation :—"That this meeting desires to convey to Mr. Gladstone the regret felt on ac- count of his enforced absence,asd hopes that he will soon be able, with renewed health and strength, to resume his invaluable work as leader of the Liberal party. (Cheers)." Mrs. Broadley Reid then moved a resolution, approv- ing of a national system of free education, but stating that the system would be incomplete until it comprised the total remission of fees for all standards, and a pre- per control by the ratepayers of the expenditure of their money. This was seconded by Mrs. W. Philips. and supported by Mrs. W. P. Bayles, of Bradford, and carried. The meeting closed with a vote of thanks to Mrs. Gladstone for presiding.

THE GRAND LODGE OF GOOD TEMPLARS.

The Grand Lodge of Good Templars commenced their annual sessions in Edinburgh on Tuesday, Grand Temp- lar Turnbull, Glasgow, presiding. Delegates attended from Germany, Scandinavia, Africa, America, and various other parts. The meetings, which will mainly be private, will last a week.
