div.head: VISIT OF THE GERMAN EMPEROR.
div.p: VISIT OF THE GERMAN EMPEROR.

On his forthcoming visit to England, the Emperor William will pay a visit to the Queen of Holland in Ams- terdam. The Empress, who will accompany her consort to England, will, of course, be with him in Amsterdam. His Majesty will not be attended by Chancellor Caprivi on this journey, but by the Foreign Secretary, Baron von Marscliall, and the ordinary retinue, with the addition •f a few other persons. The Emperor wishes to have the most important incidents of his visit to England per- manently recorded on canvas, and for this purpose has requested one or two painters, including Herr Rudolf Wimiser, of Munich, to proceed to Loadon in advance.

div.head: COLLISION ON THE MERSEY.
div.p: COLLISION ON THE MERSEY.

TWO STEAMERS SUNK AND SEVERAL LIVES LOST. A disastrous collision took place on the Mersey on Saturday evening about half-past ten, when the weather was hazy and the river choppy with a strong tide running, resulting in the sinking of the steatnship Lestris, 1,065 tons gross, belonging to the Cork Steamship Company, and the coasting steamer Mersey, belonging to Rogers, Bright, and Co.. of Liverpool. The Lestris was built at Sunderland in 1872, and carried a crew of 21 hands, being commanded by Captain I'. Matthews, while the Mersey had a crew of nine hands, her master being Captain Helton, who resided in Liver- pool. The Mersey was almost cut in two, and sank in a few minutes, abreast of the Sandon Dock, while the Les- trig, which was badly injured at the bows, and was rapidly filling, drifted towards the Cheshire shore and sank off Egremont. Altogether six live 3 were lost.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: INQUEST.

An inquest was held on Wednesday at the Liverpool Coroner's Court before the Deputy-Coroner, Mr. C. S. Samuel!, on the body of Francis Woodlands, second mate of the Cork steamer Lestris, who died as a result of the collision on the Mersey on Saturday night last between that steamer and the coasting steamer Mersey. The evidence of Captain Matthews, master of the Lestris, was to the effect that shortly before 11 o'clock on Satur- day night, his vessel left the Salisbury Dock and pro- ceeded down the river on her way to sea. When about opposite Egremont he noticed the lights of an approach- ing steamer. He first saw the red light, then the green light, and then the red light again, which showed that the approaching vessel was altering her course. As she approached he ordered full speed astern, but the other vessel, which proved to be the Mersey, casne up ansi struck the Lestris amidships. Both vessels foundered shortly afterwards.—William Elton, captain of the Mersey, gave evidence as to the course he steered, and stated that the Lestris altered her coarse when the two vessejs were close together and so rendered a collision inevitable.—After some discussion between the legal gentlemen engaged, it was arranged not to go further into the case, as it would be the subject of legal proceed- ings in another court, and the jury returned an open verdict of " Death fvom immersion."

div.head: FATAL FIRE IN LONDON.
div.p: FATAL FIRE IN LONDON.
DEATH OF LORD ROMILLY AND TWO SERVANTS.

Shortly after Midnight on Saturday a disastrous fire occurred at the residence of Baron Rotnilly (son of a late Master of the Rolls) at 38, Egerton Gardens, Bromp- ton-road, London, which resulted in the deaths of Lord Romilly and two servants, and led to the serious injury of a fireman. It appears that at about 11.40 on Satur- day night Lord Rotnilly accidentally upset a paraffin lamp in his drawing-room, and, without calling for assistance, attempted to extinguish the fire which resulted in the accident. While so engaged, it is con- jectured, the unfortunate peer was overcome by the smoke and flames. On the alarm reaching the butler, Thomas Hayter, he found his master lying senseless on the floor of the drawing-room, and, from the appearance of the room, and the dense smoke which filled it, he was of opinion that Lord Romilly had been overcome by the suffocating fumes. By this time the assistance of fire- men from the Relton Mews Fire Station had been obtained, and the body was rescued and at once removed to St. George's Hospital, where the case was attended to by Dr. Comerford. A short examination by the medical man, however, was sufficient to convince him that Lord Romilly was dead. When the first fire escape could be applied and the firemen were able to enter the house, a housemaid, Blanche Griffin, aged 20, was found in one of the upper rooms lying on the floor insensible. She was at once rescued and carefully let down the fire escape, and by the constables taken to St. George's Hospital. Dr.Comer- ford:again had to pronounce life extinct. Still later another servant, Emma Lovell, the cook, was similiarly found lying insensible on the floor. By this time medi- cal assistance had been obtained, and Dr. Ryder, of rhurlow-place, Fulham-road, after a brief examination, found that Lovell, like her fellow-servant and Lord Romilly, was dead from suffocation. Superintendent Sheppard at once had the body conveyed to the Kensing- ton Mortuary. The butler and another domestic, named Jane Nappin, aged 30, escaped. The former was able to reach the street by the staircase before being overcome, but the latter had to be rescued by means of the fire es- cape. The late peer, the second Lord Romilly, was born in 1835, was educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and was also a graduate of London University. After serving for a period as a lieutenant in the 23rd Foot, he was called to the bar at Gray's Inn in 1864, and became a clerk of enrolments in Chancery. He was deputy-lieut. for Glamorganshire. Lord Romilly, who at the time of his deathtwas a widower, has been twice married —irst in 1865, to a daughter of Lieut.-General Sir John Gas- pard le Marchant. This lady died the year following, and Lord Romilly married in 1872 a daughter of the late Mr. E. H. Hanson Denison. He has issue by his first marriage, but no member of his family lived with him at the house in Egerton Gardens.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: INQUEST.

Mr. Troutbeck, coroner for Westminster, held an inquest on Wednesday at St. George's Hospital, on the bodies of Lord Romilly and Emma Lovell, one of his servants.—Thomas Hayter, the butler, aid Engineer Morris repeated the evidence given by them on Tuesday at the inquest on the body of Mary Jane Nipperd, who also perished in the fire.—Fireman Byne,whose hands were enveloped in bandages, was now sufficiently recovered to give evidence. He stateel that, having received the alarm, he proceeded to the scene of the fire with the escape. He rescued a woman who was calling for help. He afterwards attempted to ascend the escape, but was unable to proceod in consequence o; the flames. It was when making this attempt that he received the injuries. The Coroner complimented Byne upon his pluck and bravery, and the jury endorsed the coroner's remarks. Mr. Comerford, house surgeon at St. George's Hospital, stated that when brought to the institution Lord Romilly was dead. Death resulted from extensive burns and suffocation. The woman Lovell was also dead when she reached the hospital. Mr. Alfred Spencer, deputy clerk to the London County Council, deposed that he was familiar with the Petro- leum Acts. He had made inquiries in connection with the case. lie had seen the remains of the lamp and a specimen of the oil used. The oil was of the highest quality. He attributed the accident te the fact that in falling the burner of the lamp became detached, and thus allowed the oil to escape. Mr. Boverton Redwood,another expert, gave similar evidence. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death.

MR. T. W. LEGIT, M.P., AT PADGATE

On Thursday evening an entertainment was held in Padgate Church Schools in connection with the Padgate and Orford Habitation of the Primrose League. There was a good attendance including Mr. T. W. Legit, M.P. _

Mr. Legh, M.P., in the course of the evening, gave an address on political topics. He remarked that he did not personally remember any time when politics appeared to be in a duller condition than at the present time. They were, in fact, absolutely in a state of stagnation. Much more attention was given by the newspapers to such absorbing topics as the spread of influenza than to such measures as the Irish Land Bill. All this was proof that people were getting tired of political questions and of the Irish questionin particular. (Hear, hear.) Having referred to the tranquility which the country had enjoyed at home and abroad under the present Government, and to the "scramble "in South Africa, Mr. Legh went on to refer to the proposed introduction of a measure of assisted er free education. Nobody as yet knew what that measure was, and therefore it was rather premature to discuss it They Conservatives had been taunted by their opponents with having turned their coats upon that question, and with now advocating a measure they formerly did their best to resist. As far as he was concerned, he had nothing to do with English politics in 1885, when th 3 measure was formerly before the country, and had hardly expressed an opinion on it. But the position of the Conservative party with regard to that question was quite different to that of their opponents. The original proposers of free education—the advanced Liberals-- brought it forward obviously with the intention of des- troying the voluntary schools, while the object of the Conservative party was precisely the reverse. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Their object was to support the denominational schools to the best of their ability, and he should certainly not give his vote for any proposal which would involve any harm to the present system of voluntary schools. (Applause.) But, as he nad said before, they had little idea as to what the measure was. Personally he should be inclined to think it would be a much more modest measure than people supposed. Whether the government had done well to bring it in at the present moment was a point open to discussion, as they appeared to be rather over- loading the ship in bringing in such an important measure at this stage of the Parliamentary session. Whatever the measure was it would be represented by their opponents as a bribe to the agricultural com- ' munity, in the hope that they should persuade them to vote for the Conservatives at the next election. But he thought it must be evident to most sensible people that a policy of bribing was not much use. Although they might offer a bribe of that kind and might please people at the time the feeling of gratitude would very soon die out, and it was highly probable that before the next election arrived the boon or bribe would be entirely for- gotten by the electors. And, besides, however much they might do in the way of bribing they could always be beaten by their opponents,because they were in the habit of promising anything at the expense of a third party. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Legh next referred to what he termed the" entire disappearance" of the Irish ques- tion, and concluded by expressing a hope that he would be again returned to Parliament by that constituency. (Applause.)

the programme of music which had been prepared for the evening was very well rendered. Amongst those who were down to take part in it were the Misses Birtles, Mrs. G. Comber, Mr. W. Pierce, Mr. W. B. div.head: MANIPUR DISASTER.
div.p: THE MANIPUR DISASTER.
CAPTURE 015 THE SENAPATI.

dispatch received at C. 3,lcutta from Manipur states that the Senapati, who was the chief cause of the recent massacre, has at length been captured. He was taken by Major Maxwell in the Chassad Hills. The latest des- patches received state that the Senapati was captured quietly at a village not half a mile from the Akame Palace, in Manipur. He was disgmised as a Nuga coolie. Although crowds of Manipuris were about at the time of his capture, there was no attempt at rescue and no popu- lar demonstration. Slight cholera still continuos among the troops in Manipur. According to information received at Rangoon from Assam, tho Senanati was taken on Saturday by the British. Subadar Kelendra Singh, of the Surma Valley Police, effected the capture after a severe struggle.
THE GOVERNMENT AND FREE EDUCATION. LETTER FROM SIR WILLIAM HART-DYKE.

Sir William Hart-Dyke's attention having been called by a correspondent to a report of a speech delivered at Bexley Heath recently by his Radical opponent for Dart- ford, Mr. J. Lyon, wherein he is reported to have said that in the election address of Sir William Hart-Dyke, their member plainly stated that he was entirely opposed to the principle of free education, has replied as fol- lows

notige Of CottniOns, May 22. Dear hope soon to introduce the Education Bill. The scheme of free education which I denounced in my address was that of the authorised Radical pro- gramme, which would have destroyed the voluntary schools, and, as I stated, upset the settlement of 1870 (Mr. Ferster's Act). Five years' experience at the Edu- cation Office has caused me to modify my views in regard to this question, and lam in no way ashamed to admit this. The difficulty ef enforcing attendance, and the wretched system of payment of fees for non-pauper children through the poor law, are some of the reasons which convince me that a change is necessary.—l remain yours faithfully,
W. HART-DYKE.

div.head: TERRIBLE CRIME AND INSTANT PUNISHMENT.
div.p: A TERRIBLE CRIME AND INSTANT PUNISHMENT.

The " Times " publishes the following Dalziel telegram from Sandy Hook, Kentucky :—One of the worst crimes ever committed in this State has just come to light at this place, the victim, Miss Maud Fleener, aged twenty-one, who was on a visit here from Richmond, Virginia. Miss Fleener, who was reputed to be wealthy, had three admirers—namely, John and Henry Wilcox and Amos Queen. She be- came engaged to the last-named, and the Wilcox brothers swore they would be avenged. On April 14 Miss Fleener left her home on horse- back to visit some friends at a place fifteen miles distant. As she never reached her destination and did not return home, search parties went out to look for her. On Saturday last one of these parties came upon a hut in an unfrequented part of a wood Hearing groans from within, they entered the hut, and found the object of their search stretched on a filthy cot, and bound to the floor by heavy chains fixed to her ankles. The story she told was one of daily outrage, and she added" The Wilcox boys did it." She died before she could be removed. When Miss Fleener started to visit her friends she weighed Ost. 91b., when found by a search party she weighed only sst. 51b. and her left arm and leg were broken. The post-mortem examination showed that she had been subjected to extraordinary vio- lence, and her mental and physical suffering must have been terrible. As soon as the guilt of the men dawned upon the searchers, a number of them went to find the Wilcox brothers. When apprehended the latter denied any knowledge of the crime, but afterwards admitted their guilt and made the followilg confession in writing : "We were going down the road when we saw the girl coming. We both hid, and she did not see us until we jumped from the bushes. The horse shied, throwing the girl, and then bolted, dragging her for some distance, until the girth broke. When we came up to her she was unconscious. Henry brought water from a spring and bathed her face, and after a while she opened her eyes.- She cora- plained of her leg and arm hurting. We examined the limbs. and found them both broken. We were frightened and did not know what to do. John proposed that we should take the girl to the cabin and niake her marry one of us. As both wanted rto marry her, we drew straws, and John won. ir John told her she would be married to him and taken care of, and that if she did not consent we should keep her locked up until she did. She said she would rather die. When we pickiid her up she fainted,and was unconscious until after we got to the cabin. We set h9r leg and arm as best we knew how. As one day she tried to escape, we chained her to the floor. She became worse and worse,until we decided to tell her where she was and then leave the country. If she had not been found within the ; next six hours we would have told her all and run away."
The brothers ‘Vilcoek then nervously asked, " What are you going to do with us?" In reply Amos Queen stepped forward, and, raising Ins repeating rifle, blew out the brains of both scoundrels.

THE PARNELL-O'SHEA. DIVORCE SUIT.
THE DECREE MADE ABSOLUTE,

In the Divorce Division, on Tuesday, Mr. Justice Jeune made absolute the decree nisi granted by Mr. Justice Butt on the 17th of November last to Captain O'Shea for the dissolution of the marriage on the ground of hiewife's adultery with Mr. Charles Stewart Parnell, M.P. All that transpired was a formal pronouncement that six months having elapsed since the decree nisi, and there being no intervention, the decree was made absolute.
SHOCKING TRAGEDY IN GLOUCESTER- SHIRE.

Late on Tuesday night a shocking tragedy was dis- covered near Thornbury, Glotnestershire. A woman about thirty-five years of age, was found lying in the road in the outskirts of the town with her throat cut, and on examination life was found to be extinct. Close by was a man, also with his throat badly cut, but he was alive, and was removed to the Thornbury Police Station, where his injuries were attended to. The parties are apparently tramps, and their names are not at present known.
ENGLAND AND PnitrUGAL IN SOUTH
AFRICA.
THE BRITISH ATTACKED AND SEVEN OF THE PORTUGUESE KILLED.

Her Majesty's cruiser Brisk, which has just anived at Lorenzo Marques, reports that the Chartered South Africa Company's Expedition, under the leadership of Mr. Johnson, has been attacked by a Portuguese Military Post on the River Pungwe. Seven Portuguese are re- ported to have been killed. The loss sustained by the expedition is not known. Her Majesty's cruiser Magi- cienne and the gunboat Pigeon are at Beira. A force of two hundred Portuguese and five hundred natives reached Massi-Kessi en May 11th, and finding that the plate had been evacuated by the chartered company's officers, pushed on across country in the direction of Fort Salisbury. On the way, they met a detachment of sixty men of the chartered company's police, and a collision ensued, in which the Portuguese were defeated, with the loss of seven killed and several wounded. it is added that the Pungwe route to Mashonaland has been again closed by the Portuguese authorities.
ATTACK BY THE-SOUTEI AFRICAN CO.'S FORCES.

LISBON, THURSDAY —A private despatch received here from Lourenzo Marques, dated yesterday, reports that fighting has occurred between the British and Portuguese on the banks of the Bembre River, the result of which was uufavourable to the Portuguese.

div.head: FOItEIGNERS IN CHINA.
div.p: FOItEIGNERS IN CHINA.
MISSION HOUSES SACKED AND PILLAGED.

The Shanghai correspondent of the " Times" tele- graphs :—The popular movement against foreigners is spreading with somewhat alarming rapidity. Following on the outrages already reported, the Christian houses at Nankin have been attacked and pillaged, the inmates having narrow escapes for their lives. The agitation is ceasing to be local, and considerable apprehension is felt for the safety of the foreign residents at the Treaty ports of the Yangtze River.

div.head: DESPATCH OF A BRITISH CRUISER.
div.p: DESPATCH OF A BRITISH CRUISER.

A Shanghai telegram says :—The popular movement against foreigners is spreading with somewhat alarming rapidity. Following on the outrages already reported, the Christian Mission houses at Nankin have been at- tacked and pillaged, the inmates having narrow escapes for their lives. The agitation is ceasing to be local, and considerable apprehension is felt for the safety of the foreign residents at the treaty ports of the Yangtze River. There can be no doubt that some or all of the secret societies with which China abounds, and which play so important a part in the development of the domestic affairs of the couhtry, are at the bottom of .the present mischief.

Further particulars received from Mankin of the riots in that city state that European ladies and children have left the city. The girls' school attached to the Methodist mission was fired and looted by the rioters. Other mis- sibns were attacked, but the mob was finally dispersed. Her Majesty's cruiser Porpoise has started for Nankin, and Chinese troops have alse been despatched. News has been received at Shanghai that a band of rioters attacked the City of Kan King, on the Yangtze Kiang, and pillaged many of the houses.

div.head: TEE NORTH WALES MYSTERY.
div.p: TEE NORTH WALES MYSTERY.
DUNCAN BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES

'Richar-d Coolidge Duncan, was on Saturday brought before Captain Wvnne Griffiths., Messrs. J Menzies,John Robinson, D. P. Williams, and Dr. Taylor Morgan, at the Carnarvon County Magistrates' Court, and charged with having attempted to murder his wife, Kato Dun- can. at Dolwyddelen, on the 10th inst. The prisoner was brought from the precincts of :the prison along the corridor leading to the Assize Court. He appeared ex- tremely pale and depressed, but glanced occasionally round the court, which was filled by spectators. Captain Wynn Griffiths asked Superintendent Williams what was the nature of the application about to be made with re- ference to the case. Supt. Williams replied that he applied for a remand of the prisoner upon the charge that on the 10th inst. Duncan unlawfully attempted to kill his wife, Kate Duncan. He had been remanded until that day by the Bettws-y-Coed magistrates. Mrs. Duncan, however, was not in a fit state to appear, and alttmigh better she was not yet out of danger. However, she had improved wcnderfully under the circumstances. As she could not appear, he respectfully asked for a further remand until that day week at Bettws-y-Coed. Prisoner was then formally remanded, and removed to the cell in custody of the governor of the gaol. The medical men in attendance upbn Mrs. Duncan,the victim of the Bettws-y-Coed tragedy, have now pro- nounced her out of danger. Facts are cAming to light which clearly indicate that her husband entertained remarkable delusions in regard to a Welsh peerage, of which he believed himself to be the heir. DUNCAN ALLEGED TO BE INSANE.

BALTIMORS, THURSDAT.-Dr. Kempster, one of the ex- perts on insanity, who testified in the Giteau case, examined Richard C. Duncan three years ago. He says that he then discovered traces of an unbalanced mind, and advised Duncan being placed under restraint. He wrote a letter at the time to Duncan's brother, who was at the Hopkins University,recommending that he should be placed in an asylum. Duncan is a son of the Rev. Thomas Duncan, an Episcopal clergyman residing in Cecil County, Maryland. He was regarded as very ec- centric, and others besides Dr. Kempster advised the family to have him put under restraint. Travel was re- commended by his physician, who thought that variety and change might bring about a more healthy condition of mind.

Alarming collisions between the police and svmpatni- zers with the strike hands of the Paris. Omnibus Com- pany occurred on Tuesday. Traces were cut and other damage was done to the property of the company.

div.head: THEFT OF L5O BY A GIRL AT WARRINGTON. EXTRAORDINARY ADVENTURES.
div.p: THEFT OF L5O BY A GIRL AT WARRINGTON. EXTRAORDINARY ADVENTURES.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor, and Alderman Harrison, Annie Critchley, aged 14, daughter of Ed win Critchley, of 34, Allen-st., who is employed at Messrs. Rylands Brothers' wire works, was charged with stealing, on the 11th inst., £5O in gold, the chief part of which was the property of Emma Critchley, aged 65, a widow, the girl's grandmother, living at the prisoners father's house.—Chief- Constable Hunt said the prisoner, lie believed, was 14 years old last March. Her father was left a widower with seven children 12 years ago, and the prosecutrix had ever since then been his house- keeper. The prisoner was the only daughter at home, and three or four other children, boys, were also there. There was staying with the family a relative with a child three years old. About three o'clock on Monday afternoon the 11th inst., the pri- soner was playing with this little child at the front door. She was noticed by her father and grandmother who were in the kitchen to go upstairs. She came down without their knowledge, and it was afterwards found she had left by the front door, taking a small bundle with her. No notice was taken of her absence until about half-past four, when, as she did not come home to tea it was thought she had gone into the park, not far from which her father lived. Dur- ing the evening he went out for a walk, and returned about half-past nine, when the grandmother told him that the girl bad not come in. His son aged 13 told her that he had seen his sister spending money. In conse- quence of that Mrs. Critchley went upstairs and found that a certain drawer which was then locked had been unlocked and that two purses containing about £5O in gold, that was,from 10e. to 20s. more than £5O, had been stolen, with their contents. The money belonged mostly to Mrs. Critchley and some of it to a sister of Mr. Critchley. Mr. Critchley r£s belonged to the sister.— Mr. Hunt proceeded to say that every possible enquiry was made and information given to the police, but no- ing was heard of the girl until Wednesday, the 20th when Mr. Critchley received a telegram from the St. Pancras Workhouse, London, stating that his daughter was there. He (Mr. Hunt) heard from the London police on Thursday morning, and from them, and by enquiries, had ascertained the girl's movements. It appeared that on the Ilth inst., the girl went from Warrington to Roby, and then took the train to Liverpool, and the midnight train from there to London, reaching there between six and seven next morning. She then went to a coffee tavern, and got some coffee, and walked about during the day, taking lodgings at the coffee house at night. She took the train next day back to Liverpool, reaching there about half-past five p.m., and returned to London the same night by the midnight train. She strolled about London, going to different places, and was out late on Saturday night. About one or two o'clock on Sunday morning, she was wandering about in Regent's Park- road, and observing a policeman was hastening towards , her, ran away. He ran after her and caught her, and I took her to the Albanv-st. Police Station. She was. subsequently handed ovcir to the parochial authorities, an it was not until then that she told her right name , and address. Her fattier was communicated with on Wednesday night, and he (Mr. Hunt) received a letter from the police authorities, informing him of the eir- cumstances, and that the girl had confessed to stealing £5O at her father's house. He (the Chief (,onstable) for- warded the letter to Mr. Critchley, and he went on Saturday to London and brought her back,and found to his great surprise, that she had only a 14s. Md. cut of the £5O. The girl had told various stori es to account for what had become of the money. In the Workhouse she i said she had the money in a handkerchief n her pocket, and that when she was running away from the police- man she lost it. Every possible inquiry was made by the police in London and Warrington as to the missing money, but without avail. No charge had at first been preferred against her, but on Saturday night the grandmother called at the police station and said from what had transpired durine the week as to the girl's naughtiness, and as things had been missing,some- thing would have to be done with her, and the father having heard such a bad character of her at St. Pancras Workhouse, they were determined to bring the case before the Bench and ask them to do something to put a check upon the girl.—Mr: Critchley had had a letter from one of the authorities in which he said he was amazingly surprised that she had not come to any worse harm than she had done.—Mr. Critchley, who was pre- sent, said he was in such a position that he did not know what to do with the girl.—Alderman Harrison: I think the best place would be to send her to a reformatory.— Mr. Critchley: p i leave tin your bands.--In reply to Alderman Harrison, he said the girl had been going to Wycliffe school. She was uni:nageable at home, and would not work. She had manifested no contrition for her conduct.—Mr. Hunt: You can get very little out of i her. She s very stubborn.—Alderman Harrison: A most extraordinary case.—The deputy magistrates' clerk asked the prisoner whether she had anything to say, but she did not appear to reply, though an officer standing by her said she pleaded guilty.—The Mayor said a girl who would do such extraordinary things ought to be dealt with in some way, because they did not know what she /night not do if left at large. it was a most remarkable thing for a girl like that to go off to London, and come back,then go back to London. It appmred that she could not be sent to a reformatory unless first eentto prison. He asked the father if he would consent to her going to a reformatory.—Mr. Critchley: Oh ves.—ln reply to Alderman Harrison, Mr. Critchley said-he had never seen any !lens of mental derangement in the child, and she was quite as sharp and intelligent as any ordin- ary girl of her age. A woman in court: She is only stupid now: she Is sharp enough.—The girl was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment and ordered to be subsequently sent for five years to a reformatory.

div.p: PROPERTY SALES AT WARRINGTON.

On Wednesday at the Blue Bell Inn, llorsertarket- st., Warrington, Mr. T. Tunstall offered for sale several lots of property in and near IVarrington. Th.:4 first two lots comprised shops and. dwelling- houses 69 and 71 Bridge-st., Warrington, the former being in the occupation of the Anglo-Danish Dairy Company at the yearly rental of £65; and the latter in that of Mr. Geo. Ambrose, at a yearly rent of £45. Both lots were withdrawn, the highest bid for the shop if the Angle-Danish Dairy Company being £l,lOO, and for the other, £BOO. Lot three included four dwelling. houses and coach-house, Nos. 34 and 36, Upper Bank-st., and Nos. 1 and 2, Chrimes-yard. The highest bid for this was £340, and the lot was withdrawn. Fora field of land lying between Howley-lane and the river Mersey, containing about five acres, £5OO was bid, but, this not coming up to the reserve, the lot was not sold. A similar sum—£so0—was the best bid for the next lot which consisted of meadow land and rope walk at Poulton-witit-Fearahead and containing an area of 214 acres, and the property was withdrawn. The last lot offered consisted of two fields situate in Howley, and comprising seven acres,but for this there was no bid. The solicitors for the vendors of the above property were Messrs. Barlett and Atkinson,of Liverpool. On the same day Mr. Tunstall offered for sale 6 cottages fronting Pad- gate-lane, and a garden and croft adjoining, comprising in all la. Or. 354 p. For this piece of property there was a smart competition. It began at £2OO, but it very quickly ran UP to £940, at which sum it was knocked down to Mr. .Tacob Sankey, of Church-st.

LECTURE ON THE "DARKEST ENGLAND" SCHEME. On Monday evening, a deeply interesting lecture was given by Staff Captain Potts, from the head- quarters of the Salvation Army in London, in the Wycliffe Chapel, kindly lent for the occasion, on the present aspect of the "Darkest England" scheme. Mr. C. E. Parker, of Penketh, in the absence of the Rev. J. Yonge, presided, supported by Staff-Captain Potts, and Mr. J. Taylor and Mr. John Bate, local Salvationists. There was a good attendance. The "War Cry was largely sold among the audience. A Salvation Army hymn, with an accompaniment by the Army band, opened the proceedings, and, after prayers, the Chairman delivered an address. Ile expressed his regret that Mr. Yonge was not present, remarking that there was no one in Warrington who had taken such a warm interest in the social movement of the Salvation Army as he had—("God bless him ")—and commenting on the endeavours he had made to induce the Warrington people to support the work.—Staff-Captain Potts in commencing his address explained that Mr. Yonge had consented to preside on condition that he had not to accompany l.is invalid wife to the seaside, which he had since had to do ; and read extracts from a latter from him expressing the deepest sympathy with the movement being carried on by the Salvation Army, and the hope that the audience would respond lilogrally to Mr. Potts's appeal. The Captain then explained more clearly, and at considerable length the progress of the army's scheme for the relief and elevation of the "submerged" masses. It embraced, he said, the establishment of industrial workshops, a labour bureau, for providing situations for those out of employ- ment, a prison gate home for the assistance of discharged prisoners, a farm colony in England, and an over-the- sea colony, to which persons might be sent to get a new start in a now world. Experiments had been mad. In Londou in each department except the last, and desper- ate efforts were being made to commence the like work in the large provincial towns. The institutions were being °paned in Bradford and Leeds, and he Liverpool there would very shortly be shelters and food depots, and a labour bureau provided. It had been determined nisi% to commence the work in Hull. Manchester, and other large towns. General Booth had asked for a million to carry on his work, but not more than £llO,OOO to £115,000 had been collected. and £30.000 per annum was required to carry on the work. There were four food depots in London where, meals were supplied from a farthing upwards to children, and to men breakfast from id. to 3d., dinners for 4d. and tea for 3d., paid for out of the earnings of the indus- trial factories, which range from 9s. to 255. a week. The Captain gave a most encouraging account of the willingness of those relieved to work and their submis- sion to discipline. Out of 4,477 applicants for work 836 had been provided with permanent situations Sweating was altogether discouraged, no one being allowed to go from the labour bureau to work at less than the standard rate of wages—(applause)—and where this had been inadvertently done the men had been withdrawn. A match factory had been established at which 41. per gross of boxes was paid, lit ,er lid. mere than the sweating price. There was every reason to believe that General Booth's most sanguine hopes would be morl than realised by the scheme.—After another hymn and some further remarks by the chairman, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Staff-Captain Potts, on the motion of the Rev. .T. Davies, seconded by Mr. G. Wallington. About £4 4s. was collected in boxes from the audience, and promises were made on slips circulated in the chapel of about 105., £lO per annum being pro- mised by the chairman. The Doxology concluded the most interesting proceedings.

div.head: WARRINGTON WORKING-MEN'S PER. MANENT BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON WORKING-MEN'S PER. MANENT BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY.
ANNUAL MEETING.
The annual general meting of the members of this society was held in Uolborne-st. Schoolroom on Monday evening, the chair being occupied by Mr. John Hatton. There was a fair attendance of mem- bers.

MR SOCIETY'S MAJORITY. The CHAIRMAN remarked that this was one of the most important meetings of the society which had yet been held, namely the 21st. The society had now attained its majority, and if the members read the report, they would see that the year had been a most suace:sful one. He hoped the society would continue to prosper. (Hear, hear.)

THE ANNUM'. RHPOPT The 21st annual reporc or the managers, read by the SNCRUTART (Mr. Peter Dalton), stated that the sum of £2,320 Bs. 11d, had bean rereivel in sub- scriptions during the year, and £1,894 94. 6d. for re-pay- ments, making the total receipts £4,214 is, 5.i The withdrawals during the year amounted to £575 2s and the sum of £3,000 had been advanced to members dur- ing the year. There were 225 subscribers, holding 3261 shares, and 32 borrowers holding 154 shares, making 252 members holding 488 i shares. The profits for the year, I including £26 13s. Bd. from last account, after deduct- ; in" working expenses, amounted to £5BB 2s. 2d. out of which the managers recommended a dividend of 5 per cent., which would take £462 6s. 11d., leaving a balance of £lO5 15s. 3d., which they directed should be dealt with as follows: £5O to be carried to the contingent fund, £5O to the reserve fund, and the remaining £5 15s. 3d. to be carried forward to the next year's accounts. The reserve fund amounted to £450, and the contingent fund to £2OO. Mr. Dalton Also read the balanee sheet.— Mr. EDWARD WALLINGTON, in moving the adoption of the report and statement of accounts, remarked that he theught the members might congratulate themselves iupon the satisfactory report which had been read by the !Secretary. (Hear, hear.) There had been an incense in every desirable item. There had been a large decrease in the withdrawals, of nearly £9OO. That must mean that trade had been better, wages good, and that people had not been obliged to go to the society to withdraw their savings, and it also meant an increase of con- hdence in the society. There had been an increase in the number of members, an increase of 13 in the num- ber of subscribers, and an increase of 17k shares. They had only one borrower more than this time last year, but when they took into consideration the number of members who had paid off, and the increase of one, it meant a total increase of something like six or seven new purchasers this year. There was an increase in the dividend. Last year they paid ill ; this year they pro- posed to pay five. That was a promise made last year if the business of the society was successful. Looking at the report, he thought it was, on the whole, most satisfactory. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Edward Fenton seconded the adoption of the report, which was adopted, after some questions had been asked and answered.

TILE DIVIDEND Mr. ROBERT ISITERWOOD moved that a dividend of five per cent, be paid. He said he had been a member of the .Society for many years, and hi ideas had developed more than he had anticipated they would. There were, many working-men who yet required to be taught how to save, even if it were only a shilling a week. If they would show working-men how simple it was to put a shilling a w they would gain an object. Som. workng-mee:k dibinot think a Society like this was in ex- istence at the present time, but he did not think there, was a manager who had not tried during the past yeas- and every year in fact, to bring as many workiticr-men as possible into the Society. When men had be;un to save they had remarked that they did not think it was so easy .to put a shilling a week, or 52i. a year by (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Joux HAVIOUR seconded the motion, which was carried.

PRESCOT UNION.—APPOINTMENT OF CLERK. 41- The Guardians of the Prescot Union intend at tiheir meeting on the 4th June next to proceed to the election of a Properly qualited person, n.otanore than 45 years of age, to , act as CLERK to the Guardians. Candidates must be prac- tically acquainted with the laws and proceedings relating to ' the administration of the Poor Law Union Assessment Com- mittee Acts, Public Health Acts, and the Elementary Educa- • tion Acs ,and be bully competent to keep the various accounts' in strict accordance with the orders of the Local Government I Board, to examine, check, and be responsible for the accuracy of all stocounts, to prepare all returns required by the Local Government Board and tio Guardians, conduct the official correspondence of the Board and to supervise all the office arrangements. The person elected will hold the offices of Clerk to the Union Assessment Committee, Rural Sanitary Authority, and School Attend- ance Committee and will also receive the appointment of Superintendent Registrar. He will be required to devote the whole of his time to the duties of the several offices and will not be permitted to take any other public position. Salary £3OO per annum out of which sum the necessary office staff must be provided. Other emoluments estimated at 2301 . security to the amount of £5OO to be given. Applications stating age accompanied with copies of testimonials to be addressed to the Chairman of the Board, trnion Offices, Whiston, and sent in by 10 o'clock on Monday, the Ist June next. marked "Clerkship." Canvassing the Guardians will be a disqualification. Selectedcandidates will , have notice to attend on the day of election. By Order, A. F. MANN, Acting Clerk. THERE has been a considerable Sunday Trading. amount of petty persecution in the past under a Statute of Charles the Second which was framed to put down Sunday Trading; and that the Act is in disrepute was confirmed by the action of the magistrates at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday. A butcher named Connolly was summoned for carry- ing on his business on Sunday ; and it transpired in the course of the proceedings thatsornebutchers in Warrington actually go tl:e length of replenish- ing their stock with a view to Sunday trading. Alderman I:IARRisoN frankly said he was not pre- pared to convict in the case before him. Be thought the law should be abrogated ; and refer- red to the fact that "anyone could go into an hotel or public-house, and buy a cigar, drink, and other things that might possibly be done without on a Sunday." It certainly seems odd that the law should in effe et say—" You may buy beer on a Sunday, but you shall not buy beef." The in- consistency is glaring, and it is the reverse of creditably to our law-makers. But what is to be the remedy? Shall we, because publicans are permitted to carry on their business, allow Sunday trading and Sunday working to become 'general? Qr shall we not rather insist that the publicans, like other business men, shall cease their traffic on a Sunday? It seems to us that the latter is the right course to take; for, apart from any question of Sabbatarianism, we hold that it is in the interest of the community, and especially of the workers, that there shall be a relief from toil and trade at least one day in seven. It is no use advocating shorter hours of work during the week if we are to open wide the door to trading on Sunday.

But, touching the legal side of the case, if magis- trates will not convict under the Act of Charles 11 because they think it a bad one, what becomes of that fine old doctrine which has been preached from the Bench a thousand times to the effect that the duty of magistrates is to take the law as it stands —that their business is to administer the law, not to make or to alter it? Are we now under a new dispensation which permits of every magistrate becoming a law unto himself? It is not very encouraging to the police to be told that what they have done is perfectly legal—but they cannot have a conviction. For our own part, we would urge, without wishing to make the Act an instrument of oppression, that the police should persevere in summoning tradesmen who make a practice of Sunday trading. It is not sufficient to plead that some people pay wages late on Saturday night!. Certainly no consideration should be shown to the butchers who replenish their stocks on Sunday; and the police will be undoubtedly neglecting their duty if they tolerate such an objectionable state of things. It is unfair to the butchers who respect themselves and respect the law; and, despite what the Mayor had to say about its being " mean to instigate the police," we should say that a butcher who keeps the law would be doing no more than his duty as a citizen if he galled attention to the fact that another butcher was an habitual breaker

of the law. But tho main consideration is that we have enough of moil and toil without trespas- Sing on Sunday. The world is too much with us; late and soon, Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers. We need Sunday as a day for the repair of wasted powers—a day of rest and re-creation.

THERE has been a good deal of The Primrose boasting of late about the strength League. of the Primrose League on the grouhd that the number of members throughout the country is said to have reached one million. But does this mean that the League really has as many members as there are names on the books? The "Westminster Review" answers this question in the negative; and it affirms that the published report of membership "includes all who have joined in the space of seven years." Taking off Child members, and estimating the loss by death, marriage and" fallen off," the conclusion come to by the" Westminster " is that there is" an actual Personality of less than 140,000." This is certainly an extraordinary "come down," and it is indicative of what is known to be the fact in certain cases, and that is that the League in some towns is little more than the proverbial "local habitation and name" which is "given to airy nothing." Myths often die hard, but the myth that the primrose was Lord BEACONSFIELD'S "favourite flower" seems to have died an easy death. There has been little or nothing heard of it during the recent celebration, from which it may be inferred that a ray of intelligence has at last dawned upon the benighted Leaguers. It is told of the late Cynical leader of the Tory party that a visitor to ilughenden painted out on one occasion that the peacocks were eating the primroses. "Never mind," said the Earl, "I like peacocks better than primroses." Under the circumstances, and seeing that the primrose is played out as "his favourite flower," how would it be if the name of the insti- tution were changed to that of the Peacock League? It would be much more appropriate. Besides emphasising what is known to have been Lord BEACONSFIELD'S predilection, how fittingly a suggestion of the spread tail and showy f eathers harmonises with all we know about the sayings and doings of the Knights and Dames of the League! What if it be said that the pea- cock has no voice to speak of, is there anybody who will venture to assert that the League ever voices anything worth hearing? There is noise and there is display on the part ef the feathered as on the part of the dressed biped; and in both cases the object is to attract attention and gratify vanity. Young people, es- Pecially, delight in watching the proud strut of auno's bird; and with regard to the League does not Mr, RADOLIVFE COOKE, M.P., who is an active Yllernber, tell us that" the young folk join because it affords amusement, and gives them opportunities of meeting which they would otherwise be with- Out ?" There is a pairing season with Leaguers as With birds, for nature orders nothing in vain. We are told that "a fruitful smiree of diminution in members is, strange to say, marriage, for it is the general experience of Primrose Leaguers that great numbers of the spinisters members fall sadly away after that consummation has been affected." But Why "strange ?" When the pairing is complete, there is less need of the fine feathers and "oppor- tunities of meeting." Every little system has its day, and this is the day of the League; but call it—oh, call it the Peacock League—and its name, like that of Crosfield's soap, will be "perfection."
THE House of Commons met on "A N. ational Object." Monday, after the Whitsuntide

recess, and proceeded, on Tues- day, to discuss a motion for adjourning]: until Thursday, because of a horse race. Could anything present our legislators in a more ridiculous light? Mr. CITAPLIN, a member of the Government, actually argued that Derby Day was a national object and a national ad- vantage. From all we have heard of the racing at Epsom, we are convinced that there is more betting and blackguardism—more infamy, in short—on Derby Day, than on any other day of the year. So far from being a national advantage, it would be all the better for the nation if there Were no such carnival as Derby Day. But even if the proceedings at the races were unobjectionable, the question still arises—why should there be a 811apension of the business of the Legislature? Granted that there are members of the House of Commons who can go to Epsom and be no worse for it, it does not follow that it should be specially Patronised by the House as a whole. There arc a score of theatres open every night in the metropo- lis/ and it sometimes happens that there are more 11.P.'s in them than are to be found at St. tephen's ; but folly has not hitherto gone so far as to demand that those who would work, shall tot work, because the majority are idle! Yet there is this to be said for the worst thea- tre, that, as a means 41 recreation, it is ill almost every respect to be preferred to the best Race Meeting. What makes the 463 ourn m ent the more annoying to those fact that legislation as a serious business is the 'act that Wednesday should have been devoted to discussion of the Welsh Veto Bill. Perhaps that Was a reason why the Ministerialists voted for the adjournment. They have temperance often ell°llgh on their lips, but their actions show that their hearts are far from it. When Parliament l ueeomes more democratic, as it will be after the riPt general Election, there will be an end of the "grading idleness resulting from such a motion a 4 'Was adopted on Tuesday n*ht. There ought 4,,, be a weeding out of the House of Commons of 'e fashionable loungers who care mor3 about or,elog than they do about law-making. One way getting rid of them is for working-men to note voted for the adjournment, and take care that these members of Parliament receive EO vote of theirs when they come before them at the next e`eetion.. Men who regard horse-racing as "a ational object " should be afforded the opportun- -It3' of devoting the whole of their time to it.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Mr. John Aitkin is credited with the discovery of how to count the dust particles in the air, and a very pretty revelation we get. The lowest num- ber counted was at Lucerne, and that ran out to 3,500 to the cubic inch. At Glasgow, the ordinary air is said to contain seven million particles per cubic inch. " Prodigious ! " Who can say of any- thing, after this, that "It's not so dusty."

Mr. Stansfield, M.P., who has been interviewed on the subject of poor-law reform refers to the need of abolishing plural votink,„ and adopting the one-man, one vote system, along with the ballot. Elections of Guardians, as at present conducted, are about as bad as bad can be; they are a sur- vival of old-fashioned Toryism, where everything goes to the tune of "Property, property, pro- perty."

The money-grubbers are being looked up ; they are not to have it all their own way in the future as in the past. Mr. Grant Allen says :—" Men should recognise that the way they spend tkeir 'money is a stamp and a symbol which shall mark them after of whose fold they be—Christ's or Satan's, humanity's or the slave-drivers." This is a true saying and worthy of all acceptation. Let rich men ponder it.

Here is a good story told of the late Peter Cooper,of America, who made a pile Of money, and gave the famous Cooper Institute :—" Mr. Cooper, is there such a thing as luck? ", I once asked him. " There is. The greatest piece of luck I ever had was investing the first surplus Money I earned in a lottery ticket." "And you won? " " No, lost ; but I gained this experience, that the wheel of fortune is only turned by common sense applied to common events."

The strike of the Paris 'bus drivers is over; concessions have been made, and the men have returned to work. The agreement provides for the reinstatement of the discharged employes, the recognition of the. union' and the fixing of the working day at twelve hours. Good; but is it wholly good when workers of any kind require to strike to have their hours reduced to twelve per day? They must strike again next year, and got the hours still further reduced.

An article by Mr. Charles Scott in the "Juridical Review" is in the nature of an eye-opener to those who advocate the abolition of capital punishment. Everywhere, he says, where the death penalty has been altogether or almost abolished, murder has increased in an extraordinary degree. In proof of this, he gives statistics as to Belgium, Prussia, and Switzerland. There is no arguing against these hard facts. If life is to be taken in one form or another, it is best apparently to take the lives of the assassins.

The prevalence of influenza has naturally given rise to the question as to whether the malady is infectious. Some medical men have restored con- fidence—misplaced confidence, it would seem—by denying the infectious character of the disease. A question on the subject was put in the House of COmmons, on Tuesday. Mr. Ritchie, in reply, stated, that he was advised influenza was an in- fectious disease and therefore came under the previsions of the Act dealing with infectious dis- eases. This ought to be sufficient to cause peaple, at any rate, not to incur unnecessary risk...

"If at first you don't succeed, try, try again." This seems to be the motto upon which the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer is acting in the matter of the new coinage, for artists are being invited to send in designs. The double florin finds no favour, and presumably it will be withdrawn. It is cer- tainly confusing, differing so little in size, as it does, from the five shilling-piece. It would be a great improvement if -every coin had its value clearly indicated, as is the case with the shilling. Why should busy people have to hesitate for even a moment in determining whether a coin is a half- crown or a florin ?

The Tories are sorry they spoke on the question of Free Education. As the bye-elections show, it isn't the trump card they expected it would be. They feel as if they had signed a promissory note, and were getting nothing for it. They are like Simple Simon when he sought to get honey out of the mustard pot, for we are told that— He bit his tougue until he cried And that was all he got.

Then there is the inconsistency to be faced of adopting a proposal which they have previously denounced. Ohallenged on this point, Sir Wm. Hart-Dyke tries to get out of the tight place in which he found himself by saying the Free Educa- tion which he denounced was that of the "authorised Radical programme." This is hard, very hard, upon Mr. Chamberlain. The Tories have stolen a plank from his platform; and now when they are caught in the act they would seek to make it appear that the timber they are using is of a totally different kind !

Speaking at Padgate on Thursday evening, Mr. T. W. Legb, M.P., showed himself to be, like the rest of his party, in an unhappy frame of mind on the subject of Free Education. They had, he said, "little idea as to what the measure was," and yet" the object igif the Conservative party was precisely the reT7n-se " of that of " the advanced Liberals ! This is the thin sort of stuff that is served out at Habitations of the Primrose League. However, we can forgive Mr. Legh, for he stumb- led on the truth when he said—" Whatever the measure was, it would be represented by their opponents as a bribe to the agricultural commun- ity." Just so.; and, because the fish doesn't rise to the bait, the Tory fisherman sets his teeth wrathfully and makes remarks.

Mr. F. A. Burr, writing in an American maga- zine has a good word to say for the Prince of Wales, describing him, in fact, as "the ideal representative of his people." This is suggestive of what Tennyson said of the Prince Consort : And indeed he seems to me Scarce other than my own ideal Knight, Who reverenced his conscience as his king; Whose glory was redressing human wrong; Who spoke no slander, no, nor listened to it ; Who loved one only and who clove to her. H.R.H. is not quite the "ideal Knight" ; but he improves with age—despite baccarat and racing— and everybody is glad to see it.

At the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture, en Monday, Mr. Roger Bate read an interesting paper oa "Farm Labourers and Domestic Service." Mr. Thomas Finchett disputed the statement that labourers were leaving the country to live in towns; but what of that? It simply means that he is ignorant of a notorious fact—a fact confirmed by the recent census returns. The Chamber as a whole took a more intelligent view of the situation as was shown by the adoption of the following motion 1—" That in the opinion of this Cham- ber a better supply of cottages with land attached, sufficient to keep a cow, would tend to improve the condition of the agricultural labourer, and would further tend to attach the rising generation to the land, and thus benefit farmers by increasing the number of capable farm servants."

Who could believe it that in Boston U. S. A., "the hub of the Universe," a respectable citizen and his wife would be arrested for kissing in the street? "It seems the couple have not long been married, and, happening to meet in the street after a few days' separation, they could not help saluting each other with a kiss. By this act they brought themselves amenable under one of the old Puritan Blue Laws, which have never been re- pealed." Ali, those Puritans, they didn't always know what was good for themselves. Their ordin- ance as to kissing should have died with them. It had too much of "the vale of tears" in it. It wasn't a Puritan—it was Lady Mary Wortley Montague—who wrote— Be plain in dress, and sober in your diet; In short my deary ! Kiss me and be quiet.

At the Southwark Police Court,on Thursday afternoon, Franz Joseph Much, 31, a baker, was committed for trial on the charge of having wilfully murdered Jas.Hickey,a native of Manchester, by shooting him on the morning of 23rd of April. The prisoner pleaded not guilty.

At Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, Isaac Johnson, was sentenced to seven days' hard labour for begging from P.C. Worth while on duty in plain clothes. . _

The members of this club, which is connected with Brunswick Wesleyan Improvement Class, opened their second season on Saturday afternoon, when about 6C) paid a visit to the grounds of Foxhill, the residence of Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., at Frodsham. Although the weather was very showery, a pleasant afternoon was spent in the sylvan spot. Tea was provided at the Fox- hill Farm of Mr. Eaton.

div.head: FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS AT WIDNES.
div.p: FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS AT WIDNES.

The deputy coroner, Mr. W. T. Husband on Monday, held an inquest at Widnes Police Court on the body of Edward Sweeney, a stone breaker, aged 55 years, who had lived at 6, Victoria-st. On the afternoon of the 18th inst. the deceased was found lying at the bottom of the stairs unable to move. He said he had fallen down five steps. He was attended by Dr. Hudson until his death oti the 22nd. The deceased walked with a crutch, hav- ing had his left leg amputated, and on the day of the accident he had had some drink.—A verdict of "Acci- dental death" was returned. SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at j. it. W. DUTTON' Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. ROBBING A WIDNES PAWNBROKER.

Mary Dukes, of 86, Church-st., Farnworth, was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Monday charged with having stolen a quantity of wearing apparel from the shop of Mr. G. I. Neil, pawnbroker, Widnes-road, at different times between the let October, 1890, and May 20th of the present year. The articles stolen were live pairs of trousers, four vests, one dress bodice, and one cardigan jacket. It was ascertained that the whole of the articles had been pawned by the prisoner at Mr. Neil's shop in Ann-st. She was sen- tenced to two momths'.hard labour.
LAWN MOWERS.—Gariand, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington. and at Barlestown.—Advt.
ASSAULT ON A GIRL AT WIDNES.

A notorious youth, named Richard Tonkics, who lives in Wright-st., was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of having indecently assaulted Catherine M‘Nicholson, 16 years of age, of 30, Cromwell-st. On Tuesday morning the girl and a com- panion were picking cinders in the yard of Messrs. Mort, Liddell, and Co.'s works when the prisoner cams up, and after pretending to pick cinders for some time, he caught hold of M‘Nicholson's companion. She, however. escaped from his grasp, and the prisoner then seized M‘Nicholson and made the attempt with which he was charged. The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. ST. JOHN'S AIIBULANCI ASSOCIATION RUNCORN

div.head: CANTRE.
div.p: CANTRE.

The following members have successfully passed the second examination in connection with the above asso- ciation : —Superintendent Large, Inspector Bowyer, Constables Bullock, Brew, and Crowder, and Messrs. Clare, Collier, Garrett. Pierpoint, and Woolley. Sergeant Costello, of Sutton Weaver, successfully passed the final examination, and is consequently entitled to the medal of the association. One of the stipulations for re-exam- ination is that twelve months shall have elapsed since the previous examination. In order to be better pre- pared for any emergency that may arise the certificate holders have decided to have a monthly practice in St. John's Schoolroom. Several of the members have already been able to turn their knowledge to a practical account. The Ladies' Classes continue to be well attended, the average weekly attendance being about 75.

div.head: AID TO WIDOWS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: AID TO WIDOWS AT RUNCORN.

With the object of increasing the fund that is being raised for the widows and families of 'Messrs. George Weedall, James Johnson, and Henry Ankers, the Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa Choir on Wednesday evening gave a concert in the Public Hall. There was a crowded attendance, and a goal' sum would be realised. The first part of the programme coßsisted of a performance of Pattison's can- tata " Sherwood's Queen," in which:the choir rendered the chorus in admirable style. The soloists were Mrs. Leathwood, Miss Heatherington, and Miss Ainsworth, Messrs. E. Worrall, J. Leathwood, J. Weedall, M.Thomas C. Leathweod, and A. Shingler,and they acquitted them- selves with credit. In the second part the choir sang a number of national airs, and songs were given by several members of the choir. The entertainment was of a most enjoyable character, and at the close cordial votes of thanks were accorded to Mr. J. Raiford, G.T.S.C. the conductor; to Mr. C. C. Le Conteur, the accompanist, and to the choir.

div.head: WILFULLV WOUNDING AT WIDNES.
div.p: WILFULLV WOUNDING AT WIDNES.

Before Colonel Gaskell, at Widnes Petty Session, on Thursday, Thomas Costello, was charged with unlaw- fully wounding Wm. McDonnell. The men lodged to- gether at 3,Nelson-st., and on the night of the 26th inst., they had a dispute in the kitchen. They commenced to fight, and in the struggle they both fell to the ground. Win. Roach, the teaant of the house, put them asunder, but a few minutes later the fight re-commenced, and in the scuffle the lamp was knocked off the mantlepiece,and the place was in darkness. Roach was hit on the breast with a heavy instrument. When Mrs. Roach had pro- cured a light McDonnell was lying on the floor in a pool of blood.and the prisoner was standing with a bar of iron in his hand. McDonnell was taken to Dr. Hutchinson's surgery,where he was found to be suffering from a severe contused wound on the forehead. Be was not in a fit condition to appear in court.—Superintendent Noblett said the prisoner had suffered considerable ill-treatment and if he were remanded fora week it would be of ser- vice to him as he could have the attention of the prison surgeon.—The prisoner was remanded.
WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

A monthly meeting of this loody was held on Wednes- day afternoon, at the Widnes Town Hall, Mr. F. H. Park- hurst presiding.—The snrveyor to the local board (Mr. Sinclair) submitted for the inspection of the members a plan of a temporary reading room for boys that it is proposed to erect at an early date, at an estimated cost of £80„ The dimensions of the room will be 17ft. by 221 t., and extra accommodation will be afforded for about 60 boys. The plan was approved.—The faurth annual report of the committee, copies of which were handed to the members, stated that the library and read- ing room had been open 306 days. The total number of attendances had been 150,175, giving a daily average attendance of 490, being a decrease on the previous year of 21 per day. To the library 566 volumes had been added during the year, making a total of 4,512 books now in the library. There had. been 52,268 books issued for home reading; 1,221 had been consulted in the reading room, making a daily average issue of 175. The total number of borrowers now on the register were 2,525. &imams P.m:from now Showing at J. & W. DurroN's, Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt.

MR,. BRUNNER, M.P., AND • TECHNICAL EDUCATION. . On Tuesday evening a letter was read at a meet- ing of the North wich Local Board from Mr. Brunner M.P., in which he states that by levying a rate of id. in the under the Technical Instruction Act, the Board has practically secured for the town the handsome endowment of another id. in the .0 from the County Council, and a grant which way amount to half that sum from the department of Science and Art. He advised that the Board should haven school of their own, in which children, after pass- ing through the elementary schools, will be thoroughly fitted for the duties of life, lie confirms with cordial pleasure. the offer he made some time ago to subscribe £5OO towards the building, and ex- presses the conviction that an appeal to the rate- payers in the same direction will meet with a hand- some response.

RAILWAY.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

Several cases of influenza are prevalent in the parish,but no deaths from the epidemic have occur- red up to the present time. The Schools.—The Board School and St. Lewis's Roman Catholic School, Croft, were reopened on Monday morning for scholastic duties, after the Whitsuntide holi- days. THE NEW HIGH SHERIFF. _ _ _

The office Of High Sheriff of the County Palatine of Lancaster, vacant through the death of Mr. G. T. R. Preston, Elle! Gransze, near Lancaster, has been offered to and accepted by Colonel W. 11. Fos- ter, of Hornby Castle, near Lancaster, and of Queensbury, near Bradford. Colonel Foster is son of the late Mr. William Foster, of Hornby Castle, who was High Sheriff of Lancaster in 1881.

div.head: SMOKING IN A COAL MINE.
div.p: SMOKING IN A COAL MINE.

On Monda—y-,-at the St. Helens Police Court, John Boardman, a collier, of Oldfield-st., was summoned by the White Cross Colliery Company, for having a pipe in his possession in Sherdley Colliery. Mr. J. 0. Swift, who prosecUted, stated that on the morn- ing of the 13th inst, the fireman, named Owen, was going his round down the mine, when he found the defendant smoking. It was a mine in which safety lamps were used, and the lamps were required to to be kept locked, but the defendant had, by some *means, got his limp unlocked. Defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined 10s. and Costs. SUMMER FA.SHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-et.. Warrington.—Advt. FATAL FALL AT ST. HELENS.

On Wednesday forenoon, William Kay, 55 years of age, a stonemason, of 14, Nebo-street, We.vertree was killed at St. Helens. The deceased man was in the employ of Mr. P. Rigby, a contractor, and was on Wedi.esday engaged in repairing a condenser at Ai`Bryde's Works. belonging to the United Alkali Company. He was standing on a scaffold about 14ft. from the ground, when he fell backwards and dropped to the floor. He alighted on his head and fractured his skull, death being instantaneous. The body was removed to the mortuary to await the inquest. The deceased man leaves a widow and several children.

div.head: MINERS' CONFERENCE.
div.p: MINERS' CONFERENCE.

Mr. Pickard, M.P., presided on VV ednesday at the Conference of the Miners' Federation of Great Britain, at Chester. Speaking of the Belgian miners' strike for the revision of Constitution,by which miners over twenty-one would have a vote, he said they had had no appeal for aid from them or official communication that. there was a strike. If such a communication had been reached by the Federation the Council would have sent them £5OO. The Labour Commission was intended to set up a great State arbitration board, to which questions affecting labour would be referred, but the real object of the Commission was to shelve burning questions.

div.head: WEATHER. AND CYCLING.
div.p: THE WEATHER. AND CYCLING.

The inclement weather played havoc with the fixtures of the local cycling clubs on Saturday. The- Roby Harriers Cycling Club had planned a cycle run to Warrington. but owing to the weather it was not carried out. The Si. Helens Recreation Cycle Club had been looking forward to a 45 miles spin to Knutsferd, via Warrington and back but they contented themselves with getting as far as Warrington. For many years past it has been the custom of the St. Helens Cyclist Club to carry out an official run to Warrington at the beginning of the season, but owing to the stormy weather which was.exnerienced this Easter the fixture was abau- doneAlor a time. It has now been arranged for the members to carry out the run on Thursday, June 4th. SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at 3. W. DUTTON'S Sankev-st., Warrington.—Advt. NEW RAILWAY STATION NEAR. ST. HELENS. On Tuesday, Colonel Rich, R.E., one of the Board of Trade inspectors, made his official inspection of the new Eccleston Park Station, between Prescot and Thatto Heath btations, on the London and North-Western line. The residents of the Eccleston Park locality had agitated for the erection of a station for some years, and the compliance with their wiblies will prove a great convenience. The work has oeen carried out by Messrs. Robert Neill and Sons, of Manchester, and the estimated expen- diture is about .V.t,000. Mr. Wm. Gibbon, late of Hindley Green, has been appointed stationmaster; and,as the Inspector found all the arrangements of a satisfactory character, the station will be opened next Monday. .
CANON DICIGLE OPPOSES FREE EDUCATION.

Canon Diggle, presiding on Wednesday over a conference of the rural deaneries of Child wall and Prescot in regard to Church schools and assisted education, said that five years ago every member of the Conservative party spoke adversely of the system of free education, and yet now they pro- posed the very thing which they then condemned. Hestia adhered to his former opinion that free education was a mistake. Mr. J. N. Stolterfoht, in the course of a paper, said his experience, both as school manager and member of a semol attendance committee, was that the children paid for were, as a rule, the most irregular and the most frequently the cause of their parents being summoned before the magistrates. The Iv. It. F. French also read a paper on the subject. BMIGRITION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canapla, China, Japan. 'Warrinaton.—Adut. • • A CHESHIRE _FARMER FINED FOR THEFT:.

AtTd—di—s-bury (Cheshire) Petty Sessions, on Mon- day, Joseph Lanceley, farmer and coal agent, of Barrow, Cheshire, was charged with stealing three spruce deal boards, valued at 35., from a wagon at the Barrow Railway 'Station of the Cheshire Lines Railway Company. Defendant was seen on the imgon, and the boards were subsequently found secreted in the railway warehouse and marked. Later on they were found in defendant's possession. The boards were consigned to the Marquis of Chol- mondeley. Defendant admitted taking the boards, but said, in defence, that he was a tenant on the Cholmondeley estate, and had a fence which wanted repairing badly. He thought if he applied to the agent there would be some delay, and he conse- quently felt that there would be no harm in taking the boards and repairing the fence himself. The Bench said they thought the justice of the case would be met by inflicting a fine of .E 5 and costs. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire—GARLAND. Warrington. —Advt. _

StrxmEa FASHIONS now Showing at 1. W. Durrox's Sankey-st., Warrington.—At. TRADES UNIONISM. Under the auspices of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union a public meeting was held on the Market place, St. Helens, on Sunday afternoon. Mr. P. Mainley presided, and was supported by Mr. W. S. de Mattos, of London; Mr. P. J. King, president of the union; and others. There was a large attendance of working-men.—Mr. MaVos I spoke at at considerable length on trades unionism and its future prospects. He remarked that the labourers of the 14th, 15th, and early part of the 16th centuries were better off than labourers to-flay, because they were associated together in Olds which protected the interests and guarded the rights of labour. He referred to the changes which had taken place in labour organisations since that Period, and said that modern trades unionism was only legal from the year 1824, and it was for many subsequent years hampered by obstructive legisla- tion. The essential objects of trades unions were higher wages, shorter hours, and improved condi- tions, and the labour movement in London had spread throughout the proyinces and the civilised world. He urged all working-men to band them- selves together in the cause of labour, and they would be able to secure the rights and privileges that were now denied to them. (Applause.) Mr. King afterwards gave an address.'
