It will be noticed from an advertisement t hat the entries for these sports close on the 6th June. The sports will take place on the evening of Friday, Jnne 12th, and on Saturday,June 13th, and as usual valuable prizes are offered to competitors, the prize money amounting to nearly £2OO.

div.head: PARAFFIN LIMP FATALITY AT CIIESTRIL
div.p: PARAFFIN LIMP FATALITY AT CIIESTRIL

On Monday morning, a young woman named Martha Roberts, residing in Cambrian-road, off Garden-lane, Chester, died in the Chester Infirmary through burns. It appears that on Sunday a paraffin lamp exploded in her residence, the flames setting her clothing on fire. She sustained dreadful injuries, and was conveyed to the Infirmary on an ambulance.

div.head: WIDNES FOOIBALL CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES FOOIBALL CLUB.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the members of Widnes Football Club was held on Thursday evening in the Hall of Widnes Conservative Club: In the absence of Mr. 11. Wade Deacon, J.P., the president, Mr. W. Ireland was voted to the chair. There was a good attendance. The report the Secretary was pre- sented and stated that durin* the past season the first team had played 31 matches, of which 13 were won, 5 drawn, and 13 lost. They had scored 13 goals, 25 tries, 72 Minors to their opponents' 15 goals, 28 tries, and 98 minors. Peters had scored 6 tries, Barber 5, Whelan, Holt, and Laws 4 each, Evans, Hartles, and Stubbs 2 each, and Brennan, Farmer, Gordon, and Harrison, one each. Barber and Drummond each dropped 2 goals, and Morris kicked a goal from a free kick, The " A "team haTplayed 19 matches, won 7, drawn 5, and lost 7. They had scored 8 goals,, 15 tries, 54 minor., against their opponents's goals, 17 tries, 35 minors. Craig, Burgess, and Holt each scored three tries, .Rushton and Tonkies two each, and Mullinger, Morris, Harrison,Min- ton, Foster, Wright,Taylor, Wade and McGurl one each. —Mr. J. Ashall, the treasurer, prosented the financial statement, which showed that the receipts amounted to £376 Bs. sid., and included £272 17s. 7d., gate money at Ist team matches, 17 16s. members' subscriptions, and £2l 19s. 6d. gate money at "A " team matches. The expenditure amounted to £4Ol 17s. 4d. The chief items were railway and hotel expenses (Ist and "A " 'teams) £96 6s. 9d. ; teas and refreshment, £5B is. 7d. ; suits for players, £4l us. sd. ; printing and posting, £36 es. Bd. • field and ground expenses, -£3O ss. 11d. ; insurance of players £2B. There was a deficit of £25 Bs. Md. Last year dr. Ashall informed the meeting the adverse balance was £26 2s. 11d., so that there had been a small profit on last season. Owing to the bad weather, five home matches had to be abandoned, caus- ing great loss to the club.—On the proposition of Mr. H. A. Richards, seconded by Mr. E. Willing, the report and balance sheet was adopted.—Mr. H. Wade Deacon was re-elected presiient, and the list of vice-presidents was passed without alteration. For the position of cap- tain of Ist team, D. Brennan and W. Evans were nomi- nated, and the former was elected by 54 vote's to 20. The voting for the position of sub-captain was as fol- lows :—H. Peters, 32 ; E. Gordon. 20 ; J. Drummond, 19 ;W. Evans, 4. W. Wolfinger was appointed captain of the second team by 47 votes to 30 recorded for G. Wright, who was elected sub-captain. Mr. J. Ashall was re-appointed treasurer, Mr. J. H. Smith, lion. sec.. Mr. F. Younge, secretary. The committee was consti- tuted as follows :—Messrs. J. A. Brown, A. Critchlev, J. E. Farrell, T. Fogg, C. Hemingway, A. Hutton, J. -J. Latham, T. Laws, and H.Rose. The salary of the secre- tary was increased from £7 10s. to £lO, on the motion of Mr. J. H. Smith, seconded by Mr. T. Laws. The ques- tion of the club colours was left to the committee. The usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

div.head: RUNCORN COTTAGE HOSPITAL.
div.p: RUNCORN COTTAGE HOSPITAL.
. THE SCAIESIE APPROVED.

A meeting of the General Committee of the Run- corn Cottage Hospital was held in the Town Hall on Monday evening to receive and consider the report of the sub-committee appointed Zo formulate a scheme. Mr. S. Tiylor presided, and there were present Messrs. P. Speakman,C.C., G. Bellamy, F. A. Lake, J. R. Frith, Jas. Frith, B. Kniveton, Captain, La Couteur, F. J. Norman, W. Shaw (missionary), W. Mellor, A. Jordan, E. Marwood, E. Imisou, E. Wynne Humphreys, E. Marshall, A. Salkeld, J. Johnson, Jas. Littler, H. White, R. H. Posnett, J. K. Digges, E. Kay, Leffler, &c. After the minutes of the last meeting had been read and passed the report of the sub-committee was presented and read as follows :

ht.—That a hospital be established to be called the Runcorn Cottage Hospital. 2nd.—That such hospital shall be under the control of the subscribers, who shall have one vote for each ss. subscribed annually (but no subscriber shall have more than 20 votes). 3rd.—That Sir Richard Brooke shall be invited to be-President of the Hospital, that all subscribers to the Hospital of £2 2s. or more annually shall be Vice-Presidents. 4th.—That the Subscribers shall at their first meeting elect a Manage- ment Committee of 12 gentlemen, being themselves sub- scribers, four of whom shall retire at the end of the first year, four at the end of the second year, and four at th e end of the third year; the order of retiring to be decided by ballot, but the retiring members to be eligible for re- election. sth. —That when any Church,Chapel, Friendly Society, or Association, or Collector shall contribute to the Funds iaf the Hospital a sum of £5 55., or more than £5 5i., or a sum of ss. or more than 55., the person through whom that pay,- , merit is made, shall for the current year be a Vice-Pre- sident, or subscriber respectively, in the same manner as if he had contributed the sum himself. 6th.—All resident Medical men, invited by the Committee and giving their services to the Hospital, shall be Hon. Members of the Committee, and possess 4 votes as ordinary Subscribers. 7th.—The Clergy and Ministers of the town shall have access to any patient desiring to see them, at such rea- sonable times and on such occasions as the Management Committee shall approve. B:h.—Each patient may ba attended by his own medical man. 9th.---A Committee of six shall be appointed to obtain donations and sub- scriptions. 10th.—In the opinion of your Committee it would be desirable to rent a house capable of containing 6 or 8 beds,to engage a Matron and Servant,and to set the Hospital in operation at the earliest possible date. 11th. That in the event of sufficient public support being ob- tained or promised, the Managing Committee shall cause plans to be prepared and recommend a site for a per- manent Institution.

SEIOOESTIONS.-I.—Your Committee have considered the suitability of various houses, but they are of opinion that no place combines so many obvious advantages as Highfield House, the property of the Runcorn Gas Com- pany, which is shortly to be vacant. 2.—They believe that such a house might be furnished for £l5O, and they estimate the annual expenditure at from £l5O to £2OO. 3.—Anxisstort OF PATlENTS.—Accidents to be admitted at once. Medical or surgical cases, (other than accidents), only upon the recommendation of a subscriber. Patients to pay not less than 59. a week at the discretion of the Committee of Management. A subscriber to have a recommehdation for each ss. 4.—The Management Com- mittee is recommended to make special terms with large employers et labour for the admission of accident cases. —Mr. Imison moved the adoption of the report; and, referring to the second clause, said there was a very strong feeling that the voting power should be in accord • ance with the political practice—the ideal political prac- tice—of one man one vote. The Committee considered there was a distinct difference between voluntary pay- ments and payments in discharge of legal obligations. If they offered large subscribers what some people might consider an undue amount of control, they might by that means get larger subscriptions, and the maintenance of the Hospital would require not only pennies but as many pounds as they possibly could get hold of. Although it might be urged that the poor man had as great an interest in the hospital as the rich man, yet it must be borne in mind that it was an institution purely for the advantage and benefit of the poor man, and if a rich man gave his pound he might reasonably consiler that he should have a greater voice in the management. After dealing with other clauses, Mr. Imison came to No. 9, which he said was the most important In the whole scheme. It was useless to attempt to hide the fact that they had come to a critical point in the history of the Cottage Hospital. Quite .in- advertently they had given the public the impression that an attempt was being made to get the affair into the hands of one denomination, so that he thought the Com- mittee would act wisely if it took care to have the greatest possible safeguard against anything of that kind, because that was the rock upon which the scheme would split. (Hear, hear.) He pointed out that if, according to clause ten, they made a start at once, people would subscribe more willingly. The Committee had considered the desirability of several houses, and he described the advantage of Highfield House. These were, however, details for a committee to I decide. In conclusion, he said he felt most firmly that if they let byegone3 be btegones, and made a vigorous effort, the success of the Hospital was assured ; and, on the other hand,if they allowed denominational influences td prevail, he felt convinced they would postpoe.e the es- tablishment of the Hospital to an indefinite period, and they would merely repeat the fiasco of 1887,7-Mr. W. Mellor seconded the motion, and said the committee had attempted to make the4sctieme as broad as possible.—On the proposition of Mr.Speakin a n ,seconded by Mr. Hum ph- reys,it was resolved to discuss the report clause by clause. There was added to the first clause "for the treatment. of non-infectious and accident cases: cases of long duratioa. shall not be within • the scope of the institution." Con- siderable discussion took place on clause 2, and ulti- mately it was decided that no subscriber should have more than ten votea.—As an adaition to clause 4, Mr. , Lake proposed" that with a view to avoid anything of a

sectarian character, it is deemed advisable not to have clergymen of any denomination upon the committee of this ir.stitution."—Mr. Bellamy seconded the motion. —Mr. Johnson: If anyone is fit to be on the committee, it is the clergymen in the different denominations.—Mr. Key said the parsons ought to be on.—Mr. Speakman said the Committee of such an in- stitution was the place for the different ministers pro- perly salected.—Captain Le Couteur : They may refuse to have a hospital Sunday.—Mr. Norman pointed out that they could not put every clergyman upon the Ccm- , mittee, and umbrage would certainly be caused if they were to make any distinction at all, and, he would be a shallow-minded minister who felt that any slight had been put upon him when he un lerstood the reason. Once the sectarian spirit crept in the whole thing went to smash.—Mr. Lake said whether they were Churchman or Chapelmen, it was unfortunately the fact that they could not get clerics to work together. There were cer. tam n questions of precedence, right orders, and wrong orders, and the end was always disorder. They had bet- ter keep them if the Committee. Whatever religious sect they as laymen belonged to they could work together.—Mr. Imison said there was. distinct advant- age in having laymen as the Committee of Manage- ment ,hut they might lose something in the way of col- lections. They were looking forward to receive a large sum from hcispital Sunday collections.—Mr. Hump- hreys said in the best interests of the hospital he sup- ported Mr. Like. As to the collections tile only people this motion could effect were the:church people. The ques- tion whether there should be hospital Sunday collections or not did not depend upon the ministers but upon the laymen of Nonconformist places of worship, and he did .not think this motion would affect the church.—Mr. Lake said at Ulverston the fact that clergymen were nof permitted on the committee did not affect the col- lections.—The Chairman said unless they were prepared to admit overyclerg.yman in the town they were sure to have friction.—Mr. Jordan stronglynpposed the motion. —Mr. Lake's motion was carried by 15 votes to 12. Clause 6 was altered to read that medical men should be ex-ojicio members of the Committee but should not possess votes as subscribers. The Com- mittee to obtain donations and subscriptions was em- powered to take the necessary preliminary steps. This Committee was constituted as follows :—Messrs. Taylor, Lake, Speakman, unison, Frith, Thos. Riley, and F. W. Nerman.—Mr. Norman said this scheme would commend • itself to everybody that he knew, and they would get his support whether he was on the Committee or not.—Mr. lmison was glad to hear the way Mr. Norman had spoken of the scheme. It was very encouraging, and even an augury of its success.—After some further details had been dealt with, the meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.
A VICTIIf TO DUTY AT RUNCORN.

Yesterday, at Runcorn Burial Boardroom, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest on the body of a sailor, 18 years of age, named John Lup- ton, who was found drowned in Fenton Dock, on Wednesday night. On the 16th inst., Hugh Doran, captain of the schooner Western Maid, of Peel, Isle of Man,reported to the police that Lupton was mis- sing. He said on the previous evening Lup- ton went into a boat to learn to scull, and he bad not been seen since. The boat was afterwards found and the oar was inside it. The description given by the captain was as fol- lows :—Height 5 feet, hair aark brown, stout build, age 18 years; dressed in a cotton shirt, brown checked tweed trousers, black cloth vest, silver ring on one of his fingers and brass one on another, low shoes. P.S. Crowder said the body found fulfilled this description, and no doubt it was that of the missing man. The captain said he had been a tailor at Radford in Yorkshire, and had run away to join the ship. He was very anxious to learn his duties as a sailor, and that was the reason he went out to scull.—P.C. Pettinger deposed to recovering the body from the dock. There was 16s. 6d. in his pockets, two purses, and four tickets.—A verdict of "Found dead "was returned.

div.head: NEW MAGISTRATES.
div.p: THE NEW MAGISTRATES.

It is now stated that Mr. John Geddes will acccept the position which has been offered him of Justice of the Peace for the borough of Warrington He is one of the three Liberals who were reported last week to have declined the honour; but it would seem that the misconception as to his alleged refusal arose through his not having replied to the official communication from the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancashire.

div.head: WARRINGTON LIBERAL BAZAAR.
div.p: WARRINGTON LIBERAL BAZAAR.

Mr. J. C. J. llolmes, hon. sec. of the Liberal Bazaar Committee is in communication with vari- ous leading Liberals throughout the country with a view to securing their patronage for the forth- homing bazaar, and so far his applications have been very successful. Mr. T. B. Potter, is giving his patronage; he also adds that he should be pleased on behalf of the Cobden Club Committee to furnish the bazaar with £2O worth of books, the publica- tions of the Cobden Club. This is a gift which will be the means of bringingin money, and at the same time disseminating knowledge amongst the electors of the town. - .

The decorating and arranging of the bazaar stalls has been placed in the hands of Mr. G. M. Bridges, of Kings Lynn, who has a high repute as a bazaar artist. The plan adopted is that which is known as a "Grand Ice Carnival," and the Public Hall will be specially fitted up, to represent this highly picturesque scene. A description of the Carnival, has been furnished us, as follows: " On entering the hall, the visitor at once finds himself in a novel and enchanting scene. On each side of the hall are picturesque buildings representing the homes of England, Norway, Switzerland, Russia, Siberia, Germany, and Canada. At the east end of the hall is a splendid representa- tion of one of the famous ice palaces of Montreal On the platform is portrayed the mighty St. Lawrence and its numerous islands,rapids, and cat- aracts, with a background of lofty mountains tipped with snow, their sides covered with vast pine forests. The whole is a grand and realistic picture of mid-winter, the snow and ice sparkling in every view." There is every reason to believe from the work which is in progress that there will be ample material for the various stalls, as the Ladies' Com- mittee are alike industrious and enthusiastic in promoting the objects of the bazaar.

FORTHCOMING LABOUR DEMONSTRA- TION AT WARRINGTON. The preparations for a great labour demonstration which is to be held in Warrington on Saturday the 13th June, are now well-nigh complete. The demon- stration is being promoted by the Warrington Trades Council and will be taken part in by about twenty societies. The arrangements are for a gathering to take place on the vacant ground near Holy Trinity Schools, and from here, about half- past two in the afternoon, the procession will ! begin. After parading the principal streets of ' the town, the processionists will return to the same place, where an open-sir meeting will be held, if the weather be fine, but if not the Theatre in Sankey-St. will be the meeting place. The meeting will be presided over by Mr. Malkin, a member of the local Trades Council, and the principal speakers will be Mr. John Wilson, M.P., Mr. W. blatkin, of Liverpool (chairman of the Trades Union Congress held in Liverpool last year), and Mr. John Jenkins, of the Manchester and Salford Trades Council. Efforts have been made to secure as speakers at the demonstration, Mr. John Burns, Mr. Tom Mann, and other prominent labour leaders, but these popular speakers have been prevented from attending by press- ing engagements. It should be added that there will be a good deal of the scenic element about the demon- stration. Several bands will be engaged, many banners will be displayed, and, in additimt to this, some of the trades will exhibit some of tke machinery or processes of their respective handicrafts. The final Arrangements as to the order of procession and other details will be made at a meetinc, this evening. It may be mentioned that the Warrington Trades Council now represents about 1,400 members.. There has lately been a rapid increase of membership, as may be gathered from the fact that within twelve months ago there were not more than 700 members.

The main resolution to be proposed at the meeting 'will read as follows :—" That this public meeting of Warrington workingmen rejoices to know that in many townsand places fair wage clauses are being inserted in the public contracts, and respectfully re- quests the Warrington Corporation to insert fair wage clauses in their contracts, the same clauses to apply to all contracts which may be sub-let,and as far as practicable, to give such contracts to Warring- ton persons, firms, and Companies; and also desire the Corporation to consider this important subject as soon as possible, so that clauses may be inserted in the public contracts, which will be one great step towards abolish- ing that cruel evil known as the sweating system." A second resolution is in. the following terms: " That this meeting agrees to make the fair wage contract clauses the test question at al municipal elections, d pledges itself to support only those candidates who are prepared tin to vote for this measure being returned to the Town Council."
THE INFLUENZA AT ITAYDOCK .—Dr.ilay ward, the medi- cal officer of health for flavdock, is conflued to his bed, suffering from influenza.

div.head: "HIS YED WUR TUCHT A BIT !"
div.p: "HIS YED WUR TUCHT A BIT !"

A SUNG. Eaur Rodger wur as nice a lad As ever stept shoon ; He wur a fine musicianer, An' invented mouy a tune. 'Tw'uz only upo' polliticks seemt to loze his wit; His brains went avr wool-getherln', For his yod wur tucht a bit. lfi feyther made him, like hissel,
A gatter to his trade; An aw the "tiles " abeawt eaur tea,

Wur wot eaur Roger made. Aw th' swells coom rewlin' to eaur shop, He're such a fost-rate fit; AD' ev'ry one wuz sorry that His yed wur tucht a bit. He wur a Tory; hot an' strung, An' woc a lot that means! It seems to smack o' pigs an' poork, An' pratoes, beef an' green/. He wee a fossil, true and blue,
An' no ameaunt o' skit Would make him change his note, becoze His yed wur tucht a bit. Owclpizzy wur his fay'rite mon,
An' Glaastone's name wur like A taste o' colic reawnd his ribs,
An' nearly made nim skrike. He allus swore as Church an' State
Wur towt i' Holy writ, But then—as aw've remarkt befoor—
His yed wur t Licht a bit. Poor, dear owd Roger's deead neays, An', wheer he may be gone, If they shud want some Tory help, He's just the very mon ; An aw'm quite sure, he'll ne'er be damned
Becoze he'd little Wit; 'Twuz his misfortin, not his faut, His yed war tucht a bit !
TUII 0' PEGS.
Warriton, May 29th, 1891.
PRESENTATION TO A FOOTBALL PLAYER..

Last evening, at a well-attended meeting of the Committee of the IVarrington Football Club, an in- teresting•presentation was made to Mr. W. Hayes. The gift was a very handsome timepiece,which had been subscribed for by members of the club ; and in the absence of the President, Mr. W. Tinsley, the presentation was made by Councillor Pierpoint. lie referred in highly complimentary terms to the valu- able services rendered by Mr Hayes, who was a playing member of the first team for about six years, and up to two years ago. The recipient tendered his thanks in a suitable manner for the valuable present, which he said he should always especially prize as a token of the esteem of the members.

div.head: TOWNSMEN IN AMERICA.
div.p: TOWNSMEN IN AMERICA.

We learn that Mr. Joseph Ellison who left War- rington: some weeks ago for Boston has accepted a temporary engagement on the staff of the " Daily Telegraph" Worcester, U.S.. Mr. John S. Green, printer and stationer, who went out at the same time on a visit to the States,in a note to hand,dated May 7th, says :—" I. left Mr. Ellison in 130410 n a week ago, and came on here (Utica), to my cousin. Whilst here the weather has been just frightful— snow, hail, and rain, in May! I leave, however, in a day or so for Chicago, to see my old editor, Mr. H. H. Barker. Both Mr. Ellison and I are quite Mr. Barker was formerly editor and part proprietor of this journal. He is now in business in America, trading with a partner under the style of the Acme Publishing and Engraving Co.,' and will, we are quite sure, be glad to see Mr. Green who served, under him as reporter."

div.head: INFLUENZA.
div.p: THE INFLUENZA.

There can be little doubt that this malady is still very prevalent in Warrington; and in not a few cases serious results have followed. The sudden- ness of its attack is exemplified by a circumstance which occurred in connection with the Sunday- School anniversary services which were held in Cairo-st. Chapel, on Sunday. The Rev. F. K. Frees- ton had been announced to preach in the morning, and the Rev. J. J. Wright,Chowbent,in the evening. Both of these gentlemen were, however,seized with an attack of influenza, and neither was able to at- tend, and the Rev. Lloyd Jones, Liverpool, had to officiate. Dr. Adams had to give an entertainment at the Sankey bazaar, at the Conservative Club, on. Wednesday, but was prevented, we are informed.. by his having so many influenza patients to attend to. There has been an increase during the week in the rate of mortality, and four deaths have resulted from the malady.

div.head: WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

The annual meeting of the newly appointed re- presentatives on the Executive from the various wards, was held on Thursday evening, at the War- rington Liberal Club. There was a good attendance. In the absence of the Chairman (Councillor F. A. Roberts) Mr. John Walker was elected to preside. The meeting having power to elect thirty co-opta- tive members in addition to those appointed by the wards,this part of the business was proceeded with, with the result that the Committee was completed pretty much as before,sundry additions being made to take the places of persons who had died or re- moved from the town. Coun. F. A. Roberts was un- animously re-elected to the post of Chairman of the Executive; and the meeting then proceeded to the appointment of a sub-management committee,when the question was raised as to the desirability of al- tering the rules with a view to enlarging the com- mittee, and effecting some other improvements. It was finally resolved, on the motion of Councillor 11. Roberts, seconded by Councillor Flood, to defer the appointment of the sub-management commit- tee until the meeting of the General Council, which will take place in two or three weeks. k sub- committee was afterwards appointed and instructed to, in the meantime, revise the rules, with a view to presenting the results of their revision to thee General Council at its next meeting. The proceed- ings concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chair- man.
FATAL ACCIDENT AT CHEMICAL WORKS.

An inquest was held yesterday afternoon, by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at the Crown and Sceptre Inn, Buttermarkat-street, concerning the death of Patrick McLoughlin, aged 45, who lived at No. 4, Dolman's-lane, Warrington, and was employed as a labourer at Messrs. Winser and Co.'s Chemical Works.—Ann McLoughlin, the deceased's wife, said on the 28th of August she heard that he had had an accident at the works, and had been cOnveyed to the Infirmary. She went to see him there, and he told her he had slipped with a barrow of clay, which he was wheeling, and fell into the bin, and was a certain time before he was assisted out. —John Wood, of Cloth Hall-yard, deposed to witnessing the accident. The'deceased was wheeling a barrowful of China clay from the kilns to the bin, along the platform, when he fell among the material in the bins, which was sufficiently hot to burn him. It was red hot. Witness got him out, and ran for a cab to convey him to the Infirmary immediately. Nothing could have been done that witness knew to prevent such an accident.—Mr. Jackson, foreman at the works, who was present, said the platform was a good broad fone,and exactly as it had been for many years. and no previous accident had happened.—The Coroner pointed out that the Government Inspector had recently made his periodical visit to the works, and made no com- plaint as to the platform. The accident and the inquest had been notified to him.- The jury, after some private consideration, proceeded to the works to view the spot ; and on their return gave a verdict of accidental death, with a recommendation that 9. hand rail four feet high be put up along the plat- form.

THEFT OF BAGS.

Martin Mulhoyle, had to answer a charge at ths Eorough Police Court, on Monday of stealing some bags from the lock-up premises of Thomas Williams, marine Store dealer in Haydock-st. The prisoner was seen to get over the wall into the yard and then to come back ever the wall with a bag and something in it; and fpformation was given to the police who apprehended tim and discovered that he had sold the bags at Mr. 'Chorley's, marine store dealer's. He was sentenced to a sa2onth's hard labour. CHARGE OF STEALING MONEY FROM THE PERSON. At the Borough Police Court on Monday Elizabeth Ellen Fleming was charged with stealing, in Scotland-rd., an Sunday afternoon, 6s. from the person of Frederick Wood, navy, who did not apnear. Chief-Constable Hunt said Wood came to Warrington on Saturday and stayed at a respectable public-house, and on Sunday afternoon bad a strill when he met the prisoner, whom he had since charged of robbing him of 65., but that morning he bad paid for his lodgings and gone. The prisoner, who pleaded not guilty,was bound over to appear again when called upon.

THEFT OF CLOTHING. At the Borough Police Court on Monday,llarry Ander- son, Ship Canal labourer, et Latchford, and a native of tiouthampton, was charged with stealing on Saturday sight a man's jacket, value 7s. 6d., and five silk hand- kerchief!, value 7s. 6d., the property of Edgar Valentine Morton, broker, St. James's-st., Latchford. A woman named Mary Riley saw him take the articles from the door, and informed P.C. Robinson, who collared hint and found them upon him. The prisoner, who pleaded that be was drunk at the time and did not know what he vas doing, was sent to prison for a month's hard labour.
STEALING IgONET FROM A CHILD.

At the Borough Court on Thursday, Margaret Welsh, a woman, daughter of Michael Welsh, farm labourer, of irennell-st., was charged with stealing, on Saturday night, 10s. 441. from Jane Kirkham, a child. She had been sent by Mary Ann Cox, a daughter of Joseph Cox, lanyard labourer, Lennox-st., to a pawnshop to redeem a ring.and had the money wrapped in paper in her hand, and the prisoner was there pledging a silk handkerchief. There were a large number of people about the counter, and the prisoner told the child to give her her money and she would do her business for her. The little girl banded her the money, upon which the prisoner walked eut with it. Information was given to the police, and it was found that she had left the town on Monday, but she came back and gave herself up to Police Sergeant Sheeny, saying she wanted to "get it over." The pri- soner was fined 20s. including costs, in default 14 days' imprisonment.

STULING COAL Xt the Warrington Borough Court, on Wednesday, titer Ernmis, a young man, who lives in Haydock-strset, was charged with having stolen, on the previous day, lfcwt. of coal, valued at is. 11d., the property of his employer, Samuel Gough. It seemed that the defendant was employed by Mr. Gough,coal dealer,in Winwick-at., to deliver seal from a lurry. On Tuesday he was sent out with a specified quantity, which he had to deliver to certain customers, but from what Mr. Gough learned,de- fendant had sold *wt. to a Mrs. Stirrup, and received the is. 10. for it. This money he never attempted to deliver up to his employer. On being charged by P.C. Monaghan with the offence, defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. Gough said he had now another similar charge to make against the defendant. Emmis, be said, had for- merly been in his employ, but had been discharged. As be had joined the Salvation Army and appeared to re- form, he (Mr. Gough) had again taken him en. but cau- tioned him strongly against any dishonest practices. The Chairman said defendant would have to go to gaol for a month. At the same time the Bench were of opinion that the system of delivering coal loose on the lurry was not the best one. If the coal were in bags, there would not be the same temptation to do that sort of thing. Mr. Gough said the same thing could be, and was, practised, when coal was in bags. SHAMEFUL CONDUCT TO CHILDREN. At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, William Hodson, forge labourer, of Silver-st., was charged with being disorderly the previous night, by using indecent Language to Rose Rogers, aged 14, daughter of Mr. Rogers, landlord of the Blue Back beerhouse, Allen-st., Frances Hewitt, and Edith Smethurst, two other little girls residing in the neighbourhood of Bewsey-st. Chief Constable Hunt said the defendant had used expressions to the girls that were the same RS those used by him on an occasion some twelve months since as to which he had been charged at that Court.—Wm. Rogers, of the Blue Back beerhouse, said about 20 minutes to nine on the night in question he was coming homewards down Allen-st., when he saw the defendant speaking to his daughter and the two other little girls, and they ran away from him towards witness. They said the man had been using vulgar language to them, and was the same man who had been insulting to them twelve months since. Witness ran after him and overtook him near the Liberal Clubin Bewsey-st. It Aas all he could do to keep from using his stick to the man. Alderman Harrison: Have you ever been in India ?—The defend- ant : I was in Africa.—Alderman Harrison said the defendant ought to be ashamed of himself for prowling about the streets. and trying to corrupt poor innocent children, by using such filthy language.—The defendant said he was ashamed of himself, but after being a tee- totaller nine months he had broken out, and did not know what he was doingwhen drunk.—Alderman Harri- son said in the case of a is-ian like him, it was criminal to take drink. He was ordered to find two sureties of £2O each for his conducting himself properly for six months; in default six months imprisonment. —The defendant went to jail.
ANOTHER OBSTREPEROUS LONDONER.

At the Borough Police Court, on Thursday, before Alderman Sutton (chairman) and Mr. R. Garnett, Joseph Slade, a Londoner, who described himself as a cigar maker. was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Fennell-st, and with assaulting P.C. Bell, the previous nikiht. P.C. Bell said the defendant walked into the Police Office and asked to see the superintehdent, stet- in that he wanted a night's rest. Witness told him to .go to the Workhouse, and he replied, "No fear ; I en% not going there; I want to see the superintendent." Witness put him out into the street, and he commenced using threatening language, and struck himin the neck and got him by the throat. He was drunk. Witness and `Sergeant Taylor with great difficulty locked the prisoner up.—The prisoner said the witness told him he yas the inspector, and if he did not go out he would kick him out.—P.S. Taylor corroborated Bell's statement, aid said he was obliged to be a "little strict" with the prisoner •en account of his violence. He was more like a madman than anything else.—The prisoner said Bell had rup- tured him in the stomach by kicking him,and demanded a medical examination to show his injurieg.—Chief Con- stable Hunt deposed to witnessing through a window the prisoner's crnduct,and seeing him strike at Bell. The ran was so violent, that fearing he might" drop in for it" he came down. No more violence than neccessary was used. He might have got one or two blows.—The prisoner repeated his accusation against Bell, and the , Chairman said if he was kicked it was entirely his own fault.—The prisoner: It seems a concocted affair be- tween thenolice.—The Chairman : Ah, we will concoct another affair.—The Chief Constable said as to the mm ga night's lodgings, tickets for lodgings used to be given at the Police Station.—The prisoner: I was told to come here: that was the reason I came.— The pris.ner, who stated that he was on his way to Liverp,ol to look for work, was sent to prison for seven days' hard labour.

CRUELTY TO HORSES. Mr. Doughty, inspector to the Ii.S.P.C.A., brought up several persons at the Borough Police Court, yesterday, on charges of cruelty to horses. John Taylor, hawker, General-st., was the first. He had been working his horse while suffering from a lame hind leg and strained tendons. He had afterwards fired and blistered it on the advice of the Inspector. He was fined 10s. and costs, 16s. in all.—John Fairclough, farmer, Burtonwood, was the next defendant. His offence was on the 20th inst., he having been driving the horse with a trap, the animal suffering from strained tendous and an inflamed leg. He was mulcted in the costs, 6s.—Alfred Wilson, 43, Pinner's Brow, was similarly charged as to working a horse on the 23rd inst. The animal was in a poor con- dition, and had a sore under the saddle as large as a five shilling piece.—John Broadhurst, 53, Bewsey-it., the owner of a horse was charged with abetting the offence. Broadhurst conducted himself in court in a most vehe- ment and excited manner,in a stentorian voice denounc- ing the assertions of the Inspector and Detective-Ser- geant Monaghan, who corroborated him, as lies, until Alderman Harrison remarked that he thought it would be necessary to send him to the lunatic asylum.—The defendant: I have as good a name as any man. Never mind the lunatic asylum.—The defendant desired the Bench to allow Vas lad to bring the horse. Sergeant Monaghan said he wished it was brought. He never saw such a sight in his life. It was nothing but skin and bone.—Broadhurst was fined 10s. and costs and Wil- son,a boy, was ordered to pay the costs of the summons.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Mognar.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R.W. Francomb)

and Alderman Harrison. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. Ellen Terry, drunk and disorderly in Jockey-st., on Saturday night, was dis- missed on promising to go back to the Workhouse.— Charles Phillips was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly at the Central Station, on Saturday night, also with refusing to give up his ticket from Widnes to War- rington. From the evidence it appeared that he refused either to give up his ticket, pay his fare, or give his name and address; and used most abusive language. He had hia ticket upon him. The defendant said the porter used foul language to him, and he was so enraged that he would not give up the ticket. He was fined 20s. and costs, or a month's hard labour.—Patrick Moore, drunk and disorderly in Dallam-lane. on Saturday night, was fined 103, and casts, or 14 days' hard labour.—George Hopkins, drunk in Watkin-st., on Sunday morning, 10s. and costs.—John Rooney,-' for not appearing to a sum- mons for being drunk mail disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on the 18th of April, was fined 10s.—Albert Allcock, in Winwick-road, on the 19:h inst, who had been running after his mother with a knife, was fined 53.—Joseph Bad- dard, in Liverpcol-road, on the 19th inst, fined 7s. 6d.— Michael Ford, in Cockhedge-lano, on the 16th inst, ss. Michael Mahar, in Buttermarket-st., ss. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF HORSES.—George Donoghue for being drunk in charge of a horse and a lurry on the 23rd inst.. in Bridge-st., was fined 10s. FIGHTING.—WiIIiam Patten, for fighting in Napier-st., on the 19th inst. was bound over in his own recognis- ances of £5 to keep the peace for six months. FIGHTING.—John Powey, was charged with fighting in Buttermarket-st., on the 16th inst.—lt appeared that a man, a stranger to him' came up to him and butted him with his head, and the defendant had only acted in self- defence.—The Mayor remarked that he had done right. It was no man's duty to stand to be butted at by a wretched corner man. The case was dismissed. HAVING A DOG AT LAHOR UNMUZZLED.—James Addison, fustian cutter, 74, Battersby-lane, was mulcted in the costs 3s. 6d., for having a.dog at large unmuzzled on the 18th inst.
TUBSDAT.—Bofore Messrs. R. Garnett and E. J. Guest. _ __

THEFT FROM A MAEKET-STiT.L.—Edward Norman, all out-porter, living at Jolley's-yard, off Friar's-green, was charged with having stolen a cover from a stall in the market, value 75. 6d., the property of the Corporation. An officer stated that on the previous Friday night, he saw the defendant tear a part from one of the stall covers in the market, and afterwards attempt to walk away, but on seeing the officer he turned back and put the cover back on the stall. A fine of 103. including costs was imposed. ALLEGED ASSN:MT.—James Sauce was charged with not appearing to a summons, charging him with an as- sault on Mary Jane Dilly. The case was dismissed. DRUNIEBNNESS.—James Theis. Cavanagh, a Ship Canal navvy, drunk and disorderly at Market-gate, on Monday night, 55., including costs.—James Clarke, drunk and disorderly in Peter-st., on Monday night, dismissed. SLEEPING OUT.—Michael Duffy was charged with hav- ing been asleep that morning, in a closet in Gaskell's- yard, and was sent to gaol for seven days. Tim CANAL BOATS ACT.—Thomas Skelhorn, a canal boatman' was charged with having used a canal boat on the 11th May without the same being registered ; aid Richard Abel, of Runcorn, the owner, was charged with having allowed the same to be used. Mr. Percy Davies, of Warrington, defended, and Inspector Norman prose- cuted on behalf of the Warrington Corporation.—Mr. Davies contended that the boat was registered according to the Act of Parliament, it having been registered by Messrs. R. Fairclough and Son by whom it was sold to Mr. Abel about 18 months ago. This register was pro- duced. The case was dismissed.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—Ann Floyd,washerwoman Winwick-road, was find 2s. 6d. for neglecting to send her boy to schocl.—Henry Goodhead, soap boiler, Bank Quay, proved that his son was unmanageable, and the boy W 35 ordered to the training ship Clio.—Mary Hanlon, Tidy-st., was fined 2s. 6d. for neglecting to send her boy to school.—Samuel Johnson, forgeman, Stem ford-st., was fined 29. for neglecting to send his two children to school.—William Lloyd, forgema.n, Orford-lane, was fined ss. for the same offense; and William Mapp,ostler, Howley-lane 25. 6d. _ _

and Mr. J. Fairclousgh. DRSHRTERS.—John Boyer and Albert Robbins were charged with being deserters from the 2nd Cheshire regiment, stationed at Sheffield,and they were consigned to Strangeways gaol to await an escort. FBlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman),and _
Dr. Gornall.
DRUNK AND DrsormEn-L-Y-.:---G-e-r-aid Fitzgerald, a soldier, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., the previous night was handed over to the military authorities to be dealt with.
INDICCENT BBIZAVIOUR.—AIice Thomas, aged 19 for this offence in Buttermarket-st., the previous night, was fined ss. and costs.

WO3IBN'S 61-S-P-U—TES.—Mary Jane Airley, Blackhurst- st., was charged with assaulting Elizabeth Fallon on the 30th inst., and Julia her daughter, on the 21st. They were each bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace tor 6 months.—Margaret Kelly, a married woman, 102, Pierpoint-stiwas charged with damaging the windows of Hugh Brown on the 18th inst., and was fined the damage and costs, lls, in all.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TITIODAY.—Before Messrs. J. C. Parr (chairman), R. Pierpoiut, J. Marson, W. Long, and W. C. Jones. DIMNIC AND DISORDERLY.—Isaac llurst, and Isaac Lawton, big uncle, drunk and disorderly at Stockton Heath, were fined 2s. 6d. and costs each.--Frank Milling- ton. Dutcher, of Stretton, at Whitley, who had been fighting with a man named J,.iseph Mitchell, 2. 6d. and costs. Mitchell had been summoned on the like charge, but had absconded.

DRUNK IN CIIARGIR or A Hoass.—John Hampson of Cadishead, was charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and lurry at Moore, on the 11th inst.— The Con- stable who proved the case found him drunk and asleep ia the furry, and had to take charge of it and put it up, and afterwards escort him part of the way home. The defendant pleaded that he had had no sleep for a week through having to be up with his wife who was suffering from influenza. He was fined is. and costs.

BICYCLING AT NIGHT WITHOUT A LIGHT.—John William Jowett, wiredrawer. of Warrington, was charged with riding a bicycle at 11.50 p.m. on the 18th inst., without having his lamp lighted. A constable said the defend- ant was riding in Chester-road without having his lamp lit, and he called ont to him to stop him, and he did not do so, but rode actoss the road and fell under some rails. Witness put his hand up and caught him, or he would have been seriously hurt.—The defendant said the light was not quite out. He had re-lit it at Tom Paine's bridge, about 150 yards back.—The constable said the light was out, but the lamp was smoking. The defendant sounded no bell as he was turning.—Another constable said the lamp had been recently lit, but had no oil in. It was moonlight.—The Rev. T. W. Cook, assistant curate of Warrington Parish Church, said he was returring from a picnic in connection with that church and saw the de- fendant light his lamp on the road, and trim it at Tom Paine's bridge. He lighted it many times along the road, and borrowed oil from a companion.—The defendant said he had been laid up a week through his accident. He bad been to Chester with the picnic party. The Bench fined him the costs 4s. ed., the Chairman pointing out the extreme danger involved by cyclists coining quickly round corners, especially at night, without a light and Without sounding the bell. CRUELTY TO A Honsa.—John Brandwood, of Chorley- st., Warrington, was charged with cruelly treating a horse, on the 30th of April, in Chester-road, by working it in an unfit state, and James Wilkinson was charged I • with causing him to do so. They pleaded not guilty. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence. John Doughty, Inspector for the R.S.P.C.A., said the defendant was in charge of a mare attached to a spring float. The mare was very lame on the off hind leg, and was suffering from contraction of the tendons. He stopped him and pointed out the animal's condition and that he had twice stopped him before on the same account, and he replied that his master had sent him out.—By Mr. Browne: The horse was stopped by witness and Inspector Wilson some time before, and the defendant had beea summoned there on the Bth of May. There were two boxes of empty bottles in the float, which .would not be heavy.—One of the magistrates at Warnugton examined the horse and did not agree with the Veterinary Surgeon, and the other inagisti ate's opinion that it was not fit for work. The horse was now destroyed, but witness had only learnt that that morning.—Mr. Browno said at the Warrington Court another veterinary surgeon had pronounced the horse fit for work, and considering this, and that one of

div.head: EXAMINER, SAITRDAY, MAY 30, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAITRDAY, MAY 30, 1891.

the magistrates there had agreed with him, the defen- dants could not be considered guilty ot wilful cruelty. The defendants were fined 10s. and costs each. QUARREL BETWEEN TWO WOMEN.—Annie Atkinson, of Partington Common, was charged with assaulting Emmeline Taylor, at Little Leigh, on the 16th May, and Taylor by a cross summons with assaulting Atkinson, Mr. Browne appeared for the latter. Taylor said she was walking in Runcorn-road when Atkinson was coming along the road with a perambulator. She left it in the road, and came across to witness and struck her two or three times over the head and shoulder, without any provocation. She had been saying nothing about her. Mrs. Hewitt having given evidence,Mrs. Atkinson stated her case,alleging that she asked Mrs. Taylor for an explan- ation about something she had said about her. Mrs. 1 Taylor pushed her, and she pushed her in return. Mn. Elizabeth Beach corroborated this assertion, and the de- fendants were each bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months. SCHOOL CASES.—At the instance of Mr. De Prez, School Attendance officer, for neglecting to send children to school, R. Wilkinson, Great Budworth was fined 53. and costs, and in the caseof W. H. Owen,of Walton, who was charged in respect to a boy and a girl, the mother stated that they had both been ill, and that the girl had been crippled in the hand for life, and her shoulders were made black and blue by the schoolmistress, and the child was terrified of her. Mr. De Prez said the child had a lump on her hand, but the school teacher denied having ever flogged her. He also denied that the children had been kept at home through illness. The Chairman said the father had his remedy if the child had been so beaten. The defendant was lined 10s. and costs.—ln the case of Charles Delooze, charged with non-compliance with an attendance order as to his son,the Bench proposed to send the boy to an industrial school,but the mother expressed a preference for the ship Clio, to which she said the lad wanted to go, and an order was made for his despatch thereto.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY,—Before Mr. H. Reynolds and Mr. James Handley. MISCELLANEOUS.—For being drunk and disorderly Joseph Reynolds was fined ss. and costs.—Joseph Gibson was charged with being drunk and fighting in Halton- road, and he was bound over to keep the peace.— Frederick Cooper was ordered to pay ss. 6d. costs for permitting his dog to be at large without a collar.—Hy. Douglas, for allowing the chimney of his dwklling to be on firs was orclred to pay 4s. 6d. Smoot. CASES.—A number of parents were summoned by the School Board for not sending their children regularly to school and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in each case.

DEFECTIVE SEIVERING.—WiIIiaIII Statham, of Dukes Field, was summoned for allowine a nuisance to exist on premises owned by him, Nos. 19 to 41, Brackley-st., viz, defective stench traps in yards.--Mr. F. A. Lake prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Commissioners,and said the traps to take off the drainage water were defec- tive. They were made of brick ;to render them effective they should be of earthenware. There were two cases selected for prosecution out of a number of others in order to give a warning to others.—After hearing evid- ence, the Bench made an order for the nuisance to be remedied, the defendant to pay costs. A FILTHY LODOING-HOUSE.—James Kelly was sum- moned for committing a breach of the byelaws of the Runcorn Improvement Act relating to common lodging- houses.—Mr. Lake prosecuted, and said byelaw 11 pro- vided forth. removal of filth or refuse solid or liquid once at least in every day before the hour of ten in the fore- noon from every room in the lodging-house. Rule IT required that every window in every room in use as a sleeping apartment should be opened and kept fully open at least one hour in the forenoon and one hour in the afternoon of each day.—Mr. Percival, nuisance in.spec- tor.proved that these regulations were not observed by the defendant.—The defendant said he could not look after the house when he had to work for his living, and his wife was always drunk. One of the windows could not be opened.—The magis'zates imposed a fine of 10s. and costs, £l9s., or 14 days' imprisonment.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Col. Gaskell.

DRIINKENNESS.—For this offence, Thomas Greenwood, Mary Loughlin, Patrick McCabe, Patrick Mack, Thomas Houghton, and Mary McCabe were each fined ss. and costs. Bridget Oates and Michael Allen were each fined 10s. and costs; and Catherine Hynes, Wm. lieenaghar, and William Critchley were each fined 7s. 6d. and costs. WITHDRAWN.—Benjamin Thomson, of Widnes-rd ~was summoned for working a horse while in an unfit state.— The defendant promised that he would not work the animal again until it was quite well, and the case was withdrawn on payment of costs. _ _

NOT PRovEN.--.Thomas Callon was summoned for hav- ing on the 21st inst. been drunk on the liceused premises of Joseph Dixon, the Swan Inn, Waterloo-road.—P.S. Strickland and P.C. Evans gave evidence in support of the summons, but Mr. Swift who defended, called six witnesses who swore the defendant was perfectly sober. The case was dismissed.

UNCOMMERCIAL THAVELLER9.—Wm. White, of 'I horpe- st., William Williams, and George Williams, of Grenfell- st., ware summenen for obtaining drink from W. By- rom' of the Bold Arms, Bold, on Sunday, the 24th May. The defendants all pleaded guilty. It appeared that the house was under three miles away from some parts of Widnes,but was 3i miles from the Snig Pie House. The defendants represented they came from Snig-lane, and were served with beer. —A tine of 10s. and costs was im- posed upon each defendant. BREACH OF THE PEACH.—Thomas Allen, Pleasant-st., and Bartholomew Welsh, Fisher-st., were charged with committing a breach of the peace. Welsh was bound over; the case was withdrawn against Allen. Don AT LARGE.—Joseph Clare, Gerrard-st., was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, for allowing his dog at large un- muzzled.
STREET OBSTRUCTION.— John Hoey, Pear-st., James Johnston, Nelson-st., John Liston, Dock-st., and James Dicksoß, Nelson-st., were each fined is. and costs, for obstructing Mersey-st.

WARRINGTON v. LEYLAND.—PIayed at Warrington on Saturday, before about 2,000 spectators. Messrs. S. M. and J. J. Crosfield commenced punctually at two o'clock, but with the second ball S. M. was caught. Lee filled the vacancy. Runs came very slowly at first, though 50 were ultimately registered after an hour's play. Not- withstanding repeated changes of bowling, the second wicket did not fall until 98 had been scored, Crosfield's contribution being 45,made up of one 4, three 3's, six 2's, and singles. R. Smith joined Lee, and again the score rapidly rose, Lee, by means of a fine drive for four, caused the 100 to appear, and at the same time placed 50 to his credit. With the total at 129 Lee was smartly caught by Silcock for 69, which included six 4's, four 3's, nine 2's. and singles ; he was at the wicket an hour and fifty minutes, and had obtained his runs by really good cricket. Captain Manson soon placed nine to his credit, and was then bowled by Tonge. Clarke and Jolley each contributed a single. Voisey put on 10 in about four minutes before he was beaten by Tonge. With the total at 167 for seven wickets, the innings was closed, Smith taking out his bat for a well-played 27. The fielding of the visitors was a treat, especially that of Silcock. At a quarter to five the Leyland men began their innings. Kershaw was bowled by Jolley at 14. Rain was falling pretty fast at five o'clock, when the players took shelter. Tea minutes laterthey appeared again, but for only one over, when the match had to be abandoned. Full score :

The annual meeting of the members of this Club will be held at the Workmen's Club next Thursday evening. The balance sheet which will be submitted by the hon. treasurer will, we believe, compare favourably with previous balance sheets. No fewer than eight special resolution have been given notice of. Mr. D. Tinnion will propose, and Mr. H. Webster will second.—" That Rule 4 be altered to read" That the acting officers shall consist of a president, three captains, two sub-captains, honor- ary treasurer, and honorary secretary, who shall form part of the committee; such committee with the above exceptions, shall consist; of eight non- playing members and also two umpires, by virtue of their office. "A series of resolutions will deal with the annual subscriptions of various classes of members of the Club. It will be proposed "That the minimum annual subscription for honorary members joining the W. F. C., after this date shall be 15A., with an entrance fee of 55."; " That the annual subscription for ordinary mem- bers joining the W. F. C. after this date shall be 6s. with an entrance fee of ss. " ; and furti,er "That the annual subscription for playing members be reduced to 2s. 6d., with an entrance fee of 2s. 6d".

Alexander Kemp was on Wednesday sentenced at Edinburgh to seven years' penal servitude for shocking cruelty to his wife's illegitimate infant, which was found after death to have several of its bones broken.

ROYAL NAVAL EXIIIIIITION.—SCOTCH WHISIC.BY.— We were attracted and highly interested on our visit to this popular resort, by an unique exhibit in the form of a "Special Whiskey Bar," and noted with pleasure that the old-established house of Robertson, Sanderson and Co., Leith, are still to the fore with their well-known brands of this popular beverage. Of their Mountain Dew little need be said, unless that it is (if it were pos- sible) finer than ever, and it has stood the public test of half a century's use, they may therefore well and justly term it unrivalled. We were greatly struck, however, with the singular appropriateness in an Exhibition of this kind by another of their exhibits, "The Naval and Royal Marine Blend," with its exceptionally beautiful and artistic show card. This fine blend of Glenlivets is distinguished by an especially delicate and pleasant flavour, the result of a skilful blending of the finest and most matured products of Highland distilleries; it ' has all the delicacy and boquet, all the mellow- ness and softness, which are only to be had in the finest Highland Whiskey, and it is specially suited for medical purposes. Amongst others of their favourite blends is that called "Second to None" (which unques- tionably it is), all of which, we may add, can be pro- cured of the trade, from Land's End to John-o'-Groats. It must be a source of satisfaction and pardonable pride to Messrs. Robertson, Sanderson & Co., Leith, to know That the great, andever-Increasing, demand for their high-class Whiskies arises wholely and solely from their matchless quality, and not by the adventitious aid of competitive and interested exhibitions with their so- called presentation medals.

The great French road ride is now an evert of the past, and the result must lso,very satisfactory to• English cycledom, as all theEnglish:competitors were better than their opponents. The Frenchmen were complenly out- classed. G. P. Mills, .who that made so notable a name a few years ago in coneectionwith the Anfield Bicycle Club, was the first man in, having succeeded in covering the entire distance of 358 make in 26 hours, 35 minutes. He rode throughout in ,magni*ent form, and covered rale last ten kilometres (about miles) in 35 mints.

Thirty competitors -weremarshalled at the start by M. Thomas, of the Union Velocipetlique of France, an. the race began at 5.30 on Saturday morning, the five Nng- lish competitors being M. A. 111bein, G. P. Mills, St F. Edge. Twentyman,and Bates. Elllbein was a very strong favourite, and the French people- generally evinced the keenest possible interest -in the e-rent, which was quit a novelty across the Channel. The English competitors were generally recognised as the superiors of their Fremth opponents, of whom, however, it was hoped, Rousset, Coullebeuf, or Dellaval would occupy the fourth plasm. Several English riders of , slightly less ability than the competitors rendered most valuable aid in pace-making, Mills being especially favoured in this respect.

The following towns were included in the course Tours, Chateau Renault, Vendome Rambouillet, and Versailles. The roads were in many places very rough and in a bad state from recent rains, the going being very heavy. At Angouleme, Mills, Holbein,Twentyman,.. Edge, and Bates arrived together at 21 minutes past ten,. and although only 121 kildmetres (7.8 miles) had been covered, it was thus early seen that the race was -en- tirely in the hands of the ErigliSh ?competitors. MIA soon began to forge ahead, and at Poitiers was twenty minutes in advance of his fellow-competitors, the time being 3.48. He dismounted here and partook of a slight luncheon. Continuing his course, Tours was reached at 8.15, he being then 15 miles in front of his nearest op- ponent, and from this point he wenton and won easily. He rode no fewer than five pneumatics-on•the journey..

div.head: CR/CKICT..
div.p: CR/CKICT..

The first county match in which Lancashire has been engaged this season ended in defeat on Saturday,. by Surrey, but it will not be denied by any candid critic that there were extenuating • circumstances. On the second day Watson, who is suffering from a very severe strain, was unable to leave his bed, and Briggs became a victim to influenza, although the attack is not a serious one. In addition to these misfertunes, which were serious enough, Lancashire was further handi.; capped by a downright bad 'decision ,on the part of an umpire by which Barlow's innings was cut- short. The absence of Briggs and Watson ,was felt, also, quite as much in fielding as in bowling, for their respective sub- stitutes were by no means up' to county form as we understand it at Old Trafferd. Nevertheless, when all this is said, it is more than probable that Surrey would have won even if Lancashire had been abhi.to keep up its full strength,

The visitors showed some admirable batting 4 Loh-- mann's and Maurice Read's innings standing out con- spicuously; and on Saturday they bowled and fielded in a manner worthy of the highest praise.. Lancashire suffered a great loss when Sharpe left St. Helens for London, for he is certainly one of the best bowlers in the country. When the home Eleven went in for the second time on Saturday afternoon it was practically imposslble for them to get the -required, and the, only game to play, therefore, was the,•Scotton and Bar-- low type. Mr Hornby was , unlucky in obstructing his wicket, and Sugg, after playing the proper game for some time, allowed himself to fall into theArappwhich Mr. Read laid full "in sight of the bird," and' was very finely taken by that grand cricketer. If Sugg had bven content to stay "at home" 'the match mightliave been. saved, but he could not resist the temptation to hit. Albert Ward, of course. played the steady game—it is his nature; but unfortunately, he • could not keep his wicket intact, and may be said to have failed rather seriously in this match. Mr. Steel,, who has-probably not had much practice, was beaten all- the way by Sharpe, to whom Barlow and Ward also fell victims,

Mr. A. MacLaren batted very finely in both innings. Ho has learnt his cricket in one c,f-the best of schools, and some of his "Harrow drives" were a treat to see. He was not out in both innings. Mold was rather expen- sive, and Maurice Read and Lohmann scored heavily off him. Wood kept wicket splendidly, and themhole toam worked hard to secure the victory. The matchattraeted very large crowds on all three days.

A somewhat interesting match, or what might have. been an interesting match if it had not been for the rain, was played on the St. Helens Ground,,Dentons Green, on Saturday, the opponents being the past and present players of the St. Helens Club. The "'Moderns "'went to the wickets first, Roughley and Westhead facing the' bowling of Forster and Rayner. The players werodriven from the field by a heavy shower of'rain, and although play was resumed, after some time all interest in the game seemed to have evaporated.

Lord Sheffield states that he- has definitoly resolved upon taking a powerful team of cricketers to Australia next autumn. As far as the constitution of the team is concerned, Messrs. W. G, Grace, Briggs, Peel, Lohmann, aid Attewell are certainties, and further names will doubtless be published shortly. The inclusion of Attewell renders the famous quartette of bowlers complete, and with a strong complement of batsmen to support them, the team should be one that will take a lot ot, beating.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

THIIRSDAY.—Before his Honour Judge Floulkes. CLAIM FOR TENNIS RACKETS.—J. S. Garland, iron- monger, Bridge-st., Warrington, sued 11. Stuart,solicitor, Newton, for £11O& 6d., the value of tennis rackets,sup- plied to the defendant. Mr. Forshaw. (Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw) appeared for the defence. It ap- peared that on a Saturday in the summer of 1889, Mr. Clarke, milling engineer, of Newton,, was in Warrington, and having been requested by Mr. Stuart to bring him a pair of tennis rackets on approval,, he called at Mr. Garland's and got the rackets. Mr. Garland, in his evi- dence, said that he told Mr. Clarke that the rackets, if not approved, must boreturned the same day. They were, however, not returned for about ten days after, and Mr. Garland then refused to accept them, and hav- ing failed to obtain compensation, he brought the pre- sent action. For the defence, Mr. Clarke said he did not remember being told that the rackets were to be re- turned the same day if not approved, nor did he think any time was mentioned for their return..—His Honour held that the rackets had been detained an unreasonable time, and he gave a. verdict for the pinintiff for the full amount.

AN EXPENSIVE DOG. - Ann Cantrell, earthenware dealer, Sankey-st., Warrington, claimed from Peter Bradshaw, Legh-st., Warrington,. £1 is. which was the veterinary surgeon's fees for attendance on the plain- tiff's dog after having beon bitten by defendant's dog. Mr. Forshaw (Messrs. Percy Davies and Forsha w) appeared for the plaintiff. It was stated that on the evening of the 21st April, 1890; plaintiff's dog was attacked at the shop door' by the defendant's dog, which is a very large one, and severely bitten about the shoulder. The next day it had to, bd sent to Mr. Dixon, veterinary surgeon, who attended it till it was better. Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer, deposed that defendant's dog had on a previous occasion bitten a dog belonging to him. Defendant at that time paid the veterinary surgeon's fee of 2./ is. for attending the animal. There was practically no defence, and his Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed.

CLAIM AGAINST A FARMint—George Waywell, landlord of the Bull's Head Inn, Newton, claimed £6ss. 9d. from John Bridge, farmer Lawton, for /9 tons, 5 cwts, of manure supplied. Mr. IT. J. Longton appeared for the plaintiff. The defendant had paid £5 ss. 2d. into court but disputed the balance, saying that two loads charged for had not been received by him. The weights, it was stated, had been obtained from Mr. Mayhew, at the weighing machine at Messrs. B. Evans aid Company's siding,, and plaintiff booked the weights as he received them from defendant's carter. His Honour said that on the evidence he must give a verdict for the plaintiff for the amount claimed.

A DOMESTIC DISPUTE.—In this case in which John Hill wan the plaintiff, and Henry Horrocks, of Winwick, the defendant, plaintiff claimed from the defendant the whole of his household furnitureoe its value LSO. Mr. Forshaw appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. Dobson for the defendant. It was stated that plaintiff was married to defendant's daughter. Up to January of this year they lived together, but in that month plaintiff went teN work at Leigh and took lodgings there, sending mone•jc• for his wife's maintenance. On coming home to see hen- on the 14th March it was alleged the door was 610.0 against him. Be applied for his furniture to be returned. to him but that was refused, and his wife also declined to live with him. After the case had been partly heard,. his Honour saggested that an amicable arrangement might be come to, and the further hearing was conse- quently adjourned.

div.p: ST. ILA•RY'S, PENKETH SUNDAY SCHOOL
AND MISSION, --- BAZAAR AT THE WARRINGTON; CONSERVA- TIVE CLUB.

A three days' bazaar in aid of the extinction of the debt on the at. Mary's Sunday School and Mis- sion aC Penkethrwas opened in the Assembly Rbom of the Warrington: Conservative Club, on Wednes- day at noon. The committee of management were the Re' % B; S. Jackson, vicar of St. Mary's, Sankey (the chairman), the Rev. T. E. Winder lcurate) i the churchwardens and sidesmen of St. Mary's, end Messrs.. R. Beiirdman, J. Dignum, 1). Jeans,. C. H. Lewin,..ll Maintey, James Millingtcni. J. New- combe, NI H. Robinson, J. C. Routledge;tW. P.' Skel- ton, A. Ttorpe, Jt Forster (hon. secretary, and' Jt B. Aitken (treasurer). The followingl were the steward-:,--Dr. Adems, the Revs. F. C. Tit:aim, IV E. Wf,nder, and T.. Cook, and Messrs. F. 31. Appleton; E. Atkin, D..Buckton, R. Chorley, J. A. .Dan, JJ Edlesten, R. N. Foster, NV. Do Hfighes- W. D; Jeans, B. Jeans, H. S. Jonce,-.. A. H. Robinson,. B. 31gby, A. Thorpe,. H. Winder, .and Jt Wylde. The committee in the course of ttie printed programme make a statement' as to the establishment of St. Mary's schools.- Some twelve years ago;.according to this, it was ccnsi— tiered needful in consequence of the increasing 'population and the• distance between pat l of the township ofil'enketh, and the schools at Sankey, about two miles,.to provide Sunday School, faciti-i ties for the children of parents residing in, that part of the-parisht A room was rented an& a start made with some half dozen scholars. As thee num- ber- increased larger premises became necessary, and the COnservative Association kindly placed I their club room at the disposal of the management. A week eveningsereiCe in conjunction with tha,school was carried on in the club room for about eight years. Theraecommodation became so inadequate that immediate steps had to be taken to erect a, suitable building, to meet requirements, and an energetic Committee took the matter in hand. A site having been kindly presented by Mrs. Nall, Mrs. Taylor; and Miss Goodier, the new , building was-commeneed• in, October. 1888, and :completed and dedicated in Jnly,lBB9. The edifice was erected at a cost exceeding £1,400. A considerable debt remained on the structure and foL accounts •due•for work kindly permitted to be left outstanding: Hiance•the• neeeeeity_ for the bazaar.

The main feature-Of the bazaar was one whiduis a comparatively novel element in connection with such institutions. It consisted of the fashioning of, the stalls- so as to constituters reproduction of certaini antilive Warrington, buildings. The following are the, names of the stalls and the-ladies in charge :—Ye stalle at ye signe of ye• Daisie" or "Marguerite," Miss Tinsley aid Miss Mary Tinsley,, assisted by Mrs. Lewin, Mrs. RontlMgo; Misaißobinson, Miss Dutton, and Miss Fraser. Ye stale at ye-Signs of Ye Buttercup," Mrs. Skelton,assisted by Mrs, E. Caldwell,. Mrs. Hatton, Miss Skelton, Misses Warburton,. and Miss Williams. Ye booths for ye refreshment at ye sign of "ye Barley Mowee? 'Mistress Johnson, attended by ye followinv:— The Misses Johnson, Mrs. Jones, Miss Cook,. and Miss Jones. Ye stalls at ye signs of ye Mave,blossons;"' !Ars.. Houghton, Mrs. Aitken, and Mrs. Thorpe, assisted by Mrs. Murray, Mrs. H. P. C. -White, Miss Broadhurst, Miss Grange, Miss Holinger, Miss •Blanche lolinger, Miss Nita Riddel, Miss Woolfall., Ye stalle- at ye algae of ye Shamrock: Rev. E. S. Jackson, assisted by Mrs. Ridgway, Miss Ridgway, the Misses Litton,Mise- Jackson,,and Miss Nason. Ye stalle at ye, signe of ye Rose:: Miss Bolton, assisted by Mrs. J. R. Wylde,Miss A. Bolton, the Misses Miniati, the Misses Jeans, and the Misses Robertson. The Old Barley Mows stalkwasa,capi- tal representation of the ancient hostelry in-the Market Place,. and the west front of Bewsey Old Hail was.ze- produced with striking faithfulness by the -Shamrock and Rase stalls. The " Daisie" and " Buttercup" stalls- were constructed in imitation of the Market Place,. as- anciently existent, having been modelled froma picture of the spot. The old Fox Inn, still in existence in Butter- market-st.,kad its counterpart—or nearly so—for the-re- production was not perfect, in the" Mayeblossomi'stalli Behind the pia,tforin was a picture, copied fromamencii sketch, which represented old Church-st.' . with the- church as it was before the spire was added toit ;: and it wasa very artistic rendering, the painter being Mr: G. Widdie, of the Alexandra Theatre, Widnes. Thspresent- merit of so much that partook of the antique character, not merely in the stalls themselves,but also in thequaint costumes of those connected with various departments of the bazaar, gave the room an aspect of interest quite independently of the usual extraneous decorations, of which there ware but few.

The bazaar was opened on the first day: by Lady Greenall, on which occasion there- was a large. attend- ance. The Rev. E. S. Jackson presided, and an orches- tral band, under the conductorship of, Mr.. J. B. Caldwell, having played the National Anthem.. the Rev. Mr. Jackson delivered a short and somewhat- Immocous address. In the course of this-he remarked ;that Sankey formerly consisted of Great and Little Sankey, but the latter had become part and parcel of Warringtnn„ and he believed the spot he stood in was in Little Sankey or very near it. They had come from Great Sankey to Little Sankey with some nice things to show- them, and to appeal to them as old friends to admire and purchase them. The rev, gentleman mentioned that since he came to Sankey parish he had raised about azooo for church and school extensions ; and said, he- was now anxious to get £6OO more, to clear off, the mortgage that existed upon the church, and to pay certain ex- penses. Mr. Jackson concluded by handing to Lady Greenall a programme, and (tailing upon herto open the bazaar. Her ladyship then rose, and excusing herself on account of a very bad cold, from much, speaking, declared the bazaar open,, and expressed the hope that mare than the sum required would be obtained.—The Mayor (Alderman R. W. Francemb) then proposed a vote of thanks to Lady Greenall fq her kindness in coming to open the bazaar, comm@fiding her and Sir Gilbert Greenall for their readiness-to take always a foremost part in the promotion of any good work.—The Rev. F. W. Willis, rector of Warrington.. seconded, ob- serving that he had great pleasure insh,ing so because he was personally indebted to Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall for many acts of 'kindness. He also bestowed high praise upon Mr. ..Jackson and his-zuzate Mr. Winder for the indefatigable work they were doing among their parishicners.—A vote of thanks was. accorded with hearty acclamation. The Company then gathered about a May-pole, which had been erected in the centre of the room, to witness a series of dances round it by a number of children, to the music of the band. They were all arrayed in whit 4 and their dancing constituted a, picturesque scene,, and evoked much applause.

On Thursday the bazaar was opened at 2 p.m. by Mr. R. Davies. The. Rev. E. S. Jackson in a brief address invited that gentleman to perform the duty, and pre- sented him with the handbookc containing the pro- gramme. Mr::Thavies in his address said if there was one more than:another who advocated bazaars it was himself. The most beautiful things he had in his house had been bought in bazaars, and not the least beautiful amongst them were those which, he had acquired there yesterday. 41350 had already. been obtained by the bazaar, which he thought wasa, very good earnestof the success which would attendi the efforts of the pro- moters. lie never was in a. more beautiful lsaasar in his life. and his only regretwas that Mrs. Da'aies was prevented, by indisposition' from accompan7itt,g him there. He had heard its asked, what was; Sankey doing touome to Warrington,. Be believed many a good Sankey shilling came to, Warrington for la..w and other necessaries of life (lnughter)—and by the rule of reciprocity, it was quite natural to expect that the Sankey population should desire to have a,little in re- turn-o.nd that their desire was being rea..lsed the £350 wasa witness. He was, de*ghted to hear from Mr. Jackson the previous day what had been done in Sankey. Fie understood him to say that about £.7000 had been expended in the cause,ot education and religion there in a very few years. He-(Mr. Davies), felt anxious about the changes that wereconaing in our educational system., iilducatien dis soci4edfrom religion WAS a thing that, iwhether it suited the majority or nnt,vttniki not suit the !principles of Lancashire, at all events.. He hoped and 'trusted that the system of free education which we ;were promised would not interfere with religious edcua- titan. But it was, to, promote the cause of religion,not only among the young, but also antong the adultsithat Mr. Jackson hadi called them these upon that occasion. Be did not know another man he could congratulate with more pleasure than he did Mr. atekson on the promotion of these °bleats and the suucess of that excelleab bazaar. The Rev.. T. E. Winder proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Davies., Remarking on the re- presentations,of old Warrington he said they had brought back all ". the tender grace of a day that i&dead," and it was most pleasing to see these charming, reproduc- tions ot these houses of the olden times., Mr. J. B. Aitken seconded, and Mr. Jackson put,thehmotion,which was heartily carried ; and Mr. Davies thanked the meet- ing,

div.head: WIFE MURDER IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: WIFE MURDER IN SCOTLAND.

Orr Saturday morning, about three o'clock, Robert BK. of South Bridge-st., Airdrie, gays himself up to the police at Airdrie, and said he had murdered his wife.'• Inspector Jackson, the officer on duty, after questioning* :him,. locked him up, and proechled ta the house, where hs found Mrs. Bell lying on the bed irher night clothes. Subsequent investigation showed that the woman had ' been killed by a blow on the head from a poker. Bells. who has shown signs of mental aberrrution, has been re— mitted to the Sheriff. He and his wife lived on happy terms. Their three children, two boys and a girl—aged .fourteen, eleven, and seven years, respectively—were-as- - leep in bed when the woman was mundered.
THE CHARGE AGAINST MR. CHARLES ALLAN FYFFE.

At Croydon Police Court, on Tuesday, the hearing of,: the charge against Mr. Charles Allan Fyffe. M.A., •was,. - resumed before the local magistrates. The charge against. the prisoner, who is the Liberal candidate for Devizes, . was originally one of having indecently assaulted a young-: railway goods clerk named Richrannd, in a railway car-- riage, between Horsham and Cr....s.ydon five weeks ago. The case was then adjourned for a week, at theend orpf which time prisoner failed to appear, his salicitor stating:: that he was suffering from a large incised wound in the. throat. On Tuesday morning the prisoner was,brougbt. into court on a stretcher. A consultation resulted in a modification of the charge to an alleged offence under' the Criminal Law Amendment Act, so as to permit thee prisoner to give evidence. According to the. medical.l evidence, the prisoner was suffering from hallucinations. Several eminent gentlemen spoke to the prisoner's war,- blemished character. The defence was reserved. The' prisoner was formally committed for an indecent assault; bail being laid at £9OO.
