01-1 ARGE OF SUNDAY. TRADING AGAINST A WARRINGTON BUTCHER.

At the Warrington Borough ,Police Court, on , Monday, before the Mayor and Alderman Harrison, Prank Connolly, butcher, 48, Pinner's-brow, was charged with.earrying on business on Sunday, the 17th mat, this not being a work of necessity, or Charity. Janellall, a married woman, and Jane Lucas, a little girl, were charged with aiding and abetting the offence.— Mr. A. Browne appeated for the defence.—M. Jones deposed that about ton o'clock on Sunday morning, the 17th inst, be saw siX or seven people come in and ont a the defon- (lanes shop. He went near the shop and stayed a few minutes, and aaw three or four more persons Coming in, and then out with something." lapped' ruP in paper, including the defendants Ball and The assistant weighed a piece .of meat, value 25., and gave it:to the little girl, and. Hall got .1 piece value 38. sd.—By Mr. Browne: lie ad been 'spoken to by no other:butcher in the neighbourhood About taking proceedings. Mrs. Hall told lirn Os Iliad paid for the meat on Saturday, and let it at ,theshop until Sunday moaning because she had no place avlo me to keep it in ;and that she had done the like for 2/1„,,13g while. Mr. Connotly told him he had had,a bad '"ft-Saturday,and he had aysantity of meataleft. There were other shops open at the time. A young man stated It‘l,lEkt what the officer said was quite true.—lnsipeetor said he had cautioned the defendant two years ago :gunday trading when he loept a shop in Lythgoes- rne--,,-Mr. Browne said his client had been under the 'alpressiha that the police had beau prompted in the I Matter bya rival butcher. Witnesses could be called to Prove that all the butchers' shops in the neighbourhood Were open, though Mr. Connolly had been singled out from among them. The proceedings were taken under a statute of Charles 2nd which ought to be obsolete. It Was one of those statutes for conviction under which Inagistrates were ridiculed all over the country. To con- .lll 'via a man under this ancient Act of Parliament for Su- n" day trading was simply keeping up a bigoted system Which ought not to exist cow-a-days. Mr. Browne tl_unted a Latin maxim, with its translation,which was to the effect that necessity made that legal which otherwise Was not legal, and pointed out that his client was e com- tlied to get quit of the meat on Sunday as he had a rge quantity on hand, through his bad sale on the pre- 'Pious day, and if he did not it would not keep, and he could be liable to prosecution for having bad meat on his premises. The AO, under which the proceedings Were brought was one the carrying out of which was universally, ridiculed exeept by the most bigoted people. It ought to be abrogated; and no doubt it Would be within the next few months because it only continued until the 31St of December next. Mrs. Hall had been in the habit for 18 months of paying for her Meat on Saturday and leaving it at the butcher's, ,?ecause her pantry was over ron with beetles; and had moues° in this case. The meat was weighed merely to Ulake sure that it was the piece she had left. The little 1:1;r1 had also paid for her piece on Saturday.—Alderman _arrison said so far as he was individually concerned he nuld not convict in a case like that. When he consi- uaered that anyone could go into an hotel or public-house 8,1? cl latly a cigar, drink, and other things that might pos- -21313' be done without, on Sunday, it did appear to him that the law under which a man could be punished Or 4., 1' selling one of the ordinary necessaries of life on that t'a_3" ought to be obsolete. As far as he was cwicerned "11°..should most decidedly dismiss the case. He did sintuitiosaingy that the police were not perfectly justified what they had done; it was perfectly legal, but the law ought to be abolished, and he hoped it 7_o:id not be long before they saw it swept away ir ir In the statute book.—Mr. Browne said Pinner's was a neighbourhood where a lot of people ded, employed by publicans and others who did get their wages till after eleven o'clock on urday night.—The Chief Constable said that he ;Tote!arcug,lit the case before the Bench as a mat- icnr r duty, though he respected Mr. Connolly very much -1' more reasons than one, but the police had to take Who the ,n 1 they could catch. There were some butchers in B‘, town who were in the habit of getting an additional 2.4_131)115' of meat on Sunday to sell on that day; and that 1;11g1 t not to be.—Alderman Harrison: No, it should Mr. Hunt said he did not think there were many 17,0 got their wages late on Saturday night. They must ityLhave these complaints about this Sunday trading as thawtaAs going on now, from persons who had respect for "EtY• Two butchers had complained to him, and 11;‘, if others opened on :Sunday they would ' • hence, if els sort of thing were allowed, they would be having the shops open on that day.—Alderman Harrison said " Would only be a few that would be. There were many ruple who had too much respect for themselves to do business on a Sunday.—The Mayor thought there was no tter°ug case against the defendants. A little girl whocould sent to choose meat and have it weighed must be very Precocious. He did not think any other butcher would ,so mean as to instigate the police : they had probably acted on instructions. Cases that seemed very tri- tal to the magistrates were of very great weight with Hunt, because he got information that they did not. .9ere were, it seemed,butchers who actually replenished %heir stock on Sunday, in order to carry on Sunday trad- ! g. That would be very bad, and the defendant would sAoatvdsh to do that.—The defendant: No.—Alderman rri so n : if butchers all kept open on Sunday, people Would not trouble to purchase till then,and the butchers would have to work seven days instead of six.—The cases were dismissed.

REDUCTION OF BOURS OF LABOUR.

Sir,—Under the above heading we noticed in your ....sue of Saturday last a paragraph to the effect that w had unsolicited" reduced our working hours from 56 to 54 per week, the wages remaining unaltered, and also expressing the satisfaction of our men at our unasked for generosity. As the fact set forth in this way has a very misleading effect upon all persons outside the trade, 'we shall be glad if you will kindly allow us space to explain the matter, and thus remove the wrong impres- sion produced. We are afraid that we have not the smallest title to the gratitudp of our employes in this instance, for, although it is quite true .that our men did not themselves prefer the request,yet the United Kingdom Society of Operative Coachmakers did so for them, by a circular,addressed to the Master Coach Builders' Defence Association, and it was decided, after several meetings of the latter body, to grant the request of the men in this instance rather than disturb the very friendly rela- tions existing for the past eleven years. You will therc- *fore see, that what we have done in granting the reduc- tion, is simply following the lead of the other Members of our trade throughout' the country, and adhering to a general trade arrangement which was in operation in the larger towns especially, some time before it was in- augurated here, and we must admit that had it not been for the existence of such an arrangement, the reduction would never have been granted by us. Apologising for encroaching upon your valuable space with a purely personal matter,—We remain, sir, yours faithfully, MASKERY & CO. Coach Works, Warrington, May 29th, 1891.
MAGISTRATES AND POLICE COURT FINES. Sir,—Referring to an article on Stipendiary Magistrates in your issue of the 23rd instant. I would call attention to one or two matters which are not correct.

The article states that "Mr. Matthews had been under the necessity of communicating to the Warrington Magis- trates on the irregular practice of .inflicting costs where the fine was ss. only or something less than that sum." It is not an "irregular practice" to inflict costs where the fine is ss. or under. The Summary Jurisdiction Act 1879 (42 and 43 Viet. c. 49) section 8, enacts" Where a fine adjudged by a conviction by a court of summary jurisdiction to be paid does not exceed five shillings,then, except so far as the court may think fit to expressly order otherwise, an order shall not be made for payment by the defendant to the informant of any costs ; and the court shall, except so far as they think fit to expressly order otherwise, direct all fees payable or paid by the informant to be remitted or repaid to him; the court may also order the fine or any part thereof to be paid to the informant in or towards the payment of his costs." The Circular received from the Home Secretary was sent to all Benches of Magistrates throughout the coun- try, and was merely a recommendation not to ordercosts -where the costs would exceed the fine and the fine is ss. or under, but rather to fine a fixed sum including costs, in order that defendants may know at once what amount they are required to pay.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, .
GEO. F. F. WHITE, Deputy Clerk. Borough Magistrates' Clerk's Office, _Warringto n, May 28th, 1891.

[We are obliged to Mr. White for his explanation of the Home Secretary's communication, but should have been further obliged if he had given the letter in full and let it speak for itself. If the practice was not

4‘ irregular," it was regarded by the Home Secretary as either unjust, er unadvisable, or he would not have been under the necessity of instructing the " great unpaid" as to the proper execution of their duties. As Alderman Sutton frankly stated on the bench, the Warrington Court is "more in the habit than other courts in other places of imposing fines and costs " ; and it follows that there is pressing need to act on the Home Secretary's advice. If the practice has not been
"irregular," it has in certain cases been scrnething worse : it has been unjust.—En. Ex.]

div.head: A. STIPENDIARY MAGISTP ATE FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: A. STIPENDIARY MAGISTP ATE FOR WARRINGTON.

Sir,—Some months since in the course of some critic- isms on magisterial procedure in Warrington I hinted • that I should probably have something to say at some future time in advocacy of the appointment of a stipen- diary magistrate for the borough. I am pleased to see that you have anticipated me by advocating,in an article in yeur last impression, this very desirable reform. As your readers are aware, I have had occasion to point out what! consider a piece of flagrant illegality. on the part of the Warrington magistrates in the sentencing of the boy Dunbobbin to be birched, which indeed has -since been denounced by the " School Board Chronicle," ' as such; but that is merely one instance of the curious irregularities, not to say illegalities, to which our local Bench have been addicted. I think any impartial per- son reading the records in the " Examiner " of the decisions in the Warrington Police Court,and comparing one decision with another, must be struck with the comparative absence of all principle of uniformity mani- fested in many of them. There seems frequently to be no discriminating analysis of the merits of cases ; but a rough-and-ready system of peremptory dealing with prisoners on inadequately supported and even unsworn testimony prevails to considerable extent. Only a month or two since I read an account of a poor man being brought up at the Warrington Police Court, on a charge of attempting to commit suicide, and it ap-

peered that the case was disposed of without one iota of sworn testimony ; even the evidence of the medical man as to the prisoner's condition of mind not being given, according to the legally prescribed usage, on oath. In oases in which a defendant pleads guilty,all evidence,be- yond the Chief Constable's explanatory and unsworn statement, is often dispensed with; the good old princi- ple of English jurisprudence that no man shall be con- victed of any offence without a fair and exhaustive trial, being in these instances entirely lost sight of. To remedy these and other abuses I could name it has become an imperative necessity that the Warrington Bench should have some competent guiding head in the shape of a presiding stipendiary to give coherence and consist- ency to their administration, and to establish in our police court a system of jurisprudence deserving of the name.—Yours truly,
MANLIUS

A FLINT GLASS MANUFACTURERS' UNION Sir,—We are living in times of great unrest and anxiety in all branches of the manufacturing community, both at home and abroad. Trade Unionism has taken a firm hold on the industrial classes, and is continually developing new phases, and new combinations for the double purpose of reducing the hours of labour, and ad- vancing the rates of wages. On the other hand, capital- ists and employers are combining on all sides to resist the exorbitant demands of the workmen, and hope by such action to secure an adequate return on their investments, and be in a better position to do battle with foreign competitors. There is one industry in this country, howev.w, in which the manufacturers engaged seem to be strangely lacking in cohesion and effort in the midst of the fierce struggle that is now going on around them. I refer to the English Flint Glass Trade. Tho present aspects and prospects of that trade, when compared with the pros- perity of twenty years ago, are very discouraging, and assuredly point to a final collapse in the near future,unless sound and energetic measures are immediately adopted to avert such a catastrophe. I have good reasons to be- lieve that the turnover of the various works is now less by 40 per cent, than it was at the period named, and, unfortunately, the tendency is still downwards. This deplorable state of things is clearly traceable to several causes. The first, and undoubtedly most important of these, is the solid and unyielding combination of the operatives. As a Union they are indeed practically masters of the trade,. inasmuch as they regulate . and control to a large extent the conditions of service, and the wages to be paid to the various grades of workmen. Strong financially, and determined to maintain their ground at all costs, the operative glassmakers render it absolutely impossible for English makers to compete successfully with the products of continental workmen who live so comfortably and contentedly on a very much lower scale of wages than rules in this country. Then the manufacturers themselves are not without considerable blame in the matter. Tney are not com- bined in any way, and, therefore, cannot effectuallf resist the growing and unreasonable demands of their men. Every firm appears to work exclusively for its own hand without any regard whatever for the general interest. The prices of their manufactures are not based upon any common and recognised standard, glid terms and discounts are regulated by a loose kind of sliding scale dictated by customers and not by the requirements of business. And then there is the foreign competition which we hear so much about. German and other con- tinental makers are flooding the country with such low- priced goods that in many instances the English manufacturer must either sell at a loss, or be driven out of the mark,t altogether. With such facts as these before us we need not be sur- prised at the present unhealthy and precarious condition of the English flint glass trade. But surely something might be done to recover lost ground, and restore a valuable and highly artistic industry to the place it once held, and sbould still maintain, in the commercial world. In the quality and colour of their metal, and in variety and beauty of design, our English manufac- turers have very few equals, and certainly no superiors; and if they would only work harmoniously together for their common interests a change for the better would soon be apparent. Let them, then, put away the petty jealousy that now prevails, and unitedly demand from the Glassmakers' Union an entire and complete re- vision of working prices, and an increase in the number of articles made per move as may be required. Having accomplished this, their next step would be to agree upon and issue a fixed scale of prices to their customers, both home and foreign, and arrange and settle a uniform , discount to all purchasers whether large or small. Then the losses that are now entailed by empties and carriage might be obviated by making a reasonable charge for the former, which should not be returnable in any case, and requiring consignees to pay the cost of conveyance of all goods sent to them whether by rail or sea. I believe that such an arrangement as I have shadowed forth would, if loyally adherred to, greatly improve the position of the manufacturers, as it would enable them so to recast their quctations and terms as to secure a monopoly of the higher classes of goods, and at the same time match them more evenly with the foreign makers of inferior ware. In canclusion, I wculd remark that . my only motive in writine, is a sincere desire to see the Flint Glass Trade of England in a state worthy of its ; ancient prestige, and I trust that both the manufacturers and workmen interested will receive and consider these remarks and suggestions in the same friendly spirit.— Yours faithfully, BETA.

Mr. C. W. Tibbits, deputy coroner for West Cheshire, held an inquest at Ellesmere Port, on Tuesday, upon the body of a boy named David Henry Grewcock. aged 14 years. From the evidence of an engine driver named George Morgan, it appeared that the boy was employed as a fireman on his engine, and that whilst riding on the step of his engine cn Friday last, he was knocked off by a piece of projecting rock and run over. He was immc • diately conveyed to the Ship Gana' Hospital, and every attention paid to him, but he died the following day.— The Deputy Coroner, in summing up. said he thought a boy of deceased's age ought not to have been employed as a fireman, and the jury requested him to communi- cate with the company, and inform them that they were of the same opinion.—Verdict," Accidental death." EXTRAORDINARY ENCOUNTER AT ST. HELENS.
A NEWSPAPER MANAGER THRASHED BY A
TOWN COUNCILLOR.

Literary and professional circles in St. Helens were on Tuesday startled by a rumour that Mr. Led Dromgoole, manager and the son of the pro- prietor of the "St. Helens Newspaper and Adver- tiser," had been severely thrashed by Mr. Joseph Massey, a well known solicitor and town council- lor, representing South Eccleston Ward. The report proved to be founded on fact, and the unfortunate incident formed a leading topic of conversation in the business and commercial circles of the town. The affair appears to have arisen out of some comments which appeared in the "St. Helens Newspaper" regarding the starting last week of the engines at the New Kirkby Waterworks,belonging to the Corpora- tion. The comments were headed "Sad Effects of Kirk- by Water," and two of the paragraphs read as follows: The inner man, although refreshed, still sought re- pose on the homeward journey. Rest and " Scotch, please,' was found at Schows Mawdling Hall, where, to rouse the drowsy, the little Collier's Warbler sang an in- spiriting ditty of many verses, while others, overcome with sentiment and Knowsley air, sank, like Cromwell, under the table,searching for—the Lord ? No, the cork- screw. After many passing scenes, the Blackbird was reached—and from Raven caws, or some other cause, or Mr. Santa Claus—one of the victims to the rush of many waters, or mixing thereof, was, as the shades of evening were closing o'er 'em, bundled into a cab, sans chapeau, sans half a Coat, and sans &c., sent home a present, in a pretty plight, to his wife." On Wednesday a tternoon a press representative waited upon Councillor Massey at his office. Mr. Massey stated that it was perfectly true that he had thrashed Mr. Fred Dromgoole, and he considered there was plenty of justification for it. He (Mr. Massey) was consulted by Councillor Walsh in regard to the paragraphs which had appeared in the "Newspapers," and, what seemed to be the most satisfactory course, sent across for Mr. Dromgoole. On Mr. Dromgoole's arrival some conversa- tion took place in regard to the matter, and Mr. Massey pointed out to Mr. Dromgoole that the paragraphs were certainly of a scurrilous and untrue nature, and asked for their withdrawal. He (Mr. Massey) cared little about them so far as he was personally concerned ; but in regard to Councillor Walsh, who moved in religious circles, they were extremely cruel, unjust, and untrue. Mr. Dromgoole declined to withdraw the comments, and Mr. Massey informed him that if they appeared in the Friday's issue of the paper he should strongly resent their insertion. It was not journalism to be prying into private affairs—it was an abuse of Journalism. Mr. Massey then stated to the reporter that Mr. Dromgoole became abusive, and there was no doubt about it he struck Mr. Dromgoole several times. He opened the door and said to him " Get out," and Mr. Dromgoole went. Mr. Massey added that Councillor Walsh asked for a correction or a withdrawal of the ob- noxious paragraphs, but Mr. Dromgoole refused to com- ply with the request. According to Mr. Dromgoole's version of the encoun- ter he was struck about the head, had a tooth knocked out,and was kicked. More of course will be heard of this summary way of settling accounts.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. The persons who read the proceedings of the Southport Evangelical Conference, as reported in Wednesday's daily newspapers, would be startled and deeply grieved at the announnement of the Ven. Archdeacon Clarke that Mr. W. Whittaker, of Runcorn, was dead. I have made inquiries and am glad to be able to state that Mr. Whittaker is alive land well,and I shall only be echoing the sentiments of all luncornians in wishing many more years may be added to his long and useful life. The Archdeacon had fallen into an error. It appears that over a week ago Mr. Whittaker's eldest brother, whilst driving to Manchester, was thrown from his trap, and subsequently died from the injuries he received by alighting on the kerbstone. A sad event truly! He had attained about 76 years of age. The vacant clerkship of Prescot Union is causing quite a commotion in the district. The local appli- cants are likely to be very* numerous, and the Guardians will have a difficult task to decide upon the rival claims of the aspirants for the office. I believe Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner for South-West Lancashire,and Mr. C. H. Lewin,deputy magistrates' clerk are two Widnes solicitors who seek the position, which is a valuable one. Mr. 11. G. Linaker, of Frodsham, who served an apprentice- ship to the work in the Runcorn Union, is also among the applicants. Mr. W. Tyrer, registrar, of St. Helens County Court, acted with too much haste in resigning the honourable position of the Board in order that he might become an applicant for the Clerkship. The Guardians, in their wisdom, have decided that the clerk must devote the whole of his time to the several offices he will hold, and must hold no other public position. This will have the effect of debar- ring Mr. Tyrer from competing,as he will certainly not be prepared to forego his private practice and the lucrative appointment of Registrar. Perhaps the members will again reinstate him as their president. The meeting of ratepayers held at the Town Hall, on Monday evening, spent two hours and a half in I.lunching the Runcorn Cottage Hospital on to %%That all concerned hope will be a successful career. Previous attempts to establish such an institution have miserably failed, and there were fears that the present effort was doomed to a similar fate. Mr. Imison moved the adoption of the scheme of the sub-committee, at the same time inviting full and open criticism with a readiness to accept any altera- tion which might be considered to the benefit of the cause. He gave a warning note as to the rock upon which the institution might be wrecked, and strongly urged the Committee to avoid anything that would give the scheme an appearance of sec- tarian domination. Mr. I mison's calm and temper- ate language had its due effect, and the details of the scheme were discussed in the most friendly spirit, and with a single eye to the success of the movement. The greatest danger that had to be escaped was the arousing of religious jealousies, which, unfor- tunately, are apt to be raised at the slighest and ' most trivial cause; and Mr. Lake is to be compli- mented on the courage he displayed iii. proposing that ministers of religion should be excluded from the committee of management. He concealed not his thoughts in vague language,but boldly declared that they could not get clerics to work together in harmony,and that they were a source of discord in such affairs. This view was endorsed by a majority of the meeting, and ministers of religion are excluded from taking part in the management of the Hospital. They will, of course, be allowed to exercise their priestly craft amongst the patients of the Hospital, and their recommendations of per- sons whom they consider require treatment at the Hospital will always meet with the utmost con- sideration, The great fact is that laymen are to have the managemer t of the institution. Those who were against this course will doubtless by this time have come to the conclusion that it was the wisest to pursue, in face of the grave dan- ger that threatened the carrying out of the scheme. As was pointed out, it was impossible to put all the ministers on the committee ; to leave any off would have been at once taken as a slight, and jealousies and division Would have been the result. Now they are all on a level, and they can assist the Hos- pital quite aq much off the committee as they could have done on, and, being aware of the exact posi- tion of affairs in the town, I have not the least doubt they will willingly acquiesce in the decision of the meeting, and act as missionaries of the Hos- pital, and the Good Samaritan to those in need of the surgeon's knowledge and skill. This was the chief alteration in the scheme. The principle of one man one vote was not accepted, but the maximum number of votes was reduced from 20 to 10. The committee appointed to obtain sub- acriptions, and to take the preliminary -steps for establishing the Hospital, will commend themselves to the town at large. They are men of business capacity, and energy,and occupy public positions of trust, and for the present the project may be left in their hands with every confidence, and the prospect of a succesSful. re-Port from them at no distant date. I understand that Messrs. Gamble, chemical ] manufacturers of St. Helens, the only firm that did not join the chemical syndicate, have this week be- come a part of the United Alkali Company. William Pearson, joiners' labourer, employed on the extension works at Stockport Station, was cro-sing the metals at half-past nine OR Thursday morning, when he was knocked down by a train entering the station, and ) killed on the spot, being dreadfully mutilated.

Those who have seen the short cutting or "neck," near Tom Paine's bridge, which is in the future to form the entrance to the Warrington docks, will have noticed a deep excavation or groove going down each face Of the cutting, and along the bot- tom. That groove is to be fitted with the pipe line conveying the waters of the Old Quay Canal to the works of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steel, at Runcorn. That pipe line and syphon are immediately in front of the place where the dock gates will be placed at the entrance to the Warrington docks. To mary people it will be a bit of a surprise to hear of "lock gates" at the entrance to Warring- ton docks, as the general impression is that there will be an uninterrupted communication between the canal and the docks. The object of putting lock gates is simply to improve the dock accommodation. As is well known, the stretch of canal between Eastham and Latchford is partly tidal, and as a consequence of this the spring tides will raise the water in that stretch of canal some- thing between two and four feet. Were there an open " cut" between the canal and the docks, the water in the docks would, of course, rise to a cor- responding height with the water in the canal at every spring tide. Although many docks are open to the tides, it can easily be seen that there are some rather strong objections to such docks. In mooring vessels, for example,allowance will have to be made for the rise and fall of the waters, and it is easy to imagine that, under certain circumstances, a vessel may strain her moorings. The Ship Canal Company, we believe, wish to make the docks at Warrington as complete and perfect as any other part of the canal, hence their decision to protect them byiocks. No matter what fluctuations there may be in the adjoining lower reach of the canal, the water in the level of the docks will be uniform. An interesting portion of the vast and costly apparatus to be used on the Ship Canal is that of the swing bridges. The swing bridge to span the canal near Moore is now well-nigh complete, and a massive piece of workmanship. Its weight.in fact., is estimated at between 700 and 800 tons. To move this ponderous mass hydraulic motive power will be used, the bridge being operated upon from a little pit to be noticed in the masonry close to the swivelling part of the bridge. The requisite power will be derived from a water tower which will pro- bably be erected at Moore: That tower will also probably provide the power to move the swing bridge to be built near Tom Paine's bridge, and the lock gates which are, as we have.just explained, to

LORD HARRIS.

Lord Harris was born at St. Anne's, Trinidad, West Indies, on the 3rd February, 1851, and is chiefly known to fame as a first-class cricketer, though at he present time he bolds the ‘stinguished political ap- intment of Governor of fllbay. Dr. Grace, in his ,ok on "Cricket," says Lord Tris "has proved hinlself to a distinguished cricketer .nd a distinguished politician; ,n upright, true-hearted Eng- 'jab gentleman, and the best

ne has had the game more at heart, or done Inure for it ; and every cricketer in England felt it had lost one of its greatest 'supporters when, in taking farewell of the County. Cricket Council, at Lords, in December, 1889, he said, My cricket book is closed, but it contains nothing but the pleasantest of recollections.' Eton, Oxford, and Kent have had reason to be proud of him ; his county in particular; for he displayed good form as a batsman and field, and bowled occasionally with success, during the many years he represented it. There are few better judges of what consti- tutes a first-class cricketer, and as Captain of an eleven no one can spot the weakness or strength of an opponent better. He has a very free, correct style of batting; keeps up his wicket with great patience when the bowling is good, and hits freely when it is loose. Repeatedly he has scored over 100 in an innings for his county, and he played in the Gentlemen's Eleven for many years. In his younger days he was a most brilliant out-field, covering a large amount of ground, picking up tke ball quickly and neatly, and returning it smartly and accurately to the wicket; but in later years he has fielded in closer, chiefly at short-slip, and is just as successful in that positioh. No safer pair of hands can be desired, and no more willing worker ever played in an eleven. He bowls round-arm medium-pace." The offices which Lord Harris has held under Conservative administrations are that of under-Secretary for India,lBBs-6, and in Lord Salis- bury's second Government that of under-Secretary for War.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
The monthly meeting of this Council will be held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday eveniug next, when the following among other busimiss will be dealt with.

div.head: ELECTION OF ALDERMAN,
div.p: ELECTION OF ALDERMAN,
Almost the first matter on the agenda paper is the election of an alderman to fill the place of Mr. Joseph Davies who lately resigned.
INSANITARY DWELLINGS.

The Sanitary Committee will propose that proceedings be taken under the Rousing of the Working Classes Act, 1890, for the closing of a large number of houses in Rose Yard, Dial-st., Dial Court, Pilling's Court, Webster's Yard, Green's Court, Vernon's Yard, Aikin-st., and Back Aikin-st. All these houses have been reported by the medical officer of health to be unfit for human habi- tation.

div.head: CHANGES OF COMMITTEES.
div.p: CHANGES OF COMMITTEES.

The Paving andr-S-eWer-a-g;-C-O;;;ItiTe have passed re- solutions appointing Alderman Wright to be chairman, and Counciller Heaton to be deputy-chairman of the Committee,and also Councillor J. Fairclough a member of the Committee. Councillor Heaton is also appointed deputy-chairman of the Cemetery Committee and Coun- cillor Greening is appointed a member of this Commit- tee, as well as of the School Attendance Committee. Councillor James Fairclough is appointed a member of the Markets Committee, and Councillor Flood of the Fire Engine Committee.

div.head: BUYING HORSES.
div.p: BUYING HORSES.

The Sanitary Committee propose to purchase a horse from Mr. Thos. Bennett for the sum of £6B; and two from Mr. W. Tickle, of Keck wick, at the price of £159, subject to the veterinary surgeon giving satisfactory certificates of soundness.

div.head: TECHNICAL EDUCATION
div.p: TECHNICAL EDUCATION

The Museum, Library, and Arts Committee have passed a resolution to the effect that the Technical In- struction sub-committee be requested to report on the arrangements necessary for opening classes in the autumn ; and also that the name of the Committee be the Museum, Library, and Technical Instruction Com- mittee.

div.head: NEW BATHS
div.p: THE NEW BATHS

The Town Hall. Park, and. Baths -dommiteee have re- solved that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to obtain estimates of the cost of constructing Turkish baths in connection with the proposed extension of the public baths.
THE DOCKS.

The General Purposes Committee have passed the following resolution r—" That inasmuch as the Man- chester Ship Canal Company state in their letter to the Town Clerk of the sth May, that the docks at Warrington will be completed before the end of December, 1893, the Corporation will not press for the insertion in the Bill now before Parliament of the clause submitted to the Company."

div.head: WALKING DAY ARRANGEMENTS. _
div.p: WALKING DAY ARRANGEMENTS. _

The same Committee have also resolved as follows : "That on the Dccasion of the public procession of Sun- day scholars on Friday, the 26th June, 1891, no cart, carriage, lurrv, cr other vehicle (except mail carts), and no horse be allowed to remain in or travel along any of the following streets between the hours of 9 a.m. and 12.30 p.m., viz.:—Bridge-kreet, Bewsey-street, Horse- market-street, Sankey-street, Bold-street, Buttermarket- street, and Irlam-street."

div.head: SWEEPING PROPOSAL.
div.p: A SWEEPING PROPOSAL.
Councillor Dmos has given notice of his intention to move "that the members of the Sanitary Committee be required forthwith to resign."
A STIPENDIARY MAGISTRATE.

Councillor HENRY ROBERTS will move the following resolution of which he has given•notice :—" That the Parliamentary Sub-Committee be requested to consider and report upon the advisability or otherwise of a Stipen- diary Magistrate being appointed for the borough to act either for the borough alone or in conjunction with one or more of the adjacent towns.

div.head: STATE OF THE POLICE COURT.
div.p: THE STATE OF THE POLICE COURT.

Councillor BROWSE will move that it be an instruction to the Watch Committee to take into consideration the present state of the Borough Police Court, and to take immediate action for its improvement.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

THE ARLEY TROOP.—The Arley troop, belonging to the Earl of Chester's Yeomanry Cavalry, arrived at Lymm on Tuesday afternoon, and left by train for Chester. THR VOLUNTEERII.—The H (Lymm) Company of Volunteers returned to Lymm on Saturday evening. They were the only company in the battalion who were fully equipped in the camp, and further, they mustered in greater.numbers each day throughout the week than any other company. THE INFLUENZA.--It is said that influenza is very pre- valent in Lymm,dozens of the inhabitants being afflicted with it. Among the latest sufferers from it is Acting- Sergeant Griffit4s, who was seized with a very severe attack on Sunday. Several deaths from influenza have occurred during the past week. RECOVERY OF Nories.—On Thursday notes lost by Mr. John Forster, farmer, Rush-green, Lymm, between the Lancashire and Yorkshire Bank and Statham, were re- turned to Sergeant Wynne, at the Lymm Police Station, by Mr. Thomas Collyer, a master fustian cutter, of Stat- ham. The whole of the cash and the three £lO notes were intact, and the finder received the reward of £5.

CONFIRMATION AT OUGHTRINGTON.—OR Wednesday morning, at 11.30, a confirmation service took place in St. Peter's Church, Oughtrington, in which 30 girls and 19 boys of the parishes of St. Mary's, Lymm, St. Peter's, ' Oughtrington, and St. Werburg's. Warburton were con- firmed by the Lord Bishop of Chester. His lurdship gave two short addresses to the candidates. Owinz to indisposition, the Rev. W. G. Knocker, rector, was un- able to be present.

TEAM PRIZES AT THE BIND OF HOPE FESTIVAL.—The following is a list of team prizes awarded at this festival :—For the best turnout of two horses and lurry at the coronation of the Bands of Hope Queen last Thursday: Ist prize, Mr. Dutton, Heaney ; 2nd, Mr. E. Massey, Cherry-lane; 3rd, Mr. S. Heathcote, Reddish; very highly 'commended, Mr. John Marsh, Bradley Hall; highly commended, Mr. Thomas Marsh, Cherry-lane; commended, Mr. Peter Massey, Cherry-lane. For one horse and lurry : Ist prize, Mrs. Cheetham, Heatley ; commended, Mr. Joseph Ball, Statham. The judges were Hr. Richard Clarke. jun., Warburton Park, and Mr. Fred Shakeshaft, Crouchley Farm, Lyrnm. ROBBERY FROM THE SHIP CANAL.—On Monday, at the Altrincham Petty Sessions, two men, named William Raymond and James Dunn, were charged with stealing 61bs. of copper rivets, the property of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, frem the Thelwall section, on tbe 18th May.—Mr. Brandon, from the office of Meosrs. Grundy, Kershaw, and Co., appeared to prosecute.—The rivets were placed on the 16th May, by Joseph Hill, a saddler, in a hut at Thelwall. On Monday, • the 18th, Sergeant Monaghan, of the Warrington Borough Police, saw the prisoners in Church-st., Warrington. The bag of rivets was being carried by Raymond. His suspicions were aroused, and he,took the men to the Police Station, where Raymond admitted that he took the rivets from Morrisbrook. When in custody at the Lymm Police Station, the wives of the men saw them in the presence of Sergeant Wynne. Raymond told his wife that he did take the rivets, and he supposed he would have to suffor for it. Dunn told his wife that he did not steal the rivets, but that he went with Raymond to Warrington to try to sell them .—Raymond was fined al.s. and costs,and Dunn 10s. and costs. .
MR. GLADSTONE. Mr. Gladstone was yesterday afternoon able to go for a drive.
CRICKET.
Marylebone beat Oxford by nine wickets. Cambridge beat Yorkshire by four wickets.
THE CANADIAN PREMIER.
It is expected that Sir John Macdonald, the Canadian Premier, will shortly visit England to recruit his health.
THE QUEEN'S VISIT TO PORTSMOUTH.
The Queen will visit Portsmouth on July 22nd and will be present at a grand review of troops on Southsea Common.
THE CITY OF LONDON.
Yesterday the City of London Liberal Association de- cided to contest the vacant city seat, and a Committee was appointed to interview candidates.

ALLEGED MISAPPROPRIATION OF £5,700. At Hull, yesterday, Joseph Dauber, solicitor, was com- mitted for trial for misappropriating money amounting to £5,700, entrusted to him by clients, for investments.

div.head: DEATH OF LORD CLANCARTY.
div.p: DEATH OF LORD CLANCARTY.
The Earl of Clancarty died in Lot don yesterday. Ire is succeeded by his son, Viscount Dunlo, who married Miss Belle Beltin, the music hall singer.
LOSS OF A NORWEGIAN VESSEL.

Yesterday, Alexander Ellison, the sole survivor of the crew of the Norwegian barque Helga, of Tonsberg, arrived at Shields, and reported the loss of his vessel off Newfoundland, with Captain Shouldstadt and ten of his crew.

div.head: COACH OVERTURNED.
div.p: A COACH OVERTURNED.

Colonel Furnival was driving a coach along Bucking- ham Palace-road yesterday, towards Epsom, when a policeman tried to stop the leader, .and the coach was overturned, the occupants being bruised and cut by the broken glass. APPLICATION TO COMMIT AN EDITOR. _ _ _ _

Yesterday Mr. Justice Sterling heard an application to commit the editor of the s• Star" newspaper for con- tempt, by reason of an article adverse to the New As- bestos Company, which appeared while an action was pending against the company. The case was disposed qf by defendant apologizing and paying the costs of the application. - CAPTAIN VERNEY IN PRISON.

The " Dublin Express" London correspondent says: A County Middlesex juror who visited Holloway Prison on Thursday, informs me that he encountered Captain Verney. He was in the exercise yard. He was not quite dressed like the other prisoners ;he hae been supplied with a large overcoat. It appears he does not do any work, so that he must be regarded as a first-ciass misde- meanant.

div.head: LIVERPOOL TR AGEDY.
div.p: THE LIVERPOOL TR AGEDY.

John Conway, who is charged with the murder of the boy Martin, at Liverpool, has been identified by two tradesmen, who allege that he purchased a bucket and some eoda. Yesterday prisoner was brought before the magistrates and remanded, pending. the inquest.

div.head: INQUEST AND VERDIOT.
div.p: THE INQUEST AND VERDIOT.

The inquest was resumed at Liverpool yesterday on the body of the by Nicholas Martin.—Detective Colling- wood deposed to arresting the prisoner, who was in bed at his lodgings. Prisoner admitted having purchased the bag and blankets, but said he did so at the request of a foreign sailor, whom he met in the street, and who was an old man with grey whiskers, and either German or Norwegian. When afterwards charged with the murder, prisoner exclaimed, "My God! lam not guilty." Dr. Paul, who made the post-mortem, said the wound in the neck caused death, and the legs were severed some time after death. The body bore no signs of having been out- raged other than described. There was blood on the pri- soner's coat, and also on a razor, and on the scrubbing brush and rags produced. The body had not been many hours in the water.
The Coroner summed up, and the jury returned a vet- diet of "Wilful murder against Conway.
NORTH BUCKS ELECTION.--LIBERAL VICTORY.

The polling fQr the election of a Parliamentary repre- sentative for North Bucks, in the place of Captain Ver- ney, expelled the House, took place on Thursday. The candidates are Mr. H. Leon, Gladstonian Liberal, and the Hon. Evelyn Hubbard, Conservative. The result was declared yesterday as follows : Mr. H. Leon (G L) Hon. Evelyn Hubbard (C)
Majority 3Bl

After the declaration of the poll both candidates ad- dressed a larle crowd, and Mr. Leon and Mr. Hubbard respectively proposed and seconded a vote of thanks to the returning officers. Mr. Leon said the victory would give encouragement to the Liberal party and cheer the heart of the Grand Old Man. Mr. Hubbard said he had not one word to say against his opponent, but complained that statements were made behind his back which no one dare make to his face.
At the general election of 1886 the figures were : Hon. Egerton Hubbard (C) Capt. Edmund Hope Verney (G L)
Majority 7l In October, 1889, the seat was contested with the following result : Capt. E. H. Verney (G L) Hon. Evelyn Hubbard (C)
Majority 2OB The population of the division is 56,928, and the regis- tered electors number 11,407.
YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HCUSE OF LORDS, The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four.

- Tam FISIIERIES—DIFFICULTY.—In reply to Lord Norton, the Marquis of Salisbury fully explained the position in which H.M. Government stood with regard to the New_ foundland Fisheries Bill. He did not complain of the resolution passed by the House of Commons, but having regard our to treaty obligations he regretted some of the language used by the authoritative persons in the debate.
The House adjourned at five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The Speaker took the chair at five-minutes past two o'clock.

THE DISPUTE IN AFRICA.—Sir J. GORST, ii reply to Mr Eslemont, said a report had been received by Sir John Willoughby respecting the attack and stoppage at Beira of his expedition, and it was being considered. The vessels and lighters seized by the Portuguese have been released. "The Countess of Carnarvon " had also been released, on the understanding that the owners should abide by the decision arrived at by the two Governments on the subject.

THE SEAL QUESTION.—The First Lord of the Treasury brought in a Bill to enable Her Majesty, by order in council, to make special provision for prohibiting the catching of seals in Behring Sea by Her Majesty's sub- jects during the period named in the order.

- THE BUDGET AND FREE EDUCATION.—The House then went into committee on the Budget Bill.—Mr. H. H. FOWLER, in order to give the Government an opportunity to explain their intention regarding the Free Education Bill, moved to report progress.—Mr. GOSCHEN said he was prepared to put off the third reading of the Budget Bill until such time as the House had seen the Education Bill. The GovernmeNt would endeavour to secure that there would be plenty of time for its consideration, but he thought they should have- some assurnace that the pro- ceedings on the Land Purchase Bill should not be inter-. rupted.—Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN said that the Chairman, of the Executive had met the Opposition in the most handsome manner, but he could not give an assurance. such as the Chairman of the Executive had asked.—Mir. CAMPBELL BANNERMAN gave the Government a qualified assurance that no prolonged debate would take place. on the first reading of the Free Education Bill.—Mr. H. U. Fowler gave a similar assurance.—Mr. W. H. SMITH asked the Rouse to refrain from discussing the measure on its introduction. He undertook that no delay would occur in introducing the Bill.—Progress was reported at ten minutes to four.
PUBLIC Accourcrs.--Mr. JAMESON moved the second reading of the Public Accounts and Charges. Bill. The bill was read a second time.

SUPPIX.—The House went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service estimates. On the vote to complete the sum for their survey of the United Kingdom, Mr. Ron c complained of the dilatory and unsatisfactory way in which the work was done.,Mr. CaarLAIN did not think any department could be more admirably conducted than the Ordnance Survey with the means at their disposal. The one-inch scale map of England would not be com- pleted until 1895, but that ot Scotland would be cum.-

pleted in 1893, and"that of Ireland in Mt Ultimatefi the vote was agreed to, as were votes for the Caledonian Canal rates on Government property, and other rate. SALARIES IN THE LORDS.—OrI the vote for the salar- ies of officers of the House of Lords, Mr. Mosrox moved to reduce the vote, as he considered they wore doing less work than officers of the Commons. Dr. Tan tier thought if they went carefully through s the list of salaries of officials of the House of Lords and docked every other one, they would still leave sufficient officers to do the work, and save large sums to the taxpayers of the country. The reduction of the vote was negatived without a division. Dr. Clark urged an amendment of fees of the House of Lords as regarded Private Bill business. Mr. Jackson promised to look into the matter. The vote was under consideration when the Chairman left the chair, and the sitting wa suspended.
A COUNT OUT. The speaker resumed the chair at nine o'clock. The House was counted,and there being only 32 members pres- sent, the House adjourned at five minutes past nine.

div.head: LOCAL SWIMMER.
div.p: A LOCAL SWIMMER.

The "Liverpool Edo," on Saturday evening, gave a portrait and the following sketch of the career of 1 Mr. G. Barlow, the teacher of swimming at the War- rington Baths :—"Mr. Barlow is a Warringtonian by birth,and was born on the 26th April,lB6B. His first appearance as a swimmer was at New Brighton in 1882, and afterwards he swam at Liverpool, ton, and other towns. He was successful in every race be swam in for twelve months and as a result he is now always severely handicapped. This War- ringtonian is the only swimmer in England that has beaten Joey Nuttall three times. He defeated him at the Isle of Man by 4 yards in a 100 yard's-scratch race, again at Pendleton by about 6 yards in a 200 yards scratch race, and another time at Rochdale. In all he has swum with Nuttall about eight or nine times, always starting level; and to beat the champiom in three of these races is indeed a, con- veted honour. He has contested in about ai hun- dred races and has won about fifty prizes? Mr. Barlow, we may add, complains much of the severe handicapping, and says that it is this which has prevented him and other Warrington swimmers from entering for many races of late. His defeat of Nuttall at Pendleton was on the occasion of the new baths there, and this was the first time he ha been I defeated, in a competition in a swimming bath. In 1885 Barlow swam at Ashton-under-Lyne for the 500 yards championship of Lancashire. There were four competitors, including H. 11. Britain, who had won the championship of the Mersey the same year, and had twice swum the 500 yards championship race for Lancashirc. Barlow told Britain on the night of the competition at Ashton that he (Bar- low) was sure to beat him,when Britain replied that he would not be one of the first three. But the result proved that Barlow had not exaggerated his powers. Britain gave in at the seventh length, eight lengths short of the accomplishment of his task, Barlow winning by the length of the bath. 20yards. The race in which he defeated Nuttall at Rochdale, it may be mentioned, was for the cham- pionship of Great Britain. Barlow has saved about fifteen persons from drowning at the Warrington Baths, including two policemen, he expresses great satisfaction at the proposal of the Corpora- tion to provide new baths and his readiness to do all he can to make them available for the promotion of the art of swimming. Mr. Barlow is, in addition to being a swimmer, a runner and a football player, and may be pronounced a good all round athlete.

MANCHESMER HAY AND STRAW, FRIDAY.—Hay, 4d to 4d; clover, 4d to 6d : straw wheat, 2id to 3d; ditto. oat, 2fd to 3id per stone of 141 b. GLASGOW METAL, FRIDAY.— Market strong. Small busi- ness done at 58s 6d and 58s 10id cash. Closing: Buyers 58s 6d cash; sellers 58s 7td cash. Middlesborough warrants.— Closing buyers 41s 9d cash ; and 41s 100 one month ; sellers lid more. Hematite warrants.—Business done at 53s 2d cash.. Closing: Buyers 53s lid cash and 53s 31 one month; sellers 11d more. MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY. The market is not everything to be desired, and the greater portion of what trade is being done goes to easy sellers. The estimate of the day's transactions is only 7,000 bales. Yarns are slow. Some good spinnings of twist are wanted,in small parcels for quick delivery, but the general demand is sluggish and nobody wants large quantities. Cloth is not in a satisfactory posi- tion. Some inquiry is found for both Indian ana China fabrics, but business only goes to accommodating sellers. In printers and finishing goods a quiet trade goes through, but prices are not always steady, and unfavourable weather is checking the home trade demand. LONDON PRODUCE, FRIDAY. Sugar: Pieces in fair de- mand: dry goods and crystals in moderate request cane slow; beet—May 13s 31d. and sellers 13s ; June buyers 13s Old, and sellers 13s tlid - and October-December buyers 12s 4id, and sellers 12s sid. Ditto kegs: Fine •-s ; mild, —s. In the market: 908 firkins, 2 kegs, and 255 mild. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDAY. The Beef market ex- periences a dull feeling, being, if anything, a shade easier to buy. Pork has a quiet demand with previous currencies repeated. In Bacon, the demand for both home and export is still of a very restricted character, and the tendency is still against holders. Hams and Shoulders rule quiet, with previous values unchanged. Old Cheese meets with an improved inquiry, and is steady for choice parcels; new is dull at declining prices. Butter closes dull and easier. Lard is again lower, the Market clos- ing with a quiet tone. Imports of salted provisions :—Beef, 150 tierces; Pork. 63 barrels; Bacon, 849 boxes; Hams, 616 boxes; Cheese, 567 boxes; and Lard. 70 tons.

div.head: SOIIOOI, AFFAIRS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SOIIOOI, AFFAIRS AT WARRINGTON.

The School Attendance Commitlee of the War- rfrgton Corporation have just issued_ their report for the year ended Mist October, 18*. The Com- mittee state that in IMO the average attendance of children at the public Elementary schoc4s was 7,304. This year it is 7,484, showing an increase of 90. There were on the school registers at the cliose of the year, 9,599 children, but this number included 1,00 children under school age. The figures with which the Committee have, therefore, to deal are 8,505, and the average attendance of this number was 7,484, or nearly 88 per cent. The number of children attend- ing private and other schools, including the Blue Coat and Grammar Schools, is 540. Most of the chil- dren from the Workhouse Schools are in attendance at the schools at Padgate. Adding the 549 children in attendance at the private schools to the number on the school rails within the borough, the total number of chircfren attending school was 10,146: The number of children presented for examination in 1890 was 9,601, being an increase of 1,50 over the num. her presented in 1889. The increase is. somewhat re- markable, the explanation being that white in 1889 only those children were examined who had been on the school register 22 weeks, in 1890 every child in atten— dance had to be examined. The number of prosecutions during the year were 401, against 310 the year previous,. showing an increase of 91. The inspector, in his report to the committee,states that "It would be impossible to dathis work without resorting to magisterial aid, and r am very careful that no case is submitted to the magis- tretes until I am compelled by the wilful obstinacy of the parents to take that course." During the year eight boys were committed to the ship "Clio," one was discharged from the ship by order of the Home Secretary,. and one was ascharged through ill-health. Two boys were sent to St. Anne's Industrial School, Liverpool. The total number at present detained on the " Clio " is 31, and at St. Anne's Industrial School 10. Certificates were granted to 20 children, entitling them to be taken into half-time employment, and the total number of half-timers in the town is 98. The entire cost of the working of the department of the Committee for the year has been £355 13s. 11d., from which sum there should be- deducted the amount actually received for fines, zati. 17s. ; but including the sum paid by the Board of Guardians, for school fees, the total amount is under id. in the Zoo the rates. With regard to school accom- modation„ the Committee would again repeat the desira- bility of better accommodation being provided in the outlying parts of the Borough. In other respects-the accommodation is sufficient for the usual percentage-of school-going. children.

Wright,.and Shearer (clerk pro tent.) It was re-- ported that the balance in the treasurer's hands amounted t0..E83175. 4d., and that a pupil teachers' grant of .C4,had been received from the Education Department. The head master reported that the , average number on the books for the last four weeks Was 250, and the average attendance 202. WARRINGYON DISTRICtr HOMING SOCIETY. The end.of the season so far as old birds is con- cerne&was reached on Wednesday, when 46 birds ware liberated from Bournemouth at 7 a.m. The , first bird to arrive was one belonging to Mr. Locker, of Church-a. /t put in an appearance shortly after noon, completing the distance-1884. miles in five boars. This is an exceptionally fine performance,. more especially so when the dull • weather is taken into consideration. The second bird to arrive at 12.27 belonged to Mr. Forster, of Liverpool-road ;:and Mr. Locker was again promin- ent with third position. The majority of the birds arrived back the same day. As you are aware, the new Archbishop of York was an army officer before he joined the Church. He tells the following story bearing upon that curi- ous metamorphosis. He was born on the 18th of June, 1826, which date in that year happened to fall on a Sunday. "He's born on an anniversary of Waterloo Day," said to his father a confidential servant who had been an old soldier. "You must make a soldier of him." The family nurse on the other hand contended that as the young gentleman was born on a Sunday he ought to be a minister. Strange to say, both suggestions were realised. Dr. Alaclagan first served in India, and after his return home took holy orders.
